Stadium Gate Plaza.description: The way into the stadium from the campus road: a broad paved plaza at the foot of the bowl's curved outer wall, with a bus turnaround and a covered campus bus stop on one side, a row of tall glass doors and steel turnstiles under the U.A. crest, and a separate competitors' entrance down a ramp to the tunnels under the stands. Campus buses from the Campus Bus Terminal drop classes here, and the fifteen-minute walk along the campus road from the main building ends here too. The doors open only for a class or session booked through the Faculty Office, and a staff member with a tablet checks names at the turnstiles. On festival days the plaza fills: extra buses unload crowds brought up from Musutafu Station, ticket holders queue through the turnstiles past hired pro heroes on security, broadcast vans park nose to tail along the curb, and the smell of the stalls drifts out through the doors. Out of season the plaza is wide, swept and nearly silent, the turnstiles chained, the bus shelter's bench the only place to wait. Through the turnstiles lies the Concourse; the ramp leads down to the Competitor Waiting Rooms.

Arena Floor.description: The oval field at the bottom of the bowl, ringed by a running track and walled off from the lowest seats by a padded barrier taller than a person, with a wide tunnel gate at one end where competitors come out from the Competitor Waiting Rooms. On festival days Cementoss raises a square concrete stage in the middle for the tournament, and leaving its bounds loses the match; Nemuri Kayama referees from beside it, and the roar from the Spectator Stands comes down from every side at once. The rest of the year classes use the track and field for P.E., fitness tests and drills, booked through the Faculty Office, and festival rehearsals mark the turf with chalk lines and cones. Groundskeepers roll the turf early on Monday mornings. When the stands are empty, a single runner's footsteps echo around the whole bowl, and the giant screens at either end stay dark unless a technician is testing them.

Spectator Stands.description: Steep tiers of seats rising from the field to the rim, with giant screens at both ends and reserved sections near the front where pro heroes sit to scout, notebooks and phones out. Festival days fill them with tens of thousands of families, fans and agency staff, and the noise is a solid wall when a match ends. The lowest rows look straight down onto the Arena Floor, a staff stair climbs to the Broadcast Booth, and tunnels lead back to the Concourse Food Stalls. The rest of the year they are empty except for cleaning crews, camera riggers and the odd student eating lunch in the top rows, which nobody minds as long as the wrappers leave with them. From the rim the whole field is visible at once, including which pros take notes on whom. The wind across the top rows never stops, and on clear days Mount Fuji shows above the far rim.

Competitor Waiting Rooms.description: A corridor of small rooms under the stands, each with a bench, a table, a water cooler, a wall monitor showing the arena and a numbered card on the door. On festival days competitors wait here alone or in pairs until staff call them a few minutes before their turn, then walk the tunnel out to the Arena Floor; Recovery Girl's treatment room is at the end of the same corridor, and the injured come back past every door. Competitors are not supposed to visit each other's rooms, and it happens anyway: a friend with a pep talk, a rival with a warning. The rest of the year the rooms serve as changing rooms for classes using the field, with lockers that stick. Through the concrete, the crowd overhead is a constant muffled roar, and a big cheer rattles the ceiling lights.

Broadcast Booth.description: A glass-fronted box high in the stands with a commentary desk, microphones, a mixing board and banks of monitors, shared with the national broadcaster's crew and reached by a staff stair from the Spectator Stands. Present Mic calls the first-year festival events from here, and he likes to drag a reluctant colleague in beside him as co-commentator, Shota Aizawa (Eraser Head) most of all. On the day a director, a replay operator and two camera coordinators fill the back row, and the desk has a cough button nobody remembers to use. Out of season, technicians test feeds and cameras a few days a week, and the booth stays locked otherwise; its key is signed out from the Faculty Office. Behind the soundproof glass the stadium goes silent, and the only sound is the hum of the equipment and the warm smell of electronics.

Concourse Food Stalls.description: The wide ring corridor behind the stands and the plaza outside the gates, lined with shuttered stall frames, vending machines and restrooms, with ramps up into the Spectator Stands every few dozen meters. On festival days vendors fill every frame with yakisoba, takoyaki, grilled squid, shaved ice and hero merchandise, lines wind around the pillars between events, and hired pro heroes on security duty walk the crowd. Stall work is a festival-day part-time job open to anyone who applies, paid at the end of the day, and Musutafu locals take it every year for the pay and the gossip. Out of season only the vending machines and their restockers are here, and the stall frames sit padlocked. On festival mornings the smell of grilled sauce reaches the seats before the crowds do.

Unforeseen Simulation Joint (USJ).name: Unforeseen Simulation Joint (USJ)
Unforeseen Simulation Joint (USJ).basicInfo: The Unforeseen Simulation Joint (USJ) is U.A. Academy's rescue-training facility: a huge dome high in the forest at the top of the grounds, about 3 km north-northeast of the main building and ten minutes by campus bus up the winding hill road, inside U.A.'s wall; on foot the climb takes the better part of an hour. Thirteen, the Space Hero and a rescue specialist, designed it and runs it. Inside, six disaster zones surround a central plaza: flood, landslide, fire, storm, collapsed buildings and mountain. Hero Course classes come here for the rescue side of Foundational Hero Studies, in afternoon blocks booked through the Faculty Office, with Thirteen teaching and All Might or the class's homeroom teacher, Shota Aizawa (Eraser Head) for 1-A or Vlad King for 1-B, joining when the curriculum calls for it. The bus stops at the main doors, the only doors to the outside, and they stay locked unless a class or session is booked. Thirteen opens zones for extra practice on request and begins each class's first lesson with a talk on how easily a Quirk can kill. Students come here to learn rescue, practice Quirk control under lifelike conditions and be graded on getting people out: who was found, how fast, and whether the rescuer added to the disaster. Ground crews reset the zones in the mornings so they are ready for afternoon classes. Pumps, fire jets and rain machines keep up a constant rumble under the dome, and the air changes from wet to smoky to dusty from one zone to the next.
Unforeseen Simulation Joint (USJ).hiddenInfo: The USJ's alarms, phones and cameras all route back to the main campus; a Quirk that jams signals would cut the dome off, and help from the main building is at least ten minutes away by road. The only doors to the outside are at the Entrance Plaza, and every zone is built to hide people in water, smoke, rain or rubble. The disasters run on real machinery, and Thirteen insists on safety checks before every session because a stuck valve could drown or burn a student. Right now one of the Flood Zone's current pumps is new, fitted last week, and still trips its breaker when it runs at full power; Thirteen has it on her checklist and runs the lake at half current until it holds. A class's first rescue lesson here brings Thirteen and its homeroom teacher. All Might is meant to join Class 1-A's first one too, but on that day he is held up on the main campus since morning and is not in the dome when the class arrives or when the lesson starts. Thirteen's Black Hole can pull in almost anything, which is why Thirteen teaches restraint first. The control room at the Entrance Plaza can cut every zone's machinery at once, and only Thirteen and the faculty know the shutdown code.

USJ Bus Drop-Off.description: The way into the USJ from the hill road: a wide paved turnaround outside the dome's main doors, high in the forest at the top of the grounds, about ten minutes by campus bus up the winding road from the main building. Campus buses from the Campus Bus Terminal pull in under a long canopy to drop classes at the foot of a short flight of steps up to the doors, the only doors to the outside, which stay locked unless a class or session is booked. The dome fills the sky above the trees, its curved panels catching the light, and the rumble of pumps and rain machines comes faintly through the walls. Classes climb out in costume here, Thirteen or their homeroom teacher counting heads, and the bus waits at the turnaround or heads back down for the next group. A covered bench, a first-aid box and an emergency phone to the Faculty Office stand by the curb. On foot the climb from the main campus takes the better part of an hour. Through the main doors lies the Entrance Plaza.

Entrance Plaza.description: The terrace just inside the main doors, at the top of a long staircase down to the Central Plaza. From the rail the whole dome is in view: the lake and its ship, the burning block, the storm zone's enclosed dome, the rubble and the mountain. Classes gather here when the bus arrives, hear Thirteen's safety talk and get their assignments; she counts her points on gloved fingers, loses count, and then says the serious one plainly. The doors to the outside and the control room for the dome's systems are here, behind a window that looks over the whole floor. Students line up by the rail in costume, comparing gear and guessing which zone they will draw. Sound from every zone rises to this terrace at once: water, fire, rain and wind.

Central Plaza.description: A wide paved plaza at the foot of the entrance stairs, with a fountain in the middle and broad paths branching to each disaster zone: the Flood Zone, the Landslide Zone, the Conflagration Zone, the Downpour Zone, the Ruins Zone and the Mountain Zone, with the stairs climbing back to the Entrance Plaza. Thirteen uses it for briefings, triage practice and the start of combined exercises, and classes regroup here between zones, dripping, sooty or dusty depending on where they came from. It is the one place in the dome with clear sightlines in every direction and no hazards, and stretchers and first-aid kits are stacked along its edge during sessions. The fountain runs all day, and on quiet mornings it is the loudest thing in the building.

Flood Zone.description: A deep artificial lake with a stranded passenger ship in the middle, current machines along its edges and floating debris that staff rearrange between sessions. Students practice water rescue here: swimming with a victim, righting small boats and getting people off the listing ship, whose decks tilt more each time the pumps push the water. Weighted dummies stand in for victims, and some are tied below deck where they have to be found. The pumps run only during booked afternoon sessions, and the lake lies flat and still on other days, the ship's rust streaks reflected in it. The way back is the paved path to the Central Plaza. The water is cold, chest-deep near the shore and far over anyone's head by the ship, and the whole zone smells of chlorine and wet steel.

Landslide Zone.description: Hills of loose earth and rubble poured over half-buried houses and cars, with slopes that machinery can set sliding on command. Students practice finding buried victims, shoring up slopes and digging people out without bringing more earth down, working in pairs with one digging and one watching the slope. Sensors buried with the dummies chirp faintly, and the class that finds them by listening rather than digging blind gets the better grade. Ground crews reset the slopes in the mornings, so the zone is ready for afternoon classes, and a path leads back to the Central Plaza. The ground shifts underfoot, boots sink to the ankle after rain machines run next door, and the smell of wet clay clings to costumes for the rest of the day.

Conflagration Zone.description: A city block of fire-gutted buildings whose gas jets set rooms burning on demand, with smoke machines and sprinkler mains run from the control room. Students practice clearing smoke-filled floors, fighting fire with their Quirks and carrying victims down burning stairwells, keeping low where the air is clearest. The jets light only when Thirteen clears a session, with breathing gear on hand and the fires shut off between groups; a horn sounds before every ignition, and nobody enters until it stops. Ice and water Quirks are welcome here, and explosive ones are watched closely. The path back to the Central Plaza is the only clear air. The heat is real: costumes scorch, railings burn bare hands, and everything smells of soot.

Downpour Zone.description: A cluster of streets and buildings under its own enclosed dome, where machines drive heavy rain and gale-force wind. Students practice rescues in poor visibility, rising water in the streets, slick footing and wind strong enough to throw a careless flier off course, finding dummies trapped on balconies and in flooded doorways. The storm runs on afternoon bookings; otherwise the rain is off, the streets drain into pools and the inner dome's door to the Central Plaza stands open. Costumes that are not waterproof come out heavy and cold, and the Support Course gets a wave of repair requests after every session. Inside, the roar of rain on metal roofs drowns out shouted orders, so teams train with hand signals.

Ruins Zone.description: Collapsed and half-standing concrete buildings over broken streets, with voids, tilted floors and crawl spaces built in on purpose. Students practice search and rescue in rubble: listening for victims, shoring up slabs and crossing unstable floors without bringing them down, then carrying the found back along the path to the Central Plaza. Some floors are rigged to drop a few centimeters under too much weight, a warning rather than a fall. Staff rebuild sections on weekends after heavy use, and a strong Quirk that knocks down a wall to reach a victim faster loses points for the people the wall would have landed on. Dust hangs in the air after every exercise, and the zone's one firm rule is silence when a rescuer calls for it to listen for tapping.

Mountain Zone.description: A steep artificial mountain of bare rock with cliffs, ledges, a narrow summit path and bolted anchors for ropes. Students practice cliff rescue, rope work, lowering injured climbers and crossing exposed faces, with or without a Quirk that helps; the strongest climbers learn that hauling a stretcher is a different job from climbing alone. Fall nets hang under the worst drops during sessions, and climbers can ask Thirteen for extra practice after classes. Chalk marks and frayed rope ends show the favorite routes, and a path at the foot of the rock leads back to the Central Plaza. Gloves shred quickly here. From the summit the whole dome is in view, and voices from the Central Plaza carry up clearly.

Ground Beta.name: Ground Beta
Ground Beta.basicInfo: Ground Beta is one of U.A. Academy's mock cities: blocks of full-size streets, office buildings, shops and working traffic lights built for battle and rescue exercises, about 1.5 km northwest of the main building by campus bus, on the wooded slope above Training Ground Gamma, and 2 km west-northwest of the stadium; the entrance exam calls it Battle Center B. It is one of seven, Battle Centers A to G, scattered through the forest inside U.A.'s wall, and each sits behind its own security wall with a locked perimeter gate where the campus bus drops classes off. The Hero Course uses it during Foundational Hero Studies for battle trials, in which teams play heroes and villains inside a training building while the rest of the class watches on monitors, and for street exercises in pursuit, crowd rescue and fighting faux villain robots. All Might supervises Class 1-A's battle training here. Each February, part of the entrance exam's practical test runs here, with robots worth points. Sessions are booked through the Faculty Office in afternoon blocks; outside bookings the city is closed and empty, and the gate stays locked. Damage is part of the lesson, and construction crews and Cementoss repair it between sessions. A player can fight a battle trial, chase a robot down a four-lane road or watch a classmate from the monitoring room. On empty days the traffic lights still change for streets with no cars.
Ground Beta.hiddenInfo: The faux villain robots are stored in hangars at the city's edge, along with the giant Zero Pointer from the entrance exam, and only a few staff members can activate it. The robots' programming keeps impacts training-safe, but a malfunctioning one would not hold back. Right now one two-pointer in the second hangar is overdue for servicing after the February exam: a work order taped to its chassis says its impact limiter reads wrong, and it is still on the roster for street drills because the repair crew has been busy elsewhere. A monitoring room records every exercise from dozens of cameras, and the faculty grades from the footage, including how much damage students cause. Nobody guards the streets at night: the security wall and a locked perimeter gate are the only barriers, and students who want an unsupervised fight know it. All Might draws battle-trial teams by lot, from a box he made himself, and he rehearses his briefings from a cue card he thinks nobody notices. The training building's upper floors still hold a fake nuclear warhead prop, papier-mache over a steel frame, left from last year's trials and waiting to be used again.

Ground Beta Gate.description: The way into Ground Beta: a locked perimeter gate in the mock city's security wall, at the end of the campus road where it comes out of the forest, with a bus turnaround, a concrete bus shelter and a small staff booth with a card reader and an intercom to the Faculty Office. Campus buses from the Campus Bus Terminal drop classes here in the early afternoon, about a kilometer and a half from the main building, and collect them again before evening; outside a booking the gate stays shut and the turnaround stays empty. Classes line up here in costume while the teacher unlocks the gate and runs through the exercise, and through the bars the first block of the mock city is already in view: a four-lane road, a working traffic light, blank shop windows. A hose reel and a stack of hazard cones sit by the booth for the repair crews, and robot tread marks run in under the gate. Through the gate lie the Mock City Streets.

Mock City Streets.description: Four-lane roads, side streets and intersections between full-size buildings, with working traffic lights, parked cars, storefronts and bus shelters. Exercises here cover pursuit, crowd rescue, street fights and running battles with faux villain robots, which roll out of the hangars at the edge of the city with their point values painted on their sides. Classes arrive by bus at the perimeter gate in the early afternoon and leave before evening; outside bookings the streets are empty. Cameras on the lampposts feed the monitoring room in the Training Building, and fire escapes and ladders lead up to the Mock City Rooftops. The shop windows are blank, the cars have no engines, and the vending machines hold nothing. Fresh concrete patches mark every block, and robot treads have scored the asphalt.

Training Building.description: A multistory office building near the center of the mock city, used for indoor battle trials: a villain team defends a target on an upper floor while a hero team breaks in, and wrapping an opponent in capture tape counts as a capture. Each team gets a floor plan and a few minutes to plan, and the villains get a head start to set up. Its monitoring room shows every floor on banks of screens, and the waiting class watches there with the instructor, who stops a trial the moment it turns dangerous and has every student explain their choices afterward. The walls are reinforced but not unbreakable, and holes from past trials are patched in a lighter shade of concrete. The front doors open onto the Mock City Streets. Inside, every hallway looks the same, and the elevators do not run.

Mock City Rooftops.description: The flat roofs of the mock city, crowded with water tanks, air units and antenna masts, with gaps between buildings that only some Quirks can cross. Ranged Quirk users take positions here, mobile students practice crossing the skyline, and instructors watch exercises from the tallest roofs with a radio and a stopwatch. Robot targets set on the rooftops are a standard drill for students who can fly, swing or leap, and the scorch marks on the water tanks show who has tried. Fire escapes and ladders lead back down to the Mock City Streets. From up here the forest shows over the security wall on every side, and the stadium's rim is visible to the east. The wind is strong up here, and the edges have no rails.

Monitoring Room.description: The Training Building's monitoring room, on the ground floor behind a steel door off the lobby: a dim room lined with banks of screens that show every floor, stairwell and corridor of the building from dozens of ceiling cameras, plus the lamppost cameras out on the Mock City Streets. A long console with microphones lets the instructor talk to the teams through their earpieces and call a stop, and the round's timer runs on the center screen. During a battle trial the waiting class stands here with the instructor and watches the two teams on the screens; after each round the four students come down and stand in front of the class while the instructor has each of them explain their choices, and the class weighs in. Recordings of every exercise go to the Faculty Office for grading. The air conditioning hums, the room smells of warm electronics, and the only light is the blue glow of the screens. The steel door leads back into the Training Building.

Mock City Central Plaza.description: An open square at the center of the mock city, in front of the Training Building's doors, where four streets meet around a dry fountain and a ring of empty benches. This is where an instructor gathers a class inside Ground Beta: teams are briefed here, the class lines up in costume before an exercise, and at the end of a lesson the instructor gives the last words and dismisses everyone, who then walk back down the main road to Ground Beta Gate for the campus bus. A large public screen on one building face can show the monitoring room's feeds to a crowd. The fountain has never held water, the bench paint is fresh, and the storefronts around the square are as blank as everywhere else in the city. The Training Building, the Mock City Streets and the road to Ground Beta Gate all open onto the square.

Training Ground Gamma.name: Training Ground Gamma
Training Ground Gamma.basicInfo: Training Ground Gamma is a factory-like training ground of pipes, tanks, catwalks and narrow lanes, packed so tightly that sightlines rarely run more than a few meters. It sits behind its own wall about 1 km west of the main building by campus road, at the foot of the slope below Ground Beta, with the main campus between it and the stadium. The faculty uses it for close-quarters exercises: ambushes, team battles, hostage scenarios and capture drills in which students must find an opponent before they can fight one. Hero Course classes come in afternoon blocks booked through the Faculty Office, and instructors run each exercise from the Control Tower; outside bookings it is closed, and its gate is locked. The campus bus drops classes at that gate, and the walk back to the main campus takes about fifteen minutes. Exercises start with teams at opposite ends of the maze and end with a capture, a surrender or the instructor's whistle. Staff reconfigure the maze between some sessions, so memorizing it only helps for so long. Students who are good in open ground often hate Gamma, and students with small, quiet or sensing Quirks often shine here. A player can hunt or be hunted, practice a capture, learn the maze or watch from the tower. Steam vents hiss, pipes knock when the system pressurizes, and the light stays dim even at noon.
Training Ground Gamma.hiddenInfo: Most of the pipes are dummies, but some carry live water and low-pressure steam to make exercises real, and old valves leak where students have damaged them. The Control Tower can kill the lights, open steam vents and lock some gates, and instructors use those controls to change a fight mid-exercise without warning. Cameras do not cover every gap between the tanks, and older students pass the blind spots down to younger ones. Repairs come slowly: right now a catwalk at the east end of the maze sags where a student's Quirk bent it in March, and it is still in use, marked only with tape. Last weekend staff moved a whole row of tanks, so two of the blind spots the older students pass down no longer exist, and two new ones do, near the Factory Floor. Instructors know the maze is hard on students who panic in tight spaces, and they watch for it on the screens and pull a student out quietly rather than in front of the class. The steam system runs off a pressure board in the tower; if it is left on after a session, the pipes keep knocking through the night, and the groundskeepers have learned to check.

Gamma Gate.description: The way into Training Ground Gamma: a heavy sliding gate in a plain concrete wall at the foot of the slope, about a kilometer west of the main building by campus road, with a bus turnaround, a roofed bus stop and a steel stair up the outside of the wall to the Control Tower for instructors. Pipes and tank tops show over the wall, and steam drifts out of the vents above it. Campus buses from the Campus Bus Terminal drop classes here for afternoon exercises, and the walk back to the main campus takes about fifteen minutes. Teams are split here before the gate opens, one sent in at each end, and the instructor reads out the rules from a clipboard while the pipes knock behind the wall. Outside bookings the gate is locked and the turnaround empty. A first-aid box and a fire extinguisher hang beside the gate, and a whistle on a cord hangs from the reader post. Through the gate a narrow lane runs into the Pipe Maze, past the open hall of the Factory Floor.

Pipe Maze.description: The heart of the ground: lanes of tangled pipes at every height, with tanks, ladders and catwalks overhead, turns every few meters and shadows deep enough to hide in. During afternoon exercises, teams start at opposite ends and hunt each other through it while the Control Tower watches, and the instructor's voice comes over a speaker when a team breaks a rule. Some pipes are warm to the touch and some drip; a hiss from a vent is the only warning before a cloud of steam fills a lane. The maze opens onto the Factory Floor at one edge, and a ladder climbs to the Control Tower. Sound bounces off the metal, so footsteps seem to come from the wrong direction. Getting lost here is common, and getting found is the point of the exercise.

Factory Floor.description: An open hall at the maze's edge with a concrete floor, machinery mock-ups, overhead cranes and stacked crates: the one place in Gamma with room to swing a fist or a long weapon. Exercises use it for open fights, holdout scenarios and staging areas between rounds, and classes take water breaks and instructions here, sitting on the crates while the instructor goes over the last round. A whiteboard on wheels carries the day's teams and rules, and nobody erases it without asking. Its concrete floor is the only one in Gamma flat enough for Quirks that need footing, and the crates move between sessions to make new cover. The lanes of the Pipe Maze open off one long wall. Light from the high windows falls in bands across the floor, and the cranes creak overhead whenever the wind shifts.

Control Tower.description: A tower above the maze with an enclosed observation deck: banks of monitors fed by cameras in the pipes, a console for lights, vents and gates, and windows on all sides. Instructors run exercises from here and speak to teams by radio, while waiting students and observers watch the screens and are expected to say what they would do next. Students come up only when invited, by the ladder down to the Pipe Maze. A rack of spare radios charges by the door, and the instructor hands one to each team leader before an exercise. A clipboard by the console logs every session, every vent opened and every gate locked. The deck is quiet and cool, and radio traffic from the maze is the only noise, apart from the occasional groan when a team walks into the same trap twice.

Gym Gamma.name: Gym Gamma
Gym Gamma.basicInfo: Gym Gamma, nicknamed Training Dungeon Land, is a large indoor gym with a reinforced concrete floor and walls, on the main campus, a short walk northeast of the main building, about 400 meters by the path from the Courtyard. Cementoss reshapes the concrete into cliffs, pillars, pits and arenas to suit each class or student, so the training fits the Quirk instead of the other way around. Hero Course classes use it in afternoon blocks for terrain drills and special-move training, booked through the Faculty Office and supervised by Cementoss, often with Ectoplasm's clones as sparring partners. Students can request time after classes, and they sign a sheet at the door on the way in and out. It is locked whenever Cementoss or another teacher is not inside, and no one trains here alone. The building has one wide door on the campus side, changing rooms and a first-aid kit at the entrance, and a viewing gallery along one wall where waiting students sit. A session might put one student on a pillar thirty meters up, another in a pit full of clones, and a third throwing the same move at the same wall for an hour. The gym is the place to build a special move, test a Quirk's limits safely, or ask Cementoss for terrain nobody else has thought to ask for. Recovery Girl's Infirmary is a five-minute walk away, and Cementoss sends anyone with a bad landing there at once. Under the high roof every impact booms, and cement dust hangs in the air.
Gym Gamma.hiddenInfo: Hero Course requests for after-class time often outnumber the slots, most of all before the Sports Festival and exams, and Cementoss favors students who arrive with a plan, since he supervises every session himself. Terrain he leaves standing stays until he returns, and loose blocks from broken formations are a hazard to anyone training alone. The walls are rated for heavy Quirk impacts, but repeated blasts in one spot crack them, and a cracked wall closes the gym until he rebuilds it. Right now a hairline crack runs across the north wall at shoulder height, and Cementoss has chalked a circle around it and plans to rebuild it on Saturday; a student who keeps blasting that wall before then could close the gym for days. Ectoplasm's clones hold back exactly as much as the student in front of them needs and no more, and he grades from the result in two sentences. The after-class booking sheet for the next two weeks is already half full, and most of the names are from Class 1-B, which noticed it first.

Gym Gamma Entrance.description: The way into Gym Gamma from the main campus: a paved forecourt at the end of the path from the Courtyard, about 400 meters and five minutes on foot, in front of the gym's one wide door, a pair of reinforced steel doors under a concrete canopy. A bike rack, a bench and a drinking fountain stand along the wall, shoes and bags pile up beside the doors before a session, and a notice board holds the after-class booking times. The gym is on the main campus, so classes walk here instead of taking the bus. The doors stay locked unless Cementoss or another teacher is inside; students waiting for a booking sit on the bench or stretch on the forecourt, and every impact from the training floor comes through the doors as a dull boom. After a session they come out gray with cement dust and head back toward the main building or to Recovery Girl's Infirmary. Through the doors lies the Equipment Bay.

Gym Gamma Training Floor.description: The main floor of Gym Gamma, the gym students call Training Dungeon Land: a vast hall of reinforced concrete under a high steel roof, with floodlights overhead and one wide door on the campus side. Cementoss lays a palm on the floor and it rises into cliffs, pillars, pits, ramps and walled arenas shaped for whoever is training, and whatever he leaves standing waits there until he comes back. Hero Course classes take the floor in afternoon blocks for terrain drills and special-move work, with Ectoplasm's clones dropping from ledges to spar; after classes, students who booked time through the Faculty Office train under his eye, one on a pillar thirty meters up, another holding a pit against a ring of clones, a third throwing the same move at the same wall for an hour. No one trains here alone, and the gym is locked whenever no teacher is inside. On the north wall, a hairline crack at shoulder height sits inside a chalk circle, and everyone with sense aims elsewhere. Every impact booms off the roof, and cement dust hangs in the light. The Equipment Bay and the stairs up to the Gym Gamma Observation Deck both open off the floor.

Equipment Bay.description: A long, low room just inside Gym Gamma's door, between the changing rooms and the training floor, where everything the floor needs is kept in order. Stacked crash mats line one wall, with helmets and elbow guards on open shelves by size, weighted vests on hooks, timing gates and stopwatches in a locked cabinet, and buckets, wide brooms and shovels for the rubble every session leaves. The first-aid kit hangs by the door with a folding stretcher clipped beneath it, and the sign-in sheet hangs on a clipboard beside it: every student writes a name and a time going in and coming out, and Cementoss reads it before he locks up. A whiteboard lists the after-class bookings for the next two weeks, already half full and mostly in Class 1-B handwriting. Students strap on gear here before a session and come back gray with dust afterward, comparing who lasted longest against Ectoplasm's clones. Reinforced racks hold heavier gear made for students whose Quirks would tear ordinary equipment, and a hand-lettered notice asks everyone to return it clean. The room smells of rubber mats and wet cement. It opens onto the Gym Gamma Training Floor.

Gym Gamma Observation Deck.description: A raised viewing gallery along one side wall of Gym Gamma, reached by a steel stair from the training floor: rows of bench seating behind a waist-high concrete parapet topped with thick shatterproof panels, high enough to see every cliff and pit Cementoss raises below. Waiting students sit here between turns, towels around their necks, watching classmates and taking notes on Quirks that are not their own; teachers who booked the floor for a class stand at the rail to call out corrections, and Ectoplasm sometimes grades from up here while his clones do the work below. During afternoon blocks the benches fill with a whole class in gym uniforms; after classes they hold a handful of students waiting for their slot and the occasional classmate who came only to watch a rival train. The rule is simple: nobody throws anything from the gallery, Quirks included, and anyone leaning over the panels gets a quiet word from Cementoss without his ever looking up. Through the panels every blast below arrives as a dull thud felt through the bench, and dust films the rail by evening. The stair leads back down to the Gym Gamma Training Floor.

Musutafu Station District.name: Musutafu Station District
Musutafu Station District.basicInfo: Musutafu's main rail station and the busy blocks around it, where most visitors arrive. It is a Tokaido shinkansen stop: Tokyo, about 100 km northeast, is 45 minutes away and Osaka two hours. U.A. Academy's campus is about 3 km northeast, ten minutes by bus up the hill road; Musutafu Police Headquarters is about 3.5 km northwest and Hero Agency Row about 4 km east. The rail company runs the station; a police box at the north exit handles lost wallets, directions and the first report of any public Quirk use. The north exit opens on the bus terminal and a crossing of convenience stores; the south exit leads into the Hero Merch Arcade and the back alleys behind it. Commuters pack the concourse from seven to nine and five to eight; between rushes come shoppers, and after dark office workers fill the alley bars until the last train, a little after midnight. U.A. students, who live on campus, come through on weekend visits home, and Sunday evening brings a wave of them back to the buses. Local pros walk patrols at rush hour, and Kamui Woods, Death Arms and Backdraft have all answered calls here. The station is public ground and open to anyone from the first train to the last; after that the gates close and only the convenience stores and the alley bars keep their lights on. A player can work a store or arcade shift, shop, meet friends, catch a train or bus, shadow a patrol, or trade rumors. Departure chimes, hero-news jingles and the smell of fried chicken from the alley vents are constant.
Musutafu Station District.hiddenInfo: Since the news broke that All Might now teaches at U.A., reporters and camera crews have staked out the north exit, stopping anyone in a U.A. uniform for a quote on weekends, and fans wait at rush hour in case All Might commutes by train. The rail company has complained to the police box about blocked exits, and the officers on duty spend their weekends moving camera crews along. Behind the arcade, brokers who never give their names buy drinks for small-time crooks and hire for whoever pays; the police box hears most of it as bar talk. One of them works from a standing bar near the end of the lanes most weeknights after ten, asks only about Quirks, pays a cash advance on the spot and never names the client; the bar's cook knows his face and his usual time and will say so for a meal and a promise of discretion. Meanwhile both convenience stores at the north exit are desperately short of night staff; the manager of the busier one will hire anyone who shows up sober and will look the other way about a missing résumé.

Station Concourse.description: A long, bright hall of ticket gates, departure boards, kiosks and coin lockers under a curved glass roof, with the shinkansen platforms above and the local lines below. Exits lead north to the Convenience Store Corner and the bus terminal, and south to the Hero Merch Arcade. From seven to nine and five to eight the hall is packed with commuters in suits and local students in school uniforms; U.A. students come through on weekends, and on Sunday evenings they cross it in groups toward the buses back up the hill. Between rushes it holds shoppers, tourists with rolling cases and retirees waiting for friends under the big clock. Station staff watch the gates, make announcements and help lost travelers, and a cleaner with a wide mop works the floor all day. Everyone stands on the left of the escalators and walks on the right, and anyone who blocks the flow gets glared at. The departure chime for the Tokyo trains is a short rising melody that regulars can hum.

Hero Merch Arcade.description: A covered shopping arcade off the station's south exit, lined with narrow shops selling hero figures, trading cards, posters, replica costumes, signed photos and fan magazines. All Might goods fill the front shelves of every store, and since the news that he teaches at U.A. one shop has cleared a whole window for him; Endeavor, Best Jeanist and Hawks have their own displays, and Mount Lady merchandise has sold fast since her debut in the city last spring. Young fans come after school with their parents, collectors on weekends to hunt rare cards, and part-timers restock at night after the shutters come halfway down. Shopkeepers know their regulars by name and argue about the Hero Billboard Chart across the aisle. Capsule-toy machines rattle, and every shop speaker plays a different hero-news clip. The arcade leads back to the Station Concourse at one end and, through a gap between two shops, into the Back Alleys behind.

Convenience Store Corner.description: A busy crossing outside the station's north exit, where two rival convenience stores face each other across a zebra crossing, both open all night, with the bus terminal's shelters beside them. Commuters grab rice balls and canned coffee before the morning trains; local students in school uniforms buy snacks, pay phone bills and photocopy notes after classes; night-shift workers and taxi drivers come in after midnight, and the police box on the corner sends its officers over for coffee. Both stores are always short of part-timers, and shifts are easy to pick up and hard to keep; the managers poach each other's staff with an extra hundred yen an hour. A small TV over one register runs hero news on a loop, the door chimes never stop, and the fried-chicken warmer by the counter sells out by eight. The corner leads back into the Station Concourse.

Back Alleys.description: Narrow lanes behind the arcade, crowded with tiny bars, standing noodle counters, vending machines, delivery bikes and stacked crates, under a tangle of power lines and paper lanterns. By day they are service lanes for the shops, with deliveries in the morning and cooks smoking by the back doors in the afternoon. After dark, office workers drink here until the last train, and small-time crooks use the corners to make deals and settle scores. Patrol heroes cut through on foot because cars cannot fit, and the bars go quiet for a moment whenever a costume passes the door. The lanes smell of grilled skewers and garbage, and the local rule is to mind your own business: nobody here wants to be a witness. A cook who keeps the same seat by the window sees everything and says nothing for free. The lanes lead back out through the Hero Merch Arcade.

Game Center.description: A three-story game center halfway down the Hero Merch Arcade, its open front a wall of crane machines stocked with plush heroes, All Might in front and a fresh row of Mount Lady dolls beside him. The ground floor is cranes and photo-sticker booths with curtained stalls; the second floor holds rhythm games, a taiko drum cabinet and two rows of fighting-game cabinets set back to back; the third is medal games and a quiet corner of mahjong machines. Most plays cost 100 yen, and the change machine by the stairs never runs dry. Retirees take the medal floor in the mornings, local students in school uniforms crowd the cranes after classes, and the fighting-game regulars arrive after dinner and stay until the 11 p.m. close, calling out matchups to the watchers behind them. A staff member in a red vest unjams machines and nudges a prize closer when it sticks; a printed notice on every cabinet says that Quirk use on the machines means a lifetime ban, and the staff point to it whenever anyone floats a prize or freezes a claw. The noise is a wall of jingles, drumbeats and pouring medals. The front opens back onto the Hero Merch Arcade.

Karaoke Box.description: A narrow eight-story karaoke building on the north-exit crossing, its front stacked with neon and its sidewalk worked by a staff member handing out discount flyers. The ground floor is a front desk with a rack of tambourines, maracas and costume headbands to borrow; the elevator rises to floors of small soundproof rooms, each with a padded bench, a low table, two microphones, a touch-screen song pad and a wall phone for ordering fries and drinks. Rooms run by the half hour, cheapest on weekday afternoons, and an all-night package from eleven to five draws office workers who missed the last train. Local students come after classes in groups, U.A. students book the big party rooms on weekends home, and by late evening the corridors fill with off-key office parties and birthday crowds. Hero anime theme songs are the most requested tracks this spring, with a dance remix of All Might's catchphrase. A sign at the desk says Quirks may not be used to boost the volume or the scoring, and the night clerk tells of the customer who blew out a speaker. Muffled choruses leak from every door. The entrance opens onto the Convenience Store Corner.

Station-Front Cafe.description: A chain coffee shop beside the station's north exit, with a long window bar facing the bus terminal, small round tables, a wall of power outlets and a pastry case by the register. It opens at seven for the commuter rush, when the line runs out the door and the baristas call orders by cup size at a shout; mid-morning it settles into parents with strollers, retirees and freelancers who nurse one drink for hours. After classes, local students in school uniforms take the outlets to study, and on Sunday evenings U.A. students wait here in twos and threes for the buses up the hill, ordering the cheapest drink to keep a seat. A drip coffee runs about 350 yen and the seasonal sweet drinks about 600. The window bar is the best seat in the district for watching the crossing, and a pair of retired men argue about the hero rankings there every morning. The staff keep a wide stool and a tall table for heteromorph customers, and a sign by the sugar asks customers to clean up anything their Quirk leaves behind. It smells of roast beans and warm butter. One door leads into the Station Concourse, the other out to the Convenience Store Corner.

Ramen Counter.description: A twelve-seat counter ramen shop where the arcade's back gap meets the alleys, run by a husband and wife who have cooked here for twenty years, with a meal-ticket machine by the door, a row of bolted stools, a stainless counter and a pot of pork-bone broth that never goes off the flame. Customers buy a ticket, about 800 yen for the house tonkotsu and 100 more for a soft-boiled egg, hand it over and are served in minutes. The lunch line is office workers and delivery riders; after classes, students come in pairs; after ten, drinkers from the lanes come in for a last bowl before the train, and the shop stays open until one. The house rules are painted on a board above the counter: eat, pay and give up your stool when people are waiting. The husband never speaks; the wife hears everything said at the counter and repeats none of it. A strip of signed cards from local pros runs along the menu board, some faded beyond reading, and a framed photo of Death Arms with an empty bowl hangs over the register. The air is thick with pork fat and garlic, and the window fogs over on cold nights. The door opens onto the Back Alleys.

Izakaya Lane.description: A short lane off the back alleys lined on both sides with tiny izakaya, each with a red paper lantern, a cloth curtain over the door, a wooden board of the day's dishes and six or eight seats at a counter around a grill. Smoke from yakitori and grilled fish hangs under the eaves, and beer crates on the pavement serve as extra tables. From six, office workers loosen their ties over beer, highballs and skewers at about 150 yen apiece, and the counters stay full until the last train; the owners pour, cook and listen all at once. Most places charge a small seating fee that comes with a dish of pickles. Older couples come early and young workers late, and U.A. students home for the weekend get a free skewer from owners proud of the academy up the hill. The owners have a standing agreement to call the police box at the first shove, and a closing-time scuffle usually ends with two drunks apologizing to each other on the curb. Touts are not allowed in the lane; the owners chase them out themselves. Laughter, grill hiss and old enka spill from every door. The lane opens onto the Back Alleys, and the Ramen Counter's door sits at its corner.

Family Restaurant.description: A family restaurant on the second floor above the bus terminal, reached by an outdoor staircase from the north-exit crossing: booths with vinyl benches along the windows, a drink bar, a call button on every table and laminated menus with photos of hamburg steak, doria, curry and parfaits. A lunch set runs about 800 yen, and the drink bar alone about 350, which makes it the cheapest place in the district to sit for hours. Mornings bring retirees with breakfast sets; lunch brings parents with toddlers and office workers; after classes, students take the big booths to study and do not leave; late at night, taxi drivers, night-shift workers and anyone who missed the last train nurse a coffee until it closes at two. Staff greet every arrival with the same sing-song welcome. The window booths look down on the bus shelters, and on Sunday nights U.A. students watch for their bus from there. A booth by the drink bar has a wide bench and a reinforced table for heteromorph diners, and somewhere a call button chimes every few seconds. It smells of demi-glace and fryer oil. The staircase leads back down to the Convenience Store Corner.

Neighborhood Bathhouse.description: An old public bathhouse two blocks north of the bus terminal, with a tall brick chimney and split cloth curtains at the entrance, blue for men and red for women. Inside, shoes go into wooden lockers with wooden keys, and an attendant on a raised booth between the changing rooms takes the 500-yen entry and sells towels, soap and bottled milk. Past the changing rooms, rows of low faucets with stools and buckets line the walls, and three tiled baths sit under a painted mural of Mount Fuji: a hot one, a hotter one and an electric bath. Wash before you get in, keep towels out of the water and tie long hair up: the rules are painted on a board, with a newer line asking bathers not to use Quirks to heat or cool the water. Retirees come when it opens at three; after work come laborers and shop staff, and after ten come students and night workers. A wider door and a deep tub at the end are kept for heteromorph bathers. Regulars drink their milk in front of the electric fan, and old men argue about the hero rankings across the changing room. It smells of steam and soap. The street outside leads back to the Convenience Store Corner.

Coin Laundry.description: A small coin laundry next door to the bathhouse, open all night: a row of front-loading washers along one wall, stacked gas dryers along the other, a folding table down the middle, and a bench by the window under a buzzing fluorescent tube. A wash costs 400 yen, a dryer 100 yen per ten minutes, and the change machine rejects every other note. Bathhouse regulars drop a load in on the way to the bath and fold it on the way home; single office workers come late with a week of shirts; students from the cheap apartments north of the station read manga on the bench while their clothes spin. A cork board by the door holds notices for lost cats, room shares and part-time jobs, and a pile of old hero magazines sits on the windowsill. One handwritten sign asks customers not to leave laundry in the machines overnight; another asks those with heat Quirks not to use them on the dryers. After midnight it is one of the few lit doors on the street, and anyone sitting on the bench is easy to see from outside. It smells of clean cotton. The door opens beside the Neighborhood Bathhouse, a short walk from the Convenience Store Corner.

Kiyashi Shopping Mall.name: Kiyashi Shopping Mall
Kiyashi Shopping Mall.basicInfo: A large suburban mall on Musutafu's south side, about 5 km south-southwest of the station, with its own bus terminal and a multi-level parking garage; Dagobah Municipal Beach Park is about 3 km farther toward the bay. Its selling point is range: shops stock clothing and gear for every body type, including heteromorph sizes, along with sports goods, electronics, books, groceries and a movie theater. A private management company runs it and its uniformed security guards, who carry radios and have no authority to use Quirks; serious trouble means calling the police or a patrolling pro. It opens at ten and closes at nine, and the doors are locked outside those hours except the staff entrance by the loading docks. Weekday mornings bring retirees and parents with strollers; after classes, local students in school uniforms arrive; weekends are packed with families, couples and young people from across the city, U.A. students among them. The four-story atrium is the meeting point for half of Musutafu, the food court is the cheapest long lunch in town, and the upper fashion floors are where heteromorph shoppers come because they can finally find clothes that fit. A player can shop, eat, meet friends, take a part-time job in a store or the food court, catch a movie, or watch the crowd. Escalators hum, piped music mixes with announcements, and the atrium's big screen runs hero news between ads.
Kiyashi Shopping Mall.hiddenInfo: A pickpocket crew has worked the weekend crowds in the atrium for a month. One of them has a small Quirk that makes people flinch for a second, and the others lift wallets and phones in that moment; they work Saturday afternoons by the fountain, when the crowd is thickest, and leave by different exits. Mall security has descriptions but no authority to use Quirks, and the police treat it as low priority. Embarrassed, management is quietly taking bids from the small agencies on Hero Agency Row for a paid security contract; whichever pro lands it gets steady pay and a crowd to be seen by. Store staff also complain that the security company cut night guards to save money, so the loading docks are often unwatched after closing. Meanwhile Gentle Criminal and La Brava have taken a corner table in the Food Court most weekday afternoons, where she pours him tea from a thermos while they plan. They are scouting the atrium for his next video: La Brava has been probing the big screen's control system from her laptop, and Gentle wants to take it over at the busiest hour of a Saturday to broadcast himself to the whole mall. Clues are there for anyone who looks: a small woman with raspberry-pink pigtails lingering near the screen's service panel, a white-haired man in a tailcoat rehearsing bows by the escalators, and a security guard who has twice found the panel's cover loose.

Main Atrium.description: A four-story glass atrium in the middle of the mall, ringed by balconies and crossed by escalators, with a fountain and a giant screen at floor level and a skylight that lets the afternoon sun fall across the tiles. Weekend events happen here: product launches, school band shows, seasonal markets and now and then a rookie hero signing autographs at a folding table. It is the default meeting point, so friends wait by the fountain while mall security watches from the second-floor railing, and on Saturday afternoons the crowd around the fountain is so thick that people move shoulder to shoulder. Coins glitter on the fountain floor, and the screen alternates ads with hero news and the mall's own announcements. Sound carries upward, and anything said by the fountain can be heard on the balconies above. Escalators lead up to the Fashion Floors, and a wide passage on the ground floor opens into the Food Court.

Food Court.description: A broad hall of food counters around rows of shared tables: ramen, curry, crepes, takoyaki, burgers and a bakery. Several counters serve large portions, and one section has sturdy chairs and wide tables for customers with big or heavy heteromorph bodies. Lunch brings office workers and parents with toddlers; after classes, students hold the corner tables for hours over a single drink, and on weekends every seat is taken by noon. Part-timers in paper hats work the counters in short shifts, and the ramen counter is always hiring. Regulars keep their own tables, and a pair of odd ones, a white-haired man in a tailcoat and a small woman with pink pigtails and a laptop, have claimed the far corner most weekday afternoons. Trays clatter, order buzzers go off, and the smell of sweet batter from the crepe stand reaches the escalators. The hall opens back onto the Main Atrium.

Fashion Floors.description: Two upper floors of clothing stores, from cheap chains to brand boutiques, with fitting rooms and a tailor who alters clothes for tails, wings, extra arms and other heteromorph builds while the customer waits. Athletic and training-wear shops are popular with hero students, and one of them keeps a wall of shoes reinforced for Quirks that are hard on footwear. Weekday afternoons are quiet, with clerks folding stock; on weekends, lines form at the fitting rooms and friends trade opinions from the benches outside. Staff are trained to treat every body type the same, and customers notice when they do not. The music changes every few meters, the lighting is brighter here than anywhere else in the mall, and the tailor's shop smells of steam from the pressing iron. From the railing, shoppers can look straight down into the Main Atrium, and the escalators lead back down to it.

Cinema Complex.description: A ten-screen cinema on the mall's top floor, one last escalator above the Fashion Floors, entered through a dim lobby of carpet, poster lightboxes and a concession counter selling popcorn in salt, caramel and soy-butter. Tickets come from touch-screen machines, about 1,900 yen for an adult and cheaper on the first day of each month; the screens show hero action films, anime, romances and imports, and this spring a documentary on All Might's career sells out on weekends. Weekday mornings are near empty; after classes, students fill the cheap seats; weekends are packed with families and couples, and the last show lets out just before the mall locks its doors at nine. One screen has wide reinforced seats and open space at the front for heteromorph viewers, and the ushers ask winged guests to keep their wings folded so the row behind can see. Phones off, no talking and no glowing Quirks during the film: an usher with a flashlight enforces all three. The lobby smells of butter and carpet cleaner, and a trailer reel loops over the counter. The escalator leads down to the Fashion Floors, and a stairway climbs to the Rooftop Amusement Deck.

Bookstore and Manga Floor.description: A big chain bookstore filling half of the mall's second floor off the atrium balcony, with novels, cookbooks and study books at the front and the whole back half given over to manga, light novels and hero magazines. A wide table holds each week's new manga in shrink-wrapped stacks, and the hero section sells Hero Billboard Chart guides, agency yearbooks, hero-law workbooks and the thick prep manuals for U.A.'s entrance exam, which sell all year. Retirees browse the newspapers in the mornings; after classes, students stand reading in the manga aisles until a clerk moves them along; weekends bring families buying picture books and fans lining up for hero magazine special issues. Staff write hand-lettered recommendation cards for the shelves, and one clerk's cards on hero biographies are so long they curl. A notice by the register asks customers to keep Quirks off the shelves since a telekinetic browser pulled a whole row down. It smells of paper and of coffee from the small counter at the back. The doors open onto the Main Atrium's balcony and its escalators, and a wide aisle runs across to the Electronics Floor.

Electronics Floor.description: The other half of the mall's second floor, a bright electronics store under rows of white light: walls of televisions all showing the same hero news, aisles of phones, laptops, cameras, rice cookers and massage chairs, and a games corner of demo consoles. Staff in matching polo shirts push warranties and point cards, and a time-sale jingle plays every half hour. A counter at the back repairs phones and replaces cracked screens while you wait, about 8,000 yen for most models; hero students bring in phones broken in training more often than they admit, and the repair tech has learned not to ask. A shelf of Quirk-adapted goods is the floor's specialty: heat-proof phone cases, oversized keyboards, claw-friendly touch gloves and headphones for unusual ears. Retirees try the massage chairs every weekday morning; after classes, students crowd the game demos; weekends bring families comparing washing machines. When a live hero incident breaks in, every screen cuts to it and the floor stops to watch. It smells of new plastic and cardboard. Escalators lead down to the Main Atrium, and an aisle runs across to the Bookstore and Manga Floor.

Rooftop Amusement Deck.description: An open-air roof deck above the cinema, fenced with high safety netting, where the mall keeps an old-fashioned rooftop amusement corner: a small Ferris wheel of eight gondolas, coin-operated ride-on animals and hero cars, a batting cage and a stand selling soft-serve and grilled corn. The wheel costs 300 yen and, on a clear day, shows the whole city from the top: Suruga Bay to the southwest, Mount Fuji to the north and the hills of U.A.'s campus far to the northeast. Parents bring toddlers on weekday mornings; after classes, students hit balls in the batting cage and take photos in the gondolas; on weekends, families line up for the wheel, and at dusk couples ride it for the view as the city lights come on. The deck closes with the mall at nine, earlier in rain or high wind, and an attendant in a windbreaker runs the wheel. A sign at the batting cage says in large letters that Quirks may not be used on the balls, and any hit that tears the net ends the session. The wind is steady, the netting hums, and the wheel's motor whirs between the jingles. Stairs lead down to the Cinema Complex, and an elevator runs to the Fashion Floors.

Dagobah Municipal Beach Park.name: Dagobah Municipal Beach Park
Dagobah Municipal Beach Park.basicInfo: A public beach and seawall park on Suruga Bay at Musutafu's southwest edge, about 5 km southwest of the station by local bus; Kiyashi Shopping Mall is about 3 km inland and Musutafu General Hospital about 3 km to the north. Mount Fuji rises to the north-northwest on clear days, and the Izu Peninsula's hills stand across the water to the south. For years it was an illegal dumping ground: the tide carried trash in, and people left broken appliances, scrap metal and even cars. Over ten months a young man cleared it by hand, running here every day, often before dawn, and hauling out the junk piece by piece until the sand showed again; the city has since reopened it. The parks department runs it with one part-time warden. The park is public and never closes, though the restrooms are locked at night and there is no lifeguard. Dawn brings joggers, dog walkers and anglers on the seawall; families and students come on weekends; evenings belong to couples and runners. Public Quirk use is banned here as anywhere else, and a sign by the steps says so in large letters. A player can train on the sand, fish, meet someone away from the city, or rest after a bad week. Waves slap against the concrete wave-breakers, gulls call overhead, and the air smells of salt and seaweed. Older residents still call it the dump out of habit, and then look at the clean sand and correct themselves.
Dagobah Municipal Beach Park.hiddenInfo: Regulars know the young man who cleared the beach was Izuku Midoriya, now a U.A. first-year, who ran here every day from his mother's apartment about 6.5 km east; he never told anyone why he did it, and the anglers who watched him drag a refrigerator across the sand still argue about whether he was training, punishing himself or just strange. Dumping has started again: a few nights a week, a small truck backs up to the west end and leaves bags of construction waste and old appliances. It comes after midnight on weeknights, lights off for the last stretch, and the driver works fast and alone. The warden suspects a renovation contractor avoiding disposal fees, because the dumped boards carry stamped lot numbers from a building supplier, but she has no camera and no authority beyond filing a report, and the parks office has not answered her last two. A few regulars are angry enough to stake it out themselves; a retired angler and two of the dawn joggers have talked about blocking the truck in, and one of the joggers has a strength Quirk he has never used in public. If they try it without a hero or the police, someone is likely to get hurt or arrested for unlicensed Quirk use. The city would like the story of the beach's cleanup told again, and a reporter from a local paper has been asking the regulars who the young man was.

Shoreline.description: A long curve of sand between the seawall and the water, clean now except for what the tide brings in each night: driftwood, plastic bottles, tangled fishing line and the odd sandal. At low tide the wet sand stretches far out and joggers run along its firm edge; at high tide the waves reach the concrete wave-breakers stacked at each end, where crabs scuttle into the gaps. In the early morning a few people still walk the line with trash bags out of habit, and on weekends families set up umbrellas while little ones dig and squeal at the cold water. Away from the water the sand is soft and deep, which makes running or carrying anything across it hard work, and the dents of old dragging marks still show near the west end. At dusk the light turns gold over the bay and the Izu hills go dark across the water. Steps in the seawall lead up to the Seawall Promenade.

Seawall Promenade.description: A broad concrete walk along the top of the seawall, with steps down to the sand, benches, vending machines, public restrooms, a small parking lot and the bus stop back to town. Anglers line the railing at dawn with rods and coolers and trade news of what is biting; office workers eat lunch here on warm days; at dusk, couples and runners take over, and someone always stops to photograph Fuji when the sky is clear. The warden's hut sits by the main steps, usually closed, with a notice board of park rules and a faded poster about illegal dumping. The sea wind never stops, so hats blow off and the benches stay salty to the touch. After dark the vending machines are the only light along the wall, and the west end of the parking lot, where the lights have failed, is pitch black. Steps lead down onto the Shoreline.

Beach Snack Shack.description: A weathered wooden snack shack at the foot of the main steps, where the Seawall Promenade meets the sand, with a corrugated roof, a roll-up shutter, a hand-painted menu board and a few plastic tables under faded umbrellas. It sells grilled squid, yakisoba from a flat griddle, shaved ice and canned drinks, most of it 300 to 600 yen. An older couple reopened it the season the beach came back, after years with the shutter rusted shut; in spring it opens only on weekends and warm afternoons, and from July it runs every day from early morning to sunset. Anglers buy hot canned coffee and swap news of what is biting before sunrise; on weekends families crowd the tables with sandy feet and wet towels. The couple will tell anyone who asks how the beach used to look, and keep a photo of the old junk heaps taped inside the shutter beside a newer one of clean sand. A sign asks customers to carry their trash home, since this beach has had enough of it. The griddle hisses, gulls wait on the roof for dropped squid, and soy sauce and salt mix in the wind. The steps lead up to the Seawall Promenade, and the Shoreline begins at the tables.

Midoriya Residence.name: Midoriya Residence
Midoriya Residence.basicInfo: A modest apartment in a mid-rise building in a quiet residential block about 3.5 km southeast of Musutafu Station and about 5 km south of U.A. Academy's main campus; the Bakugo house is 1.3 km east and Aldera High School under 2.5 km away. Inko Midoriya lives here. Her son Izuku, a U.A. first-year, lives in the academy's dorms and comes home on weekends; his father, Hisashi, works overseas and is rarely home. Inko is warm, anxious and a good cook, and katsudon is the family favorite, made for any big day. The apartment is small and tidy: a narrow entry with shoes lined up, a kitchen and dining table, a living room where the TV is usually on hero news, and Izuku's old bedroom, still crowded with All Might posters and figures and shelves of handwritten hero-analysis notebooks. Family photos cover one wall, most of them of Izuku in All Might shirts. It is a private home: visitors ring the intercom at the building's entrance and come up only if Inko lets them in, and she rarely turns away anyone who says they know her son. Weekday evenings she is home after errands and phones her son; on weekends, when Izuku comes back, the kitchen runs all day. A player can visit, share a meal, bring news from U.A., or find Izuku on a weekend home. The hallway smells of whatever Inko is cooking, and the neighbors' doors open a crack whenever she raises her voice in joy or worry.
Midoriya Residence.hiddenInfo: Inko calls Izuku in the dorms every evening, and he keeps the calls short. For ten months before the entrance exam he ran to Dagobah Municipal Beach Park, about 6.5 km west, every day, often before dawn, and came home exhausted and bruised, so she keeps a first-aid kit by the door and watches the news for incidents near the academy. She knows his Quirk came late and is strong, and she suspects he plays down every injury; she has started noting the days his voice sounds strained on the phone, and she is working up the nerve to call the academy herself and ask what his power does to his body. Under all of it is a regret she has never told anyone: years ago, when he was small and no Quirk had come, he asked whether he could be a hero like All Might, and she held him and said she was sorry instead of yes. She backs his dream now partly to make up for that day. His notebooks on pro heroes' Quirks, tactics and weak points still fill a shelf; anyone who read them would know more about local heroes than most villains do, and the apartment door has an ordinary lock. This weekend she has bought pork for katsudon without knowing whether he will come, and if a visitor seems to know how he is really doing, she will ask, and she will not let them leave without an answer.

Midoriya Living Room.description: The main room of the Midoriya apartment, reached through a narrow entry where shoes stand in a tidy row and a first-aid kit waits on the shoe cabinet by the door. It is small and warm: a low sofa with crocheted cushions, a low table with a bowl of mandarins, a TV that is usually on hero news, and a window onto the quiet residential block below. Family photos cover one wall, most of them of Izuku in All Might shirts at every size, from a toddler in a towel cape to a first-year in his U.A. uniform. Visitors ring the intercom at the building's entrance and come up only when Inko lets them in, and she rarely turns away anyone who knows her son. On weekday evenings she sits here with the phone after her errands and calls the dorms; on weekends, when Izuku is home, the table fills with his notebooks and the TV stays on the rankings. Inko's Quirk draws small objects to her hand, so the remote, a teacup or a tissue box slides across the table whenever she reaches for it, startling first-time guests. The air smells of whatever she is cooking. The Midoriya Kitchen opens off one side and Izuku's Old Bedroom is down the short hall.

Izuku's Old Bedroom.description: A small bedroom at the end of the short hall, left as Izuku had it when he moved into U.A.'s dorms: an All Might shrine from floor to ceiling. Posters of All Might cover the walls and the ceiling above the bed, the bedspread and pillow carry his grin, an All Might clock ticks on the desk beside an All Might lamp, and shelves of figures in every pose and every era's costume line the room, with a few pale gaps where the favorites went with him to the dorm. The desk under the window holds an old computer, a cup of chewed pens and a row of handwritten hero-analysis notebooks, numbered on the spines and packed in small, cramped writing with sketches of pro heroes, their Quirks, tactics and weak points, a few of them singed or water-stained at the edges. Inko dusts the room once a week and moves nothing. On weekends home Izuku sleeps here and stays up muttering over fresh notebook pages; a guest let in on a weekday finds it very quiet, every poster smile turned toward the door. The room smells faintly of paper and the laundry soap on the sheets. The only way out is back down the hall to the Midoriya Living Room.

Midoriya Kitchen.description: A narrow galley kitchen with a small dining table pushed against the wall at one end and four chairs, though only one is used on most weeknights. The counters are crowded but orderly: a rice cooker, a deep pan that comes out mainly for katsudon, a wooden rack of bowls, a cutting board worn pale in the middle, and a calendar on the refrigerator with U.A.'s weekends circled and a magnet holding a newspaper clipping about the academy's new faculty. Inko is a good cook, and this is where she shows it: miso soup and grilled fish on ordinary days, and katsudon, the family favorite, for any big day, the cutlets spitting in hot oil while onions simmer in sweet broth. On weekday evenings she cooks for one and puts half away; on weekends, when Izuku comes home, the stove runs from breakfast to dinner, and any visitor is sat down and fed before they can say no. A pack of pork waits in the refrigerator this week. The extractor fan rattles, and the smell of frying cutlets carries down the building's hallway, where the neighbors know exactly what it means. The kitchen opens back into the Midoriya Living Room.

Bakugo Residence.name: Bakugo Residence
Bakugo Residence.basicInfo: A two-story detached house on a quiet street of family homes, about 4.5 km east-southeast of the station, 1.3 km east of the Midoriya apartment and about 5 km south-southeast of U.A. Academy's main campus; Aldera High School is under 2 km away and Hero Agency Row about 2 km. Mitsuki and Masaru Bakugo live here. Mitsuki is a designer and Masaru works in fashion, and the house shows it: clean lines, good furniture, a small front garden kept neat and a living room that looks better than the rest of the street. Their son Katsuki, a U.A. first-year, lives in the academy's dorms and comes home some weekends. Mitsuki is loud, blunt and quick to smack her son on the back of the head; Masaru is mild and keeps the peace. When Katsuki is home, he spends little time in the shared rooms, and mother and son shout at each other at full volume; the neighbors stopped noticing years ago. To outsiders the house is polite and welcoming: Mitsuki turns gracious the moment a guest rings the bell, and Masaru makes tea. It is a private home, and visitors come in only when invited. On weekdays both parents work, and the house is quiet until evening. A player can visit, deliver something, or find Katsuki on a weekend home. Katsuki's room upstairs is kept shut, and a shouted warning comes through the door before anyone gets near it.
Bakugo Residence.hiddenInfo: The spring before the entrance exam, Katsuki was taken hostage in a shopping street by a sludge villain until All Might freed him, and he refuses to talk about it; Mitsuki keeps the news clippings in a drawer. The pros at the scene, Death Arms among them, praised him afterward and offered him a sidekick spot, and he never mentions that either. Since U.A.'s acceptance letters arrived, his temper has been worse than usual, and he has not said whether he will come home this weekend. His parents suspect it has to do with Izuku Midoriya, whom he grew up with and has looked down on since childhood, but neither has asked him directly, because asking only starts a fight. Mitsuki has known Inko Midoriya since their sons played together and sees her at the shops; she has started to wonder what Izuku's late Quirk means for her own son's pride, and she half wants to ask Inko over tea. Masaru wants to tell Katsuki that he is proud of him and keeps waiting for a quiet moment that never comes. A visitor who treats Katsuki as a thug or a victim will find Mitsuki's politeness gone at once; one who speaks honestly about him may hear more from her than she has ever said to him.

Bakugo Living Room.description: The main room of the Bakugo house, open-plan and bright, and the best-looking room on the street: pale wood floors, a long low sofa in charcoal fabric, a glass coffee table with design magazines squared at the corners, a large TV and tall windows onto the small front garden. Mitsuki is a designer and Masaru works in fashion, and it shows in the lighting, the framed prints and a dining table where nothing is out of place. A cabinet holds a few photos: the family at the beach, Katsuki scowling in an Aldera uniform, Katsuki scowling over his U.A. acceptance letter. On weekday evenings, once both parents are home, Masaru makes tea and the news plays low; when Katsuki is home on a weekend, he crosses this room as fast as he can, and mother and son trade insults across it at full volume while Masaru asks them both to sit down. Guests see none of that. The moment the bell rings Mitsuki turns gracious, Masaru brings tea and a plate of rice crackers, and the visitor is seated on the good end of the sofa. The stairs to Katsuki's Old Bedroom rise from the back of the room, and the Bakugo Front Entry is through the door at the front.

Katsuki's Old Bedroom.description: A bedroom at the end of the upstairs landing, door shut, left as Katsuki had it when he moved into U.A.'s dorms; nobody goes in uninvited, and Mitsuki opens it only to air it out. Inside it is spare and orderly in a way that surprises people: a made bed, a desk cleared except for a stack of entrance-exam workbooks with every page finished, a set of dumbbells and a rolled exercise mat in the corner, and a shoebox of medals and certificates from school competitions pushed under the bed rather than displayed. One old All Might poster still hangs over the desk, its corners re-taped more than once. The curtains are dark and heavy, and a small scorch mark on the windowsill shows where someone once tested his palms indoors and heard about it for a week. When Katsuki comes home on a weekend, he spends most of his time in here with the door closed, and a shouted warning comes through it before anyone reaches the top of the stairs. Masaru sometimes stands on the landing as if about to knock, then goes back down. The room smells of laundry detergent and, faintly, of something burnt. The stairs lead back down to the Bakugo Living Room.

Bakugo Front Entry.description: The way into the Bakugo house from the street: a low gate in a trimmed hedge, a short path of flat stones across a small, neat front garden with a maple and raked gravel, and a front door of dark wood under a narrow porch light. The intercom by the gate has a camera, and visitors ring and wait; the family lets in only people they know or expect. Inside the door is the genkan, a tiled step-down where shoes come off, with a tall shoe cabinet, a slim umbrella stand, a mirror and a row of guest slippers on the raised floor.
