Both parents leave for work in the morning and come home in the evening, and on weekdays the house sits quiet in between, apart from deliveries left in a box by the step. When Katsuki comes home, his shoes land kicked off sideways, and Mitsuki lines them up again with a remark loud enough for the street. The neighbors on this quiet street of family homes stopped turning their heads at the shouting years ago, and the ward officer who cycles past in the evening only waves. The garden smells of cut grass, and the gravel crunches loudly under every step. Through the front door, the hall leads into the Bakugo Living Room.

Aldera High School.name: Aldera High School
Aldera High School.basicInfo: Aldera High School is an ordinary public school on Musutafu's southeast side, about 5.5 km from the station, under 2.5 km from the Midoriya apartment and under 2 km from the Bakugo house, with concrete classroom blocks, a sports ground, a gym and a courtyard with a koi pond. Most of its graduates go on to ordinary jobs or further study close to home. This year it boasts that two graduates, Izuku Midoriya and Katsuki Bakugo, got into U.A. Academy, a first for the school, and a banner in the entrance hall says so. Classes run from half past eight into the afternoon, and club practice fills the sports ground with shouting until six; the baseball club's bats and the brass band's scales carry for blocks. Students in navy uniforms crowd the convenience store across the road after classes and walk home in loud groups. Visitors sign in at the front office and wear a visitor badge; the gate is closed during classes, and nobody wanders the corridors without a teacher's escort. On weekends the school is closed except for club practice. A player can visit a teacher, talk with current students, watch a club match, or ask about the two famous graduates, and anyone who mentions U.A. will draw a crowd of questions. The halls smell of floor wax and cafeteria curry, and the chime is the same one every school in town uses.
Aldera High School.hiddenInfo: Teachers who ignored years of Katsuki bullying Izuku now take credit for both of them. Former classmates still tell how Katsuki blew up one of Izuku's notebooks and threw it into the koi pond, and how the class laughed when a teacher mentioned that Izuku had applied to U.A. Most of them grew up knowing Izuku as Quirkless, and they gossip about how he got in: a hidden Quirk, a connection, a mistake by the examiners. Nobody here saw his power come in, and nobody can explain it. The principal is now drafting an invitation for both graduates to come back and speak at an assembly, and the homeroom teacher who laughed loudest is the one asked to write it; neither graduate has been asked yet, and either answer would cause a scene. Two of Katsuki's old hangers-on, graduates now, still turn up at the school gate after classes to brag that they know him, trading stories for attention from the current students. They also know exactly what was done to Izuku over the years, and one of them is uneasy about it now that Izuku is at U.A. too; he would talk to someone who caught him alone. The koi pond still has a notebook-sized patch of algae the groundskeeper swears he never cleaned out.

Aldera School Gate.description: The front of Aldera High School: a wide sliding gate of steel bars between concrete pillars carved with the school's name, a short drive to the entrance hall of the main classroom block, and a bicycle shed packed tight along the fence. During classes the gate is rolled shut, and visitors buzz the front office, sign in, wear a visitor badge on a lanyard and wait for a teacher to walk them in. Inside the entrance, rows of shoe lockers face a banner announcing that two graduates, Izuku Midoriya and Katsuki Bakugo, were admitted to U.A. Academy, the first in the school's history. At half past eight a teacher stands at the gate greeting late arrivals by name; after classes navy uniforms pour across the road to the convenience store, where rice balls go for about 150 yen and the hero magazines get read standing up. A few graduates still loiter by the gate after classes, telling current students they know a U.A. first-year. A sign on the pillar says in plain words that Quirk use is forbidden on school grounds. Brass band scales drift from an upper window. Inside, the stairs lead to the Aldera Classroom and on up to the Aldera Rooftop.

Aldera Classroom.description: An ordinary homeroom on the top floor of the classroom block, the room where Izuku Midoriya and Katsuki Bakugo spent their final year: rows of wooden desks, a green chalkboard, a teacher's lectern, a wall of windows over the courtyard and its koi pond, and cubbies along the back wall. Current students fill it from half past eight with homeroom and lessons until the afternoon; at lunch they push desks together over bento boxes and convenience-store bread, and after the last chime the cleaning rota sweeps the floor before club practice. The teachers who taught both famous graduates still teach here and tell the story of the U.A. admissions to every new class, each version kinder to themselves than the last. One old desk by the window has a faint scorch mark the custodian has never managed to sand out, and whoever sits there now gets asked about it. A printed notice by the door reminds everyone that using a Quirk in class means a call home. Chalk dust, floor wax and the crack of the baseball club's bats through the open windows fill the room. The corridor leads down to the Aldera School Gate and up the stairs to the Aldera Rooftop.

Aldera Rooftop.description: The flat roof of Aldera's classroom block, reached through a steel door at the top of the stairs: a wide stretch of weathered concrete, a tall chain-link fence around the edge, water tanks and air-conditioning units along one side, and a few benches someone dragged up years ago. The door is unlocked at lunch and after classes until club practice ends, and a duty teacher checks it at six; the rule painted on the inside of the door says no climbing the fence and no Quirks. At lunch, students who want space from their classmates eat up here in twos and threes, and after classes it belongs to friends with secrets, the occasional couple and anyone avoiding someone downstairs. From the fence the koi pond in the courtyard looks like a small green coin, and on a clear day the forested hills of U.A. Academy show to the north beyond Musutafu's rooftops, which some current students stare at longer than they would admit. The wind is always stronger up here than below and rattles the fence, and crows squabble over dropped bread crusts on the water tanks. The steel door leads back down to the Aldera Classroom and on to the Aldera School Gate.

Musutafu Police Headquarters.name: Musutafu Police Headquarters
Musutafu Police Headquarters.basicInfo: The city's main police station, a plain six-story concrete building on Musutafu's northwestern edge, about 3.5 km northwest of the station, run by the prefectural police. It handles patrols, investigations, custody and the paperwork behind every arrest a hero makes in the city: officers investigate and hold suspects, while violent Quirk crime is left to licensed heroes, who hand captured villains over here. The front desk is open around the clock to anyone; the upper floors are staff only, and visitors go up only with an officer as escort. Patrol cars leave from the yard at the back, and a city bus stop sits out front. Detective Naomasa Tsukauchi, whose Quirk tells him when someone is lying, works major cases from here and knows many pros personally; Sansa Tamakawa, a cat-headed officer, is often at his side. Shifts change at eight in the morning and eight at night, and the night shift is thin. The building also holds the traffic division, the community affairs office that runs neighborhood police boxes across the city, and a records room for Quirk registrations. Officers do not use their Quirks as weapons on duty, and heroes who bring a villain in give a statement before they leave. A player can report a crime, give a statement, hand over a captured villain, help an investigation, or visit someone in custody. Phones ring, printers run, and the lobby smells of floor wax and vending-machine coffee.
Musutafu Police Headquarters.hiddenInfo: The detectives' office always has more files than time, and Tsukauchi keeps his own short list of cases he will not let go. Morale on the night shift is low; officers do the paperwork while heroes collect the credit and the pay for each arrest, and some resent it. The holding cells are built for ordinary prisoners. Anyone with a strong or dangerous Quirk is supposed to be moved to a secure facility within a day, and a weekend with a strong Quirk user in the basement is when things go wrong. Tsukauchi's Lie Detector tells him only that he has heard a lie, never what the truth is, and the officers who work with him know a short pause before his next question means he caught one. When something touches U.A. Academy, Principal Nezu calls Tsukauchi first, and Tsukauchi calls All Might.

Front Desk.description: The ground-floor lobby: a long counter behind scratched acrylic panels, rows of plastic chairs, wanted posters, Quirk-registration forms and a number-ticket machine. Desk officers take lost-and-found reports, traffic complaints, crime reports and walk-ins who just want to talk to someone, and Sansa Tamakawa takes statements here between cases, writing everything down. Heroes bring captured villains through the side door and sign them over here; the stairs up to the Detectives' Office and down to the Holding Cells are behind a locked door at the end of the counter. Mornings are busy with paperwork; nights bring drunks, worried parents and the occasional hero still in costume. A wide chair at one end is built for larger heteromorph visitors. Raised voices get exactly one warning.

Detectives' Office.description: An open-plan room on the third floor with desks pushed together in pairs, whiteboards covered in photos and arrows, filing cabinets and a coffee machine nobody cleans. Detectives work here from morning until late, interviewing witnesses in two small side rooms and calling hero agencies for statements. Tsukauchi's desk sits by the window, unusually tidy, with a single folder he keeps closed when visitors are near. Visitors come up only with an escort, by the stairs from the Front Desk. Case files on Quirk crimes are stacked by date, the oldest on top of the cabinets in boxes, and a wall map of Musutafu bristles with pins. The evening shift orders noodles from the same shop every night. The phones never stop ringing, and nobody lies to Tsukauchi twice.

Holding Cells.description: A basement corridor of short-term cells with steel doors, bare benches and cameras in every corner, plus one reinforced cell lined with thick steel for detainees with strong Quirks. Suspects wait here for questioning, transfer or release, usually overnight, and each is logged in and out by the minute. Two officers watch the monitors at all times, and detainees with dangerous Quirks wear heavy restraint cuffs. Belongings go into numbered plastic trays in a locker by the stairs and come back only on release. Visits happen through a window at the end of the corridor, by appointment from the Front Desk upstairs, and they end the moment anyone raises a voice. The lights stay on all night, the air smells of disinfectant, and every cough echoes down the corridor.

Musutafu General Hospital.name: Musutafu General Hospital
Musutafu General Hospital.basicInfo: The city's main hospital, about 5 km west of the station and about 3 km north of Dagobah Municipal Beach Park: a large white complex with an ambulance bay, outpatient clinics and several hundred beds. Its staff know Quirk injuries well: burns, fractures, toxins, mutations gone wrong, and the damage people do to themselves by pushing a Quirk too far. The hospital is public and open to anyone; the wards keep visiting hours from one to eight, and the emergency ward never closes. Visitors sign in at each ward's nurses' station, and a few long-term private rooms on the upper floors admit only visitors on the patient's own list. Doctors and nurses work long rotating shifts, some with Quirks that help them diagnose or ease pain, though none heals the way U.A.'s Recovery Girl does; serious cases from the academy come here when her care is not enough. Heroes come in with injured victims or for their own treatment, and police officers wait in the corridors to take statements. Ambulances arrive from across the city, and the hospital bus stop has its own line to the station. A player can be treated, recover, visit someone, work as an orderly or volunteer, or ask the staff about recent injuries. Monitors beep, carts squeak on polished floors, and everything smells of disinfectant. The lobby has a coffee stand, a florist and a gift shop selling hero-themed get-well cards, and the elevators are always slow.
Musutafu General Hospital.hiddenInfo: The emergency ward is short of night staff, and after midnight anything less serious than a broken bone waits for hours. In a private room on the third floor, a burglar arrested last week by a local pro is recovering from a broken jaw under police guard. The night officer slips up to the rooftop garden for long breaks, and a man claiming to be the burglar's cousin has called the ward three times to ask about visiting hours and which room he is in. Nobody has told the police, and the triage nurses are too busy to notice who walks in with the evening visitors. The burglar fenced his goods through someone in the station district's back alleys and knows a name he has not given the police. On a quieter upper floor, Rei Todoroki, the wife of the pro hero Endeavor, has lived for years in a private room; few outside the family know she is here or why. Her daughter Fuyumi and her son Natsuo visit and bring her news, including that her youngest, Shoto Todoroki, got into U.A. on recommendation, but Shoto has not come in years. The staff keep her name off the ward board and turn away anyone not on the family's list, and they know that the mention of her husband frightens her and shuts her down for days. She is gentle, keeps to her window, and treasures small everyday news about her family.

Emergency Ward.description: The ground-floor emergency department: an ambulance bay under a concrete canopy, a triage desk, curtained bays, a burn treatment room and two trauma rooms fitted with restraints for patients who lose control of their Quirks. It is busiest at night and after big incidents, when heroes and paramedics bring the injured in together and police officers wait by the doors for statements. Triage nurses sort patients by colored tags, and nobody skips the line for being famous; a pro in costume with a cut arm waits like everyone else. The waiting room has plastic chairs, a vending machine that eats coins and a TV that is always on, and families sit there for hours without news. The sliding doors open every few minutes to sirens and a blast of outside air. Elevators and a staff corridor lead up to the Patient Rooms.

Patient Rooms.description: Several floors of wards with six-bed shared rooms and a few private rooms, each floor run from a central nurses' station where visitors sign in. Patients recover here from surgery, accidents and Quirk injuries; families visit from one to eight with fruit and clean clothes, and injured heroes sometimes check in under a false name to avoid fans. The upper floors are quieter, with a few long-term private rooms whose doors are hung with small personal touches, a pressed flower or a grandchild's drawing, and whose visitors are checked against a list. Nights are quiet except for call buttons and the nurses' rounds. Curtains are the only privacy in the shared rooms, so everyone hears everyone else's phone calls. The corridors smell of disinfectant and canned soup. Elevators lead down to the Emergency Ward and up to the Rooftop Garden.

Rooftop Garden.description: A rooftop terrace with planters, benches and a covered rest area, open to patients and visitors from morning until dusk. Patients in wheelchairs sit in the sun with their families, staff eat lunch out of sight of the wards, and people come up to make calls they do not want overheard. On clear days Mount Fuji rises to the north-northwest, and U.A.'s foothill campus shows to the north-northeast, with Suruga Bay glinting to the south. The planters are tended by a volunteer group of retired patients, who grow herbs, marigolds and a stubborn tomato vine. Smoking is banned and happens anyway, in the corner behind the water tanks, where a police officer on night guard duty has been seen more often than he should be. Wind chimes hang from the rest-area roof and ring in every breeze. A stairwell and elevator lead back down to the Patient Rooms.

Hero Agency Row.name: Hero Agency Row
Hero Agency Row.basicInfo: A short street in the riverside blocks about 4 km east of the station where several small hero agencies share one converted office block and a ground-floor garage; the Bakugo house is about 2 km away and the residential blocks of the southeast side close by. None of their pros ranks high on the Hero Billboard Chart; they handle the city's everyday calls: traffic accidents, fires, stray Quirk fights, missing persons and bag snatchers. Each agency is a licensed business with one or two pros, a few sidekicks and an office manager. They split the rent, the garage and a shared ready room, and they compete for every incident, since a hero's pay depends on the incidents they resolve. The block's pros include the rising capture specialist Kamui Woods and the rookie giant Mount Lady, who bicker in public and still work side by side, the street brawler Death Arms and the rescue specialist Backdraft, who share the garage and many patrols, the soft-spoken martial artist Gunhead, and the stern, four-armed Fourth Kind. Patrol shifts cover the morning rush, school drop-off, the evening and the night. This is where a newly licensed hero signs a first sidekick contract. The front door is open during office hours for the public and job applicants; upstairs offices are by appointment, and the garage and ready room are for agency staff only. A player can apply for work, take a patrol shift, train in the ready room, get gear fixed, or pick up calls from the dispatch radio. Radios crackle with police traffic all day, and someone is always arguing about the shift schedule.
Hero Agency Row.hiddenInfo: The agencies here run on thin margins. Sidekicks from bigger agencies have started patrolling the station district and taking calls the local pros counted on, and one agency is two months behind on rent; its office manager has started taking calls on her personal phone so the landlord cannot reach her. Kiyashi Shopping Mall's management is quietly taking bids for a paid security contract, and two of the agencies are competing hard for it; the loser may have to close. Mount Lady wants it for the crowds and the cameras, while the agency behind on rent needs it to survive, and the two offices have stopped speaking in the stairwell. Since the Hero Killer began attacking lone pros in other cities, the agencies send patrols out in pairs, which halves their coverage, and Fourth Kind openly calls the rule cowardly while following it. The police want arrest reports filed faster, and the office managers are buried in paperwork. Gunhead has started teaching an unofficial capture-hold class in the ready room on slow afternoons, and sidekicks from every office come, which is the only thing they do together. A newcomer who can take a patrol shift without complaint, file a clean report and keep out of the rent fight would be hired almost anywhere on the block.

Agency Offices.description: The second and third floors of the block, split into small offices behind frosted-glass doors along a narrow hall with a squeaky floor. Each has an agency logo, a front desk, a few work desks, a dispatch radio and a wall map of Musutafu with pins for active calls. Office managers take calls from the public and the police, schedule patrols, and handle contracts and invoices; a pro back from patrol writes reports here with one hand on the radio volume. Visitors and job applicants wait on folding chairs in the hall under framed newspaper clippings of past captures, and each office makes sure its own clippings hang at eye level. Phones and radios run nonstop, and every office keeps its door shut to the others. Stairs lead down to the shared Ready Room at the back of the ground floor and to the Patrol Garage.

Ready Room.description: A shared room at the back of the ground floor with lockers, benches, a whiteboard of patrol routes and shifts, a kitchenette, and a few mats and weights for training. Pros and sidekicks from every agency change here before and after patrols and swap news about the night's calls, and on slow afternoons the mats are pushed together for practice holds and throws. It is the one room where the agencies get along, and the rule is that rivalries stay upstairs; anyone who breaks it washes the mugs for a week. The whiteboard is a battleground of crossed-out names and arrows, and a corner of it is reserved for doodles of Mount Lady's poses that nobody admits drawing. The rice cooker is always half full. It smells of sweat, instant coffee and deodorant. Stairs lead back up to the Agency Offices.

Patrol Garage.description: The ground-floor garage the agencies share: patrol bikes, two small vans, a workbench for basic repairs to costumes and support gear, spare capture tape, first-aid kits, fire extinguishers and a roll-up door onto the street. Patrols leave and return here at shift changes, when the room fills with pros pulling on gear and calling out routes; between shifts, a part-time mechanic keeps the bikes running and listens to the radio. Support gear that needs real repair goes back to its maker. Each agency has its own painted parking spots and its own grudges about who borrowed whose tools. A drying rack by the wall holds a long yellow rescue coat and a red helmet most nights. The roll-up door rattles every time it opens, and oil stains mark every parking spot. A side door and stairs lead up to the Agency Offices.

Agency Row Coffee Stand.description: A one-window coffee stand built into the corner of the agency block beside the garage's roll-up door, with a fold-down counter, three stools and an espresso machine that wheezes before every shot. It opens at six for the morning patrol shift and closes at eight, and its drip coffee, about 250 yen, is the block's fuel: pros and sidekicks buy it in trays of six on the way out, office managers phone in orders and send whoever is newest to fetch them, and job applicants buy one for courage before their interviews upstairs. The owner trades gossip freely and keeps a tab for each agency on a clipboard, and which office has fallen behind on its tab is the worst-kept secret on the street. Kamui Woods takes his coffee black and says little; Mount Lady orders the largest size and photographs it for her followers; Death Arms and Backdraft split a bag of fried bread after night patrol, and Gunhead always remembers the owner's name. A police scanner murmurs beside the cups, and the owner turns it up whenever a call comes from the district. It smells of burnt sugar and garage oil. Its counter faces the street beside the Patrol Garage.

Endeavor Hero Agency.name: Endeavor Hero Agency
Endeavor Hero Agency.basicInfo: The agency of Endeavor (Enji Todoroki), the Flame Hero and the Number Two hero at the start of the year, who has resolved more incidents than any hero in Japanese history. It fills a glass tower with his flame emblem on the roof, about 6 km west of Tokyo Station by subway and about 3.5 km from both the Commission Headquarters and the scramble crossing of Central Tokyo Streets. The agency runs on volume: dozens of sidekicks, Burnin, Kido and Onima among them, work shifts that hand over at 6 a.m. and 6 p.m., an operations floor tracks every incident in the city in real time, and teams roll out within minutes of a call. Endeavor patrols in person every day, first out and last back. He commutes from his family home, the walled Todoroki estate on the eastern rise above Musutafu, about 85 km southwest, and stays at the office when a case runs late. The street-level lobby is open to the public around the clock; every floor above it needs an agency ID or a visitor pass issued at reception, and Endeavor's own office needs an appointment with him. Hero students intern here only by Endeavor's personal invitation. Players can apply for a sidekick contract (his trial is short and few pass), bring in a tip or a client, coordinate a joint operation, give a statement on an agency case, or train in the gym on a staff pass. Fans wait on the sidewalk for a glimpse of him at shift change, and he does not stop for them; reporters get a sentence or nothing. Inside, staff walk fast, police radio traffic plays on every floor, and nobody lingers in the halls. It is the most effective agency in the country and one of the least loved, and everyone who works here knows both.
Endeavor Hero Agency.hiddenInfo: Endeavor measures everything against All Might, and his staff know a slow week means a cold meeting. The pace burns people out: two sidekicks have quit since the new year, and the night shift is quietly short-handed; Burnin covers the gaps herself and would welcome any capable recruit willing to work nights. Endeavor expects his youngest son, Shoto Todoroki, now a first-year in U.A. Academy's Hero Course, to intern here and one day surpass All Might; senior sidekicks have been told to draft a training plan, though nobody here has heard Shoto agree to any of it, and nobody here asks about Endeavor's family. The news that All Might has joined U.A.'s faculty has made him harder to work for: he reads every report on it and says nothing. The analysts keep an unofficial file on the Hero Killer Stain, who at the start of the year has attacked heroes in several cities and vanished each time. While Stain is at large, Endeavor wants that arrest for this agency and has ordered every lead on Stain brought straight to him, which makes a player with real information very welcome and one who wastes his time very unwelcome. Right now the operations floor is also chasing a run of night-time thefts from delivery depots in the agency's district, done by someone who walks through locked shutters; the police want a joint operation, and the short night shift means Endeavor may lead it himself, which the dispatchers dread. Meanwhile a rival agency has complained to the Commission that Endeavor's teams claim credit for captures they joined late; the complaint sits on a Commission desk, and Endeavor does not know about it yet.

Lobby.description: A double-height lobby of glass and black stone behind the tower's revolving doors, with a reception desk staffed around the clock and security gates behind it that open only to an agency ID or a visitor pass. A wall screen shows the agency's running count of incidents resolved this year, updated as reports come in, beside framed police commendations and the flame emblem cut into the stone. Clients, couriers and police liaisons come and go all day; at shift change, fans crowd the doors hoping to see Endeavor leave on patrol, and security moves them along with practiced politeness. Visitors sign in and wait on hard benches, a receptionist calls each name once, and a soft chime sounds each time the count climbs. Past the gates, an elevator bank and a stairwell lead up to the Operations Floor, where every visitor is escorted and nobody wanders. The air is cool and smells faintly of floor polish and the security desk's coffee.

Operations Floor.description: An open floor of dispatch desks facing a wall of screens: police radio feeds, traffic cameras and a city map with every sidekick team marked live in orange. Dispatchers and analysts work twelve-hour shifts that change at 6 a.m. and 6 p.m.; sidekicks report here before and after each patrol and file their incident reports before they go home. Burnin and the other senior sidekicks take their assignments at the map table, and the next team out waits by the elevators down to the Lobby. Phones are answered within three rings, idle talk is not allowed, and the radio traffic never stops. A door at the back opens on the stairs to the Training Gym; a private elevator rises to Endeavor's Office, and when it chimes the whole floor straightens. Whiteboards list open cases and the night shift's empty slots, the coffee machine is never off, and the air smells of toner and burnt grounds.

Training Gym.description: A reinforced gym two floors high, lined with heat-resistant panels, with sprinklers in the ceiling and a fenced sparring ring scorched black at the center. Weight racks, a running track around the upper gallery and a row of cold-water showers fill the edges. Sidekicks train here between shifts: weights, sparring, endurance runs and supervised Quirk drills logged on a clipboard by the door, which every user signs. Endeavor trains alone before dawn and uses the ring for new hires' trials, which rarely last a minute; outsiders with a staff pass may train here once he has gone out on patrol. The ventilation roars whenever someone uses a fire Quirk, the air stays hot long after he leaves, and the mats smell of scorched rubber. A board by the door posts the fastest endurance times, and sidekicks who slip down it hear about it. The stairwell leads back up to the Operations Floor.

Endeavor's Office.description: A top-floor corner office with floor-to-ceiling windows over the city, a steel desk, two hard chairs for visitors and almost nothing personal. The one thing on the walls is a framed print of the latest Hero Billboard Chart, hung where Endeavor sees the Number One name from his desk. He reads reports here late into the night and sees senior sidekicks, police commanders and partner agencies by appointment, booked in short blocks. Staff knock once and wait, and nobody sits until he tells them to. A cot folds out of a cabinet for nights when a case runs late, and the heat he gives off keeps the room warmer than the floors below, whatever the thermostat says. The only way in is the private elevator from the Operations Floor, which needs his clearance. Meetings here are short; he asks for results, not reasons, and a visitor who answers a question with an excuse is shown out.

Todoroki Estate.name: Todoroki Estate
Todoroki Estate.basicInfo: A large traditional Japanese house behind a long wall in the hills on Musutafu's eastern edge, about 9 km east-northeast of the station and about 6.5 km east of U.A. Academy's main campus, at the end of a quiet residential road on the wooded rise. It belongs to Enji Todoroki, the pro hero Endeavor, Number Two on the Hero Billboard Chart at the start of the year; his agency is in Tokyo, about 85 km northeast, and he spends many nights there. His youngest son, Shoto, a U.A. first-year, lives in the academy's dorms and comes home some weekends. His daughter Fuyumi, an elementary school teacher, lives here and keeps the house running, and her brother Natsuo, a student who lives elsewhere, comes for family meals and leaves early. The estate has tatami rooms along wooden corridors, a private dojo and a walled garden with a pond. The wooden front gate stays shut and has an intercom; visitors come by invitation, and Fuyumi answers it far more often than anyone else. When Endeavor is in the news, reporters park along the wall outside and get nothing. A player can visit Fuyumi, find Shoto on a weekend home, train in the dojo with permission, or try to see Endeavor. Weekday mornings Fuyumi leaves early for school, and evenings are when the house has people in it. The house is very quiet: floorboards creak, and the garden water runs all day.
Todoroki Estate.hiddenInfo: The family is not well. Endeavor expects Shoto to outshine every rival at U.A. and says so whenever they are both home; Shoto comes back only when Fuyumi asks and spends those weekends alone in the dojo. Fuyumi keeps trying to arrange family dinners, and Natsuo will not stay in a room with his father for long. Rei Todoroki, Shoto's mother, has lived in a hospital for years, ever since she scalded the left side of young Shoto's face with boiling water; the scar remains, and Shoto has never visited her. He blames his father, who married Rei for her ice Quirk and drove him through brutal training in the dojo to make him an heir who could surpass All Might. Shoto has sworn to become a hero with his mother's ice alone and refuses to use his fire in a fight. Right now Fuyumi is planning the first family dinner since Shoto moved into Heights Alliance, for this coming Saturday: she has messaged Shoto twice and has no answer yet, Natsuo has said he will come only if their father is not there, and Endeavor's office has told her he may be home that night. In a back room a family altar holds the photograph of the eldest son, mourned as dead since Shoto was very small, and nobody speaks of him at the table.

Main House.description: The main building: sliding paper doors, tatami rooms along a polished wooden corridor, a formal room for guests, a family dining room and a modern kitchen that Fuyumi runs. Shoto's room stays spare and neat between his weekend visits. Mornings and evenings are when the family crosses paths; when Endeavor is home, the house goes quieter still and meals are short. Fuyumi cooks for whoever comes, labels leftovers for her brothers and keeps the kitchen radio low. Endeavor's study at the end of the corridor stays shut when he is away, and nobody goes in. A covered walkway leads to the Dojo, and the veranda doors open onto the Garden. Shoes come off at the entrance, and Fuyumi expects guests to greet her before going anywhere else.

Dojo.description: A separate wooden training hall across a covered walkway from the Main House, with a polished floor, a weapons rack, a fire extinguisher at each door and faint scorch marks on the walls. Endeavor trained Shoto here hard from early childhood, and Shoto still trains here alone on the weekends he comes home. When Endeavor is home, he uses it late at night, and the heat from his sessions lingers in the boards until morning. A row of worn practice mats is stacked by the wall, and the deepest scorch marks date from Shoto's childhood. The rest of the family does not come in, and Fuyumi sweeps the walkway but not the floor. Guests train here only with the family's permission. The air is colder than in the rest of the house, and a thin frost sometimes covers the floor after Shoto's sessions.

Garden.description: A walled traditional garden of raked gravel, stone lanterns, maples, a pond and a small arched bridge, kept by a gardener who comes once a week. When they were small, Fuyumi and Natsuo played here while their father kept Shoto in the dojo, within sight of the window. Now family members come here to avoid each other, and Natsuo spends most of his visits on the bench by the pond, out of his father's way, with his phone and a canned coffee. In autumn the maples turn red and Fuyumi rakes the leaves off the gravel herself before the gardener can. The veranda leads back into the Main House. Koi rise for anyone who stands on the bridge long enough. The pond's inflow runs day and night, and in April the maples are just coming into leaf.

Hero Public Safety Commission Headquarte.name: Hero Public Safety Commission Headquarters
Hero Public Safety Commission Headquarte.basicInfo: The headquarters of the Hero Public Safety Commission, the government body that licenses every hero in Japan, registers agencies and sidekick contracts, coordinates heroes with the police, runs the hero license exams and compiles the Hero Billboard Chart JP. It is a gray stone-and-glass tower in the government district, about 3 km west-southwest of Tokyo Station by subway and about 3.5 km from both the Endeavor and Best Jeanist agencies, among ministries and police offices with flags out front. The Commission also owns the Hero Billboard Chart Hall, about 4.5 km to the east, and leases Takoba Municipal Stadium on the Yokohama side for its Provisional Hero License Exam. The lobby and licensing counters are open to the public on weekdays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., through security gates and a bag scanner; the upper floors need a Commission badge or an appointment, and the top floor needs both. Quirk use is banned throughout the building, and the guards enforce it. On weekdays the building fills with licensed heroes, agency managers, school officials, police liaisons, lawyers and reporters; at night only security and the duty office stay, and the duty office calls agency heads in when a crisis needs a joint briefing. Players can renew or check a license, register an agency or a sidekick contract, file incident and property-damage reports, apply for support-gear permits, attend briefings when invited, appeal a reprimand, or apply for Commission jobs. The President of the Commission, known to the public only by her title, sees visitors by appointment, and the license exams are run from the bureau floor by the official Yokumiru Mera. Inside it is quiet and orderly: polished floors, low voices, ticket numbers called over the speakers, and the feeling that every word is being written down.
Hero Public Safety Commission Headquarte.hiddenInfo: The Commission's first loyalty is to public confidence in the hero system, and much of its work is never announced. A media office scores incidents for public risk and settles property-damage claims privately when a hero's name would hurt the system. The exam office, where Yokumiru Mera is buried in paperwork, designs each year's Provisional Hero License Exam, with a first round that lets only about a hundred examinees per venue advance; academies are filing their entries now, and Mera sleeps at his desk more nights than not. The Commission also keeps files on promising students at every hero academy, and the President reads the U.A. files herself. Right now three worries dominate its meetings: rising villain incidents, agencies padding their incident counts, and the Hero Killer Stain, whose crime-scene details it keeps out of the news to deter copycats. A fourth goes unspoken: the President counts All Might's weight in the system as its greatest risk, and his move into teaching at U.A. Academy has her putting questions to Principal Nezu, who handles U.A.'s dealings with the Commission himself and answers them politely and not at all. This week a mid-ranked hero faces a license review in the Briefing Room over a building collapse during a pursuit; the media office has already paid the owners on condition of silence, the outcome was settled before the hearing was scheduled, and a junior clerk in the Licensing Bureau who processed the settlement papers is uneasy enough to talk to the right person.

Lobby.description: A tall, plain atrium of gray stone and glass under the Commission's crest, with security gates, a bag scanner and a long reception counter. Visitors take a numbered ticket and wait in rows of chairs; licensed heroes skip the line through a separate gate by scanning their license. Weekday mornings bring agency managers, lawyers and school officials; after 5 p.m. it empties except for the guards and the duty officer. A recorded voice calls ticket numbers in the same even tone all day, and every door carries a sign banning Quirk use. Ticket holders are sent through to the counters of the Licensing Bureau; badge holders and invited guests take the guarded corridor to the Briefing Room, and nobody else gets past the desk. Credentialed press wait in a roped corner for statements that rarely come. The floor is polished enough to show reflections, and voices drop on their own the moment people step inside.

Licensing Bureau.description: A long floor of numbered counters behind glass, with filing rooms along the back wall. Clerks process hero license renewals, agency registrations, sidekick contracts, support-gear permits and the applications schools file for their students to take the Provisional Hero License Exam. Lines are longest on Monday mornings, and the forms change often enough that veterans bring a spare photo and their own pen. Yokumiru Mera, the official who runs the license exams, works at a cluttered desk in the back under stacks of venue plans and answers questions when he has to, usually after mentioning how little he has slept. Applicants who reach his desk get the hard rules stated plainly and a word of encouragement at the end. The noise is steady: printers, stamps, and clerks asking for one more form. The only way out is back to the Lobby, and a clerk checks every visitor's ticket at the glass door.

Briefing Room.description: A windowless room with an oval table for thirty, wall screens and a secure line to the National Police Agency. The Commission uses it for joint briefings before large operations, for coordination between agencies and police, and for review hearings when a hero's license is in question; a hero under review sits at the narrow end of the table, facing the panel. Meetings run on the hour during the day and through the night during a crisis, when the duty office calls in agency heads and police commanders. Phones go into numbered lockers at the door, the air conditioning keeps the room cold, and nobody speaks until the chair opens the meeting. Minutes are taken on paper and leave the room in a locked case. A guarded corridor runs back to the Lobby; a second, locked door opens on the stairs up to the President's Office, and only those she has summoned use it.

President's Office.description: A wide top-floor office with a view across the government district, a single long desk, a low table for guests and almost no decoration. The President of the Commission, a composed, pragmatic woman known to the public only by her title, meets top-ranked heroes, ministers, police chiefs and academy principals here by appointment only, usually early in the morning. Her secretary's desk guards the only door, at the head of the stairs from the Briefing Room. The room is very quiet; guests are served green tea and are expected to finish their business before it cools. She speaks in policy terms and approval figures, discloses exactly what she has decided to, and ends a meeting by standing. A cabinet behind the desk holds the files she reads personally, and it is locked whenever she is out. Even top heroes straighten up at the door, and no visitor leaves with any paper she has not handed them.

Best Jeanist Hero Agency.name: Best Jeanist Hero Agency
Best Jeanist Hero Agency.basicInfo: The agency of Best Jeanist (Tsunagu Hakamata), the Fiber Hero and the Number Four hero at the start of the year, ranked just behind Hawks, who controls fibers with his Quirk and is as famous for fashion as for arrests; he has won the Best Jeanist award year after year. It fills the lower floors of a sleek building in a shopping district about 6 km south-southwest of Tokyo Station by subway, about 2.5 km from the Tokyo Broadcasting Center, where he is a regular guest, and about 3.5 km from the Commission Headquarters. Its showroom-style street lobby is open to the public in office hours; the floors above are staff-only, reached by a keycard elevator, and visitors go up only with an appointment and an escort. Best Jeanist runs it on discipline and image: sidekicks wear fitted denim uniforms, keep regulation posture and are judged on conduct as much as on results. The agency specializes in clean captures with no collateral damage, binding a villain and every bystander in its path in one motion, which keeps its approval high. Sidekicks patrol in pairs from 7 a.m. to midnight; the boss splits his days between patrol, sponsor meetings and photo shoots, and greets important visitors himself. Players can apply for a sidekick post (the interview includes a dress inspection), train capture technique, have a costume tailored in the agency's workshop, report an incident in its patrol area, or pitch sponsors and fashion media. The lobby is calm: soft light, folded denim on display, and staff who will straighten a visitor's collar without asking.
Best Jeanist Hero Agency.hiddenInfo: Best Jeanist believes talent without discipline is a danger, and he watches every U.A. Sports Festival for gifted, unruly first-years he could straighten out through an internship; he has already told his staff to keep his schedule clear for this year's broadcast. His standards cost him: three sidekicks have resigned after conduct reviews this year, and the agency is short on night patrols, which keeps its incident count below those of the agencies ranked above it. His main jeans sponsor is renegotiating and wants more commercials and fewer patrols; so far he has refused, and the sponsor's people are due in the lobby again this week with a richer offer and a shooting schedule that would take him off the streets for a month. Junior sidekicks complain privately that the inspections never end, and one of them is quietly interviewing at other agencies, but the agency has the lowest rate of bystander injuries in Tokyo, and he knows it. The night gap is real: between midnight and 7 a.m. his district leans on neighboring agencies and the police, and small-time thieves have started to notice. He admits none of this in public. His Quirk needs fibers within reach, so a villain in bare skin or fiber-free gear gives him little to grip, and his sidekicks drill to cover that weakness.

Agency Lobby.description: A bright street-level lobby fitted out as a boutique: pale wood, polished concrete, and glass cases of folded denim and past costumes on headless forms. A reception counter faces the door, with a pressing station behind it where staff steam uniforms before each shift. Sponsors, fashion editors and job applicants wait on a leather bench, and Best Jeanist greets important visitors himself, often with a remark about their posture. Tourists come in to photograph the costumes and buy the agency's licensed jeans at a small counter by the window. The air smells of new indigo cloth and hot steam, and nobody in a wrinkled shirt gets past the counter without a remark. A keycard elevator behind the counter rises to the Training Floor; staff ride it freely, visitors only with an escort. At closing a sidekick lowers the blinds, refolds the display pieces and checks every seam.

Training Floor.description: An upper floor lined with full-length mirrors, padded mats and training dummies wrapped in rope and cloth. Sidekicks run capture drills here every morning before patrol: restraining a struggling partner without bruising them, moving a crowd out of danger, holding posture through fatigue, and pinning a partner dressed in fiber-free gear, the drill everyone dreads. Best Jeanist supervises when he is in, correcting stance and angles in a level voice and reaching for thread metaphors. Bolts of fabric and coils of cable hang on wall racks for the drills, and the agency's tailoring workshop at the far end mends whatever tears. The room is quiet except for the creak of stiff denim and the snap of fabric pulled tight, and anyone caught slouching starts the drill again. The elevator back down to the Agency Lobby is the only way in or out, and a card beside it lists the day's patrol pairs.

Central Tokyo Streets.name: Central Tokyo Streets
Central Tokyo Streets.basicInfo: The capital's busiest shopping and entertainment district, about 7 km west-southwest of Tokyo Station by subway and about 3 km from both the Endeavor Hero Agency and the Commission Headquarters: a scramble crossing under giant screens, an avenue of hero billboards and a row of flagship department stores, with side streets of cafes, karaoke boxes, ramen counters, game centers and hero goods shops around them. It is public ground, patrolled by the Tokyo Metropolitan Police from a corner police box and by the agencies that work the area, and heroes treat it as a stage: an arrest here can reach the evening news within the hour. Top pros pass through often; Mirko lands on Billboard Avenue whenever a fight draws her, and Edgeshot and the armored veteran Yoroi Musha are regular sights along the department-store row. Office workers and shoppers fill it from morning until the last trains; tourists, students and hero fans come on weekends, and the side streets stay busy late into the night. The stores open at 10 a.m. and close at 8 p.m.; the bars and the screens run long after. Using a Quirk in public without a license is illegal here, as everywhere, and street cameras cover every corner. Players can shop, eat, meet contacts, take part-time work in shops and cafes, hand out flyers, patrol as a licensed hero, sell footage of heroes, or chase pickpockets through the crowd. The district's subway station opens straight onto the crossing. The noise never drops: crossing chimes, advertising jingles, shop announcements and thousands of footsteps.
Central Tokyo Streets.hiddenInfo: A fan account posts live sightings of famous heroes around the crossing, and a pickpocket crew uses it to work wherever the heroes are not: three or four of them, one with a Quirk that dulls the feel of a hand in a pocket, working the crowds whenever the account puts a hero at the far end of Billboard Avenue. Rookie heroes pay informants for early tips on incidents near the big screens, and at least one informant has started causing small incidents so they have something to sell: a car alarm here, a staged shoplifting there, and lately a trash-can fire that got closer to a crowd than intended. The ward office wants crowd-control rules after two agencies scuffled over who made an arrest in front of the cameras, and the police blame heroes who play to the crowd. Mirko ignores all of it and goes where the fight is; Edgeshot has noticed the staged incidents and is quietly noting who arrives first at each one. The news that All Might now teaches at U.A. Academy has set off a buying craze: vans selling unlicensed All Might teacher goods park near the crossing and move every hour to stay ahead of the police, and the department stores' licensed counters are losing sales to them. Yoroi Musha's event appearances draw an older crowd who have followed him for decades; the stores pay well for them, and he never takes the helmet off.

Scramble Crossing.description: A huge intersection where every crosswalk opens at once when the lights change, about every two minutes, and thousands cross in all directions. Giant screens on four buildings show news, hero clips and ads, and the subway exits pour more people onto every corner. Commuters own it at rush hour, tourists and fans at midday, and night crowds after dark; police watch from a corner box, and licensed heroes stand on the corners to be seen and photographed. When an incident starts, the crowd turns and raises its phones before anyone runs. A chime sounds each time the signal changes, and street performers and flyer handers fight for the same patch of sidewalk until the police move them on. People meet under the biggest screen, and the line on the stairs of the coffee shop overlooking the crossing never ends. One side opens onto Billboard Avenue, lit by hero faces ten floors high; the other leads to the row of Department Stores.

Billboard Avenue.description: A wide avenue of high-rises covered in hero advertising: All Might's grin across the tallest tower, Endeavor's flames ten floors high, Best Jeanist in denim, Hawks with his crimson wings spread over a sports-drink ad, and newer faces such as Mount Lady and Kamui Woods on fresh boards. Agencies rent the boards by the month, and fans photograph each change. Hero goods shops fill the ground floors, selling figures, trading cards and replica capes, and are busiest on weekends and after classes let out. Mirko is a frequent sight here, dropping onto the median from a rooftop when a fight draws her and leaving the same way. The boards stay lit all night, so the avenue never gets dark, and people waiting at the lights argue about the rankings out loud. Street sweepers come through at dawn, the only hour the sidewalks are empty. The avenue runs back to the Scramble Crossing.

Department Stores.description: A row of flagship department stores, eight to ten floors each, with basement food halls, fashion floors and rooftop gardens. Hero collaboration counters sell licensed goods, and agencies hold signings and promotional events on the event floors on weekends; Edgeshot and the armored veteran Yoroi Musha are often seen here, on patrol along the row or as guests at events. Office workers buy lunch in the basements at noon, and families shop on Sundays. Staff bow to the first customers at 10 a.m., the basement halls mark down boxed meals in the last hour, and a closing melody plays fifteen minutes before the doors shut at 8 p.m. Guards in white gloves watch the jewelry floors, and store detectives work the crowds in plain clothes. The rooftop gardens are quiet, with benches and a small shrine. The basements smell of grilled eel, fresh bread and sweets, and the row's main doors open back onto the Scramble Crossing.

Underground Nightclub.description: A basement club under an office building off Billboard Avenue, reached by a steep stairway papered with flyers, past a door where two broad bouncers check IDs and stamp hands. Below is one long black room: a bar of backlit bottles, a sunken dance floor, a DJ booth on a riser, curtained booths at the back and a sound system that pushes bass through the floor into the ribs. Entry is about 3,000 yen with a drink ticket on weekends, less on weeknights; it opens at ten and runs until five, so most people who come stay for the first trains. Office workers, students and tourists fill it on weekend nights, and the odd rookie pro comes in street clothes, hoping to be recognized. Touts on the street steer people toward it on commission, and closing time brings shoving matches on the stairs that the bouncers end fast. The house rule, printed above the door, is no Quirk effects on the floor however good they would look, and one bouncer has hands large enough to carry a grown man up the stairs by the collar. The air is sweet with fog fluid and spilled cocktails. The stairway climbs to Billboard Avenue, and a back exit opens into the Ramen Alley.

Rooftop Bar.description: A bar on the roof of a hotel tower above the Scramble Crossing, reached by elevator from the hotel lobby, with a glass wind barrier, low sofas, heat lamps and a marble counter where bartenders in black vests shake cocktails. The giant screens on the surrounding buildings are close enough to light the tables in shifting colors, and from the rail the crossing turns into a river of heads, or umbrellas, every two minutes. Cocktails run about 1,800 yen with a seating charge after eight, and a dress code turns away sandals and tracksuits. Couples come at sunset; after work, agency staff, broadcast producers and executives talk business on the sofas, and weekend celebrations take the tables by the glass. Pros who want to be seen without being mobbed drink here, and the staff are trained not to stare or ask for photos; now and then a broker entertains a client in the far corner and pays in cash. A lit landing mark off the north edge is reserved for licensed heroes on a call, and everyone else, wings or not, takes the elevator. The crossing chime floats up thin and faint. The elevator returns to the hotel lobby on the Scramble Crossing.

Theater Row.description: A pedestrian street behind the department-store row lined with theaters: a grand playhouse with a lantern-hung facade for kabuki, two mid-sized houses running musicals, a basement stage for comedy and a rakugo hall with a hand-lettered program board. Posters cover every wall, and this spring the biggest shows a hero musical, with a tall actor in a gold-and-blue costume striking All Might's pose. Matinees start at one and evening shows at half past six; tickets run from about 3,000 yen at the comedy house to 15,000 for the best seats at the kabuki, and a same-day booth on the corner sells returns at a discount and has a line by noon. Retirees fill the matinees; office workers hurry in still in suits; between shows, actors in half makeup buy rice balls at the corner convenience store. Flying scenes and fire effects come from wires, harnesses and machinery, since the theaters will not risk the permit process for Quirk effects on stage. Fans wait at the stage doors with bouquets, and a uniformed attendant keeps them in a neat line. The street smells of roasted chestnuts from a cart. At its end it opens back onto the Department Stores.

Hero Theme Cafe.description: A themed cafe on the second floor above a hero goods shop on Billboard Avenue, decorated as an agency dispatch room: a big wall map of Tokyo with blinking pins, a mock dispatch radio, replica costumes in glass cases and staff in sidekick-style uniforms who greet each table as a new recruit. The menu is all puns: latte art of hero faces, a tall red-white-and-blue parfait for All Might with a gold wafer for his hair, a curry named for Endeavor that comes with a heat warning, a winged omelet for Hawks and a denim-blue soda for Best Jeanist, each with a random collectible coaster. A drink and dessert run about 1,800 yen, seatings last ninety minutes, and fans trade coasters by the door to finish their sets. Tourists, couples, collectors and student groups make up most of the crowd, and agencies pay for limited-time menus when their heroes climb the chart. Every hour the staff stage a mock emergency call, and the whole room shouts the response on cue. A rule card on each table asks guests not to use Quirks to snatch coasters or chill their drinks. It smells of syrup and espresso. A narrow stairway leads back down to Billboard Avenue.

Twenty-Four-Hour Manga Cafe.description: A manga cafe filling three floors of a narrow building just off the Scramble Crossing, open around the clock: a front desk where a clerk checks ID and hands out a booth number, floor-to-ceiling shelves holding tens of thousands of manga volumes, a free drink bar, a soft-serve machine and long rows of private cubicles with reclining chairs or flat mats, a computer and a thin door. Time is sold in packs, about 500 yen for the first hour and a night pack from ten to eight for under 2,000 yen, with showers and blankets for rent. Afternoons bring students and office workers killing time with a stack of hero manga; after the last train it fills with people who missed it and travelers saving on a hotel, plus a quieter set who live here week to week and keep everything they own in a bag under the desk. The cubicle floors stay dim, voices drop to whispers, and the house rule is no phone calls inside the booths. A hero-news ticker scrolls across the computer screens, and the night clerk knows which regulars to wake in time for their shifts. It smells of instant noodles, shampoo and paper. The front desk opens onto the Scramble Crossing.

Ramen Alley.description: A narrow passage under the elevated rail tracks a block from the Scramble Crossing, lined with about a dozen ramen counters packed shoulder to shoulder under the arches: a soy-broth shop with a forty-year line, a spicy miso counter, a dipping-noodle place and a counter whose pork broth simmers for two days. Meal-ticket machines stand by every door, bowls run about 900 to 1,400 yen, and some counters have only six stools. Office workers come at noon in waves; tourists photograph their bowls in the afternoon; after the bars close, clubbers, cab drivers and night-shift workers fill the stools until the last counters shut near dawn. Trains rumble overhead every few minutes and shake the steam above the pots. Cooks call out orders in rhythm, and the unwritten rule is to slurp, eat fast and give up the stool. A row of signed boards from pro heroes hangs in the oldest shop, Endeavor's among them, and the owner says he finished his bowl without a word and never smiled. Steam, pork fat and charred garlic hang in the air. One end opens onto the Scramble Crossing; at the other, a back door leads down into the Underground Nightclub.

Hero Billboard Chart Hall.name: Hero Billboard Chart Hall
Hero Billboard Chart Hall.basicInfo: A concert hall owned by the Hero Public Safety Commission, about 4 km southeast of Tokyo Station by subway and about 3 km from the Tokyo Broadcasting Center, where the Hero Billboard Chart JP is announced live twice a year. The chart ranks licensed heroes by incidents resolved, social contribution and public approval, and the top ten are invited onstage. The chart in force at the start of the year puts All Might at Number One, Endeavor at Two, Hawks at Three and Best Jeanist at Four, with Edgeshot and Gang Orca among the others in the top ten. Commission staff run the building: the public enters only with event tickets, the press only with Commission credentials, and guards check both at the doors. Between charts the hall is rented for agency press conferences, hero debuts, award shows and Commission seminars, mostly on weekday afternoons; tickets for chart night are allotted by lottery and gone within minutes. Players can attend or staff events, cover them as press, hold a press conference for their own agency, or watch the next announcement from the gallery. The building is a curved glass front over a plaza where fans gather with banners on announcement days, with a box office and a small shop selling chart programs. Empty, the hall is cold and echoing; on chart night it seats four thousand guests and broadcasts live to the whole country.
Hero Billboard Chart Hall.hiddenInfo: The tally for the next chart is already being compiled in a back office behind the stage, where Commission analysts work with the blinds down. They are auditing agencies that count joint arrests twice, and several agencies in the top thirty stand to drop when the corrections post. Approval scores come from surveys run by a contracted polling firm, and a freelance reporter is asking whether its samples favor the big cities; she has two former survey callers willing to talk and needs someone inside the hall to confirm when the raw numbers arrive. Agencies lobby the hall staff for seats near the stage and better camera angles, because a good shot on chart night can lift approval for months, and gifts arrive at the stage door every week. A stage manager is selling rehearsal schedules to tabloids, meeting a stringer in the plaza cafe after the Thursday sound checks. All Might's move to U.A. Academy has the analysts arguing over how to score a Number One who now spends his days teaching, and nobody has yet told the President which way the numbers lean.

Stage.description: A wide stage under a lighting grid, backed by a screen three floors high that shows the rankings on chart night. Ten numbered marks are taped across the boards for the top ten, with Number One at the center. Most days the stage sits dark or is set for a weekday press event with a podium and a backdrop of sponsor logos, and stagehands test lights and sound in the mornings. By old superstition, no one stands on the Number One mark during rehearsals, and the crew walks around it. The wings hold cable runs, prop cases and a narrow green room where heroes wait to go on, watched by a Commission stage manager in a headset. On chart night each hero walks out as their number lights, and a hero who skips the ceremony leaves an empty mark the cameras linger on. The lights are hot enough to make costumes sweat, and steps at the front lead down into the Press Gallery.

Press Gallery.description: Tiered seating facing the stage, a long camera riser across the back and a fenced press pen at the front, with power outlets at every seat. Reporters, photographers, agency publicists and broadcast crews fill it for press conferences and pack it on chart night, when ticket holders fill the upper tiers behind them. Commission staff check credentials at the door and run the microphones; questions are taken only when the moderator points, and anyone who shouts out of turn loses the microphone for the rest of the event. During announcements the gallery is loud with camera shutters firing in bursts, and the coffee urns run dry within the hour. Between events the seats sit empty under work lights while cleaners collect forgotten lanyards and lens caps. The pen's gate opens on the steps up to the Stage, and a guard lets nobody through without a nod from the stage manager.

Tokyo Broadcasting Center.name: Tokyo Broadcasting Center
Tokyo Broadcasting Center.basicInfo: A national TV network's headquarters, about 6 km south of Tokyo Station by commuter rail and about 2.5 km from the Best Jeanist Hero Agency: a tower of studios, a 24-hour newsroom, a video archive and a rooftop helipad for news helicopters. It makes hero news, ranking-debate panels, talk shows, commercials and live incident coverage, and it carries the U.A. Sports Festival, now a bigger broadcast than the shrunken Olympics, along with the twice-yearly Hero Billboard Chart. Morning shows go live at 6 a.m. and the evening news at 7 p.m.; the helicopters lift off whenever the scanners report a big incident. Celebrity heroes are regular guests: Uwabami, as famous for her commercials and magazine covers as for her rescues, shoots here often and turns any visit into a photo session. Staff badges open every floor; guests and studio audiences sign in at the ground-floor security desk and are escorted, and the newsroom and archive are closed to anyone without a badge. Players can appear as guests, give interviews, join a studio audience, sell footage, work as runners or crew, or search the archive with a staff member's help. Fans wait outside the guest entrance in the evenings for autographs. Red on-air lights burn over the studio doors, police scanners chatter in the newsroom, and every hallway screen shows the network's own feed.
Tokyo Broadcasting Center.hiddenInfo: Since word spread that All Might has joined U.A. Academy's faculty, a producer has been demanding an exclusive at any cost. U.A. refuses every interview request, so the producer has crews working Musutafu's station district instead, offering cash to anyone with footage or stories from inside the campus, and an intern has been told to find a first-year willing to talk on camera. The newsroom pays cash for incident footage, including clips filmed closer to fights than police allow, and the night desk does not ask how a shot was taken; two freelancers have already been hurt chasing better angles. A segment on heroes' collateral damage is in production and needs an insider willing to talk, ideally someone who has seen a Commission settlement; its producer suspects the Commission buries the worst cases and cannot prove it. Uwabami is negotiating a weekly segment of her own, which the news division resents, though her snakes have found more missing people on live broadcasts than the network likes to admit. The archive holds raw footage the network never aired, including unedited incident tapes from years back, and a staff badge with archive access is worth real money to the wrong buyer.

Broadcast Center Lobby.description: The ground floor of the Tokyo Broadcasting Center: a tall glass atrium with a polished stone floor, the network's logo in brushed steel over a long security desk, and turnstiles that open only to staff badges. Giant screens on every wall run the network's own feed, hero news, ranking panels and commercials, Uwabami's among them. Guests and studio audiences sign in at the security desk, show ID, receive a numbered pass and wait on low benches until a runner comes down to escort them; nobody goes past the turnstiles alone. Mornings bring early guests and makeup crews before the 6 a.m. shows, afternoons bring audience lines and couriers with drives, and in the evening fans gather outside the guest entrance hoping for autographs as heroes leave. A small shop by the doors sells network goods, mugs with show logos and last year's Sports Festival highlights on disc for about 3,000 yen. The guards know every regular courier by face, and a lost pass means a fifteen-minute wait while they phone upstairs. Announcements for audience groups echo off the stone. Escorted guests go up to the Studio Floor, and badge holders to the Newsroom.

Studio Floor.description: A long floor of soundproofed studios behind heavy double doors, each with a red on-air light above it that silences the corridor the moment it burns. In the biggest studio the set for the hero ranking panels takes up half the floor: a curved desk, a giant screen for the Hero Billboard Chart and tiers of seats for a studio audience; next door are a living-room set for talk shows and a white backdrop for commercials and magazine shoots. Cameras glide across taped marks under a dense grid of hot lights. Morning shows go live at six, talk shows tape in the afternoon in front of escorted audiences, and the evening news goes out at seven from its own set. Uwabami shoots here often and turns any visit into a photo session, posing a passing guest beside her before they know it while her three snakes turn to the lens. The floor director's rule is absolute: phones off, silence under the red light, and no Quirk use on set without a producer's sign-off. Cables snake across the floor, and the air smells of hot lamps and hairspray. The corridor leads back to the Broadcast Center Lobby and across to the Newsroom.

Newsroom.description: A wide open-plan floor that never closes: rows of desks under a wall of monitors showing every network's feed, police scanners chattering on the assignment desk, and a big screen that relays live pictures from the news helicopters whenever they lift off the rooftop helipad. Producers, writers and editors work in shifts around the clock: the morning team arrives in the dark, the evening news team takes over in the afternoon, and a thinner night desk keeps watch until dawn. When a big incident comes over the scanners, the whole room stands up at once and a crew is out the door within minutes. The night desk buys incident footage from freelancers and passersby, paying cash at a counter by the door and asking few questions about how a shot was taken. Whiteboards track segments in production, and one corner is buried in files and tapes for a feature on the damage hero fights leave behind. Staff badges open the doors, and visitors come in only with an escort. Cold coffee, warm printers and the constant murmur of scanners fill the air. The corridor leads back to the Broadcast Center Lobby and over to the Studio Floor.

Tokyo Station.name: Tokyo Station
Tokyo Station.basicInfo: Japan's main rail hub: a red-brick station over a maze of underground concourses at the center of Greater Tokyo, run by the rail companies, with IC transit cards opening the gates. Shinkansen run southwest through Musutafu, the stop for U.A. Academy (about 100 km, 45 minutes), and on to Shin-Osaka, about two and a half hours out, and Hakata, and northwest to Deika and Jaku, about an hour and a half; express lines reach Hosu, 30 km north and half an hour away, and Kamino Ward and Yokohama to the southwest. Fukuoka is also a short flight from Tokyo. Subways reach every Tokyo agency within forty minutes, and the Commission Headquarters is about 3 km away. Rush hours run 7-9 a.m. and 5-8 p.m., when the concourses move like rivers; station police and patrolling heroes watch the gates, and pros on their way to joint operations pass through all day, Ryukyu, the Dragoon Hero, among the familiar faces. Underground there are shopping streets of boxed-meal stands, hero goods shops, ramen counters and banks of coin lockers; above ground, the brick facade faces a plaza and the towers of the business district. The gates stay open through service hours, and the last trains leave a little after midnight. Players can travel, meet contacts, buy boxed meals and hero goods, work kiosk shifts, or look for someone in the crowd. Departure melodies play on every platform, announcements repeat in four languages, and the smell of grilled eel and rice drifts up from the food halls.
Tokyo Station.hiddenInfo: Coin lockers on the lower concourse are a known dead drop: brokers rent them by the day and pass keys through a bento stand that asks no questions, and the stand's night clerk keeps a private ledger of who collects which key, which would be worth a great deal to the police. Luggage has been vanishing from the shinkansen platforms for weeks, taken by someone whose Quirk keeps small objects from being noticed, and the short-staffed station police have asked local agencies for help; nobody has taken the job yet, because the case pays little and the credit would be small. The thefts cluster on the Musutafu-bound platforms during the evening rush, and the stolen bags turn up emptied in lockers two levels down, so whoever does it knows the locker trade. Ryukyu passes through often enough that station staff know her by sight; she is polite to everyone, between engagements more often than not, and the kind of pro who would hear out a young hero with a real lead. Station security has quietly doubled its patrols near the shinkansen gates since the Hero Killer's attacks in other cities, and the guards on the overnight shift are tired and easy to slip past.

Marunouchi Concourse.description: The Marunouchi side is the Tokyo Station of postcards: a long red-brick facade trimmed in white stone, with a great domed hall at each end where travelers stop to photograph the plaster eagles and zodiac reliefs high overhead. Between the domes run ticket gates and departure boards; outside, the brick faces a broad plaza, a taxi pool and the glass towers of the business district. From seven to nine in the morning office workers pour out of the gates toward the towers, and from five to eight they pour back; between the rushes come tour groups, couples posing for wedding photos on the plaza and pros on their way to joint operations, Ryukyu among the familiar faces, polite to every fan who stops her. Station police and patrolling heroes watch the gates all day. Departure melodies and announcements in four languages echo up into the domes, and after the last trains, a little after midnight, the brick glows gold under floodlights over an empty plaza. Through the gates, transfer escalators climb toward the Tokyo Shinkansen Platforms, and a long passage under the tracks runs east to the Yaesu Underground Mall.

Yaesu Underground Mall.description: East of the tracks the station sinks into a maze of low-ceilinged underground streets: a long shopping arcade, a corridor of rival ramen counters, hero goods shops with All Might figures in every window, boxed-meal stands stacked with grilled eel on rice, drugstores and cafes, and on the lower concourse long banks of coin lockers in every size. Commuters cut through at rush hour without slowing; office workers from the Yaesu and Nihonbashi towers fill the ramen lines from eleven, and in the evening salarymen buy boxed meals for the train home. Most shops pull their shutters down around ten, and after that the lockers and a small bento stand beside them keep the place lit; the stand holds parcels and keys for customers who ask, and its night clerk writes something in a notebook under the counter whenever one is collected. Attendants who clear overdue lockers sometimes find suitcases inside, emptied and abandoned. The air smells of broth and soy. Stairs climb to the Yaesu gates and the Tokyo Shinkansen Platforms, and passages lead back west to the Marunouchi Concourse.

Tokyo Shinkansen Platforms.description: On the Yaesu side, long island platforms under steel canopies hold the bullet trains: white Tokaido trains with a blue stripe leave every few minutes for Musutafu, 45 minutes away, Shin-Osaka and Hakata, and across the way the northern lines' green and red trains run toward Deika and Jaku. Painted marks on the floor show where each door will stop, and travelers line up behind them in tidy rows. When a train terminates, a uniformed cleaning crew bows it in, turns every seat around and sweeps the whole train in about seven minutes. The first trains leave around six with business travelers half asleep; daytime brings tourists and school trips; Sunday evenings bring U.A. students heading back to Musutafu. In the evening rush the queues for the Musutafu trains are so tight that bags set down beside them are easy to lose track of, and station staff have posted new signs asking everyone to keep their luggage in hand, while guards walk the gates in pairs. Departure melodies chime, and the wind of an arriving train lifts every coat. Escalators lead down to the Marunouchi Concourse and the Yaesu Underground Mall.

Hosu Downtown.name: Hosu Downtown
Hosu Downtown.basicInfo: Hosu Downtown is the commercial heart of Hosu, a dense commuter city about 30 km north of Tokyo Station. Elevated rail lines cross the district on concrete overpasses, and Main Street runs north from Hosu Station between office towers, banks, a department store, chain restaurants, pachinko parlors and electronics shops. Offices keep nine-to-six hours; the station floods with commuters at both ends of the day, lunch crowds pack the noodle counters at noon, and izakaya and karaoke bars keep the side streets busy until the last train, after which the avenue empties fast. The Hosu police, under Chief Kenji Tsuragamae, staff a police box on the Station Plaza, and pro heroes from local agencies patrol the streets on foot and the rooftops by Quirk: Native walks Main Street most days, Manual's small agency runs fixed day and night routes, and the popular Ingenium, Tensei Iida of Team Idaten, is often on the plaza, where fans crowd him for photos. The streets and the plaza are open to anyone at any hour; the office roofs are not, because building managers keep the roof doors locked. A player can shop, find office or restaurant work, meet contacts in the cafes around the station, report trouble at the police box, or follow the rooftop routes heroes use. Express trains run from Hosu Station toward central Tokyo in about half an hour; a local line reaches the Back Alleys, about 4 km southwest, in five minutes; buses run to Hosu General Hospital, about 4 km north-northwest; Manual's office is about 3 km east-northeast; and U.A. Academy is about 105 km to the southwest. Station chimes and the rumble of trains on the overpasses carry across the whole district.
Hosu Downtown.hiddenInfo: Someone has been breaking into offices along Main Street at night, coming in through roof hatches and leaving across the rooftops. The police suspect a thief with a climbing or leaping Quirk, and Manual has added rooftop checks to his night patrol, which thins his street routes. Native keeps a list of every forced hatch and has noticed that the thief takes only cash and small electronics and is always gone before the night patrol's first roof check. Hosu has few heroes for its size: the big agencies sit in central Tokyo, a call from downtown can wait ten minutes or more for a pro, and shop owners complain about it openly. Local heroes follow every report about the Hero Killer Stain.
