At the start of the year, unknown to any of them, he is already here: for several nights he has crouched among the billboard frames on the downtown rooftops, studying how Hosu's heroes work: Native's beat, Manual's night routes, the crowds around Ingenium on the plaza, how long a call takes to answer. He has chosen no one, and whether he ever does depends on what he sees. The burglar has twice glimpsed a motionless figure in a long red scarf on a neighboring roof and fled empty-handed, and a building manager found a cut padlock on a roof door where nothing was taken. The station's security office keeps camera footage for only a week, and its cameras do not cover the roofs, so anyone who wants to know who walks up there has to go up and look.

Main Street.description: A wide four-lane avenue running north from Hosu Station between glass office towers, with a department store, banks, chain restaurants, electronics shops and pachinko parlors at street level and office lobbies behind revolving doors. Office workers crowd the sidewalks at lunch and after six; delivery vans double-park all morning, and smokers cluster in the marked corners outside the convenience stores. Heroes on patrol pass several times a day, Native on foot most of all, and fans stop them for photos and autographs while shopkeepers corner them about the latest break-in. At night the towers go dark floor by floor until only the security desks and the pachinko signs are lit. Halfway up, the avenue runs under an elevated rail line, and every few minutes a passing train drowns out every conversation beneath it; regulars simply stop talking and wait. The Station Plaza opens at the avenue's south end, and service stairwells in the older buildings climb to the Downtown Rooftops.

Station Plaza.description: The paved plaza in front of Hosu Station: a bus terminal, a taxi rank, bicycle racks, the police box and a giant screen on the station front looping hero news, ranking updates and ads. Commuters pour through at morning and evening rush, thousands crossing in a few minutes; in between, the plaza belongs to students, street musicians, people handing out flyers and people waiting to meet someone by the big screen. Chief Kenji Tsuragamae is often at the police box in his dark suit, and Ingenium stops here between calls, laughing with fans while his sidekicks keep the crowd out of the bus lane. After the last train the plaza empties to taxis, a few drunks and the officer on night duty. Departure chimes and platform announcements carry across the plaza all day, the officers in the police box know the regulars by sight, and the smell of grilled corn drifts from a cart by the bus stops. Main Street runs north from the plaza.

Downtown Rooftops.description: Flat office roofs ten to twenty stories up, crowded with air-conditioning units, antenna masts, billboard frames, water tanks and window-cleaning rigs. Building managers keep the roof doors locked, so the people up here are maintenance crews with keys, patrolling heroes with movement Quirks who use the roofs as shortcuts, and now and then someone who has no business here. On the older blocks the gaps between buildings are narrow enough to jump; on the newer ones they are not, and the edge drops straight to the traffic. By day the roofs are hot, bright and empty but for an office worker sneaking a cigarette; at night the city spreads out below in lines of light along the overpasses, and a figure standing still against a billboard frame is easy to miss. The wind is hard and steady, the street noise thins to a hum, and the elevated trains pass close enough to some roofs to shake the gravel. Without a movement Quirk, the only way down is a service stairwell to Main Street.

Izakaya Street.description: A side street off Main Street running under the elevated rail line, where izakaya fill the arches and the ground floors on both sides: chain places with all-you-can-drink deals, family counters with red lanterns, a smoky skewer bar and an oden stand with steaming pots. After six, office workers pour out of the towers and in through the cloth curtains; by eight every counter is full of beer, highballs and skewers at about 150 yen each, and staff bellow a welcome at every arrival. Touts with laminated menus work both ends of the street, promising cheap courses and skipping anyone who looks local. Trains overhead rattle the glasses every few minutes, and regulars pause mid-sentence until they pass. Talk at the counters this spring is the break-ins on Main Street, the Hero Killer reports from other cities and how long a pro takes to come when you call; the owners keep the police box number taped by the phone. Closing time near the last train brings the street's only regular trouble, shoving matches on the curb that usually end before an officer arrives. Smoke, soy and beer hang under the arches. The street opens back onto Main Street.

Hosu Karaoke Box.description: A narrow karaoke building at the corner where the izakaya street meets Main Street, its glowing sign stacked floor by floor and a staff member handing out discount tickets outside. The ground-floor desk rents rooms by the half hour, about 400 yen a head on weekday afternoons and more after six, with all-you-can-drink plans and an all-night package from eleven to five that fills with office workers who missed the last train. Upstairs, rooms of every size have padded benches, two microphones, a touch-pad song list and a phone for ordering food. Afternoons belong to students and retirees practicing enka; after six, office teams arrive from the izakaya for after-parties, and the bosses sing first. The locals request the song from Team Idaten's recruiting ad whenever Ingenium is on the news. The doors have glass panels so the staff can check the rooms, and a notice at the desk asks customers to leave their Quirks out of the microphones. The night clerk calls the police box only when a fight spills into the hall. Bass and off-key choruses leak through every wall. The entrance opens onto Main Street, a few steps from the Izakaya Street.

Chain Coffee Shop.description: A two-floor chain coffee shop on a corner of the Station Plaza, with a counter and pastry case downstairs and an upstairs room of small tables and a window bar that looks straight across the plaza at the big screen and the police box. It opens at seven, and the morning line of commuters runs out the door; mid-morning, salespeople hold meetings over laptops and job seekers polish their résumés; at lunch, office workers carry their sandwiches up the stairs; after classes, local students study at the window until the staff start mopping at ten. A drip coffee costs about 350 yen and a seasonal sweet drink about 600. The window bar is a good place to wait for someone, to watch the fans gather when Ingenium stops by the screen, or to see who goes in and out of the police box, and regulars report the day's hero sightings to each other as if reading the news. Staff keep a wide chair for heteromorph customers, and a sign by the lids asks customers not to use Quirks to chill or heat their own drinks. It smells of espresso and cinnamon, and departure chimes from the station carry through the glass. The door opens onto the Station Plaza.

All-Night Convenience Store.description: A twenty-four-hour convenience store where Main Street meets the Station Plaza, with bright glass walls, a magazine rack along the front window, shelves of rice balls, boxed meals and instant noodles, a hot case of fried chicken and a pot of oden by the register, an ATM, a copier and recycling bins outside. Commuters grab coffee and rice balls before the morning trains; office workers buy lunch and pay bills at noon; after the bars close, drunks buy water and the last of the fried chicken, taxi drivers stock up, and a few homeless regulars warm up by the door until the clerk asks them to move on. Night shifts are thin, one or two part-timers, and the store has had two late-night shoplifting runs this month; the manager keeps a slip behind the register noting the times a hero last walked past, and on most nights it has long gaps. The night officer from the police box comes in for coffee around two. A small TV over the counter runs hero news, the fridges hum, and the door chime rings every few seconds until long after midnight. It smells of fryer oil and simmering dashi. The doors open onto the Station Plaza and Main Street.

Hosu Back Alleys.name: Hosu Back Alleys
Hosu Back Alleys.basicInfo: Hosu Back Alleys is an older quarter about 4 km southwest of Hosu Station, where four- to six-story concrete buildings stand wall to wall around a maze of lanes. Most lanes are too narrow for a car and are lined with restaurant back doors, stairwells, gas meters, stacked crates and bicycles chained to drainpipes; overhead, cables and laundry lines cross from window to window, and the rooftops are crowded with rusted water tanks on steel legs. Ground floors hold ramen shops, standing bars, a coin laundry and repair stalls; upstairs are cheap rooms rented by the week, small offices and families who have lived here for generations. The city owns the lanes but barely maintains them, and police and hero patrols keep to the main roads and rarely turn in. Cooks, dishwashers and delivery riders use the lanes all day, and residents hang laundry on the roofs in the morning; after dark the lanes belong to drinkers from the small bars, homeless people and anyone who wants to stay out of sight. Nothing here is gated: anyone can walk in from the main road, though the regulars notice every stranger. A player can rent a cheap room, pick up kitchen work, find a quiet spot for unlicensed Quirk practice (illegal, and a neighbor may call it in), or meet someone with something to sell. A local station on a commuter line runs to downtown in about five minutes. The quarter smells of frying oil and wet concrete, and sound carries strangely between the walls: a shout two lanes over can seem to come from right behind you.
Hosu Back Alleys.hiddenInfo: A small crew of minor villains collects a weekly quiet fee from the quarter's bars. Their lookouts sit on the water tanks and flash phone lights down into the lanes when a patrol turns in, and the crew is gone before any hero arrives. Bar owners pay because the police take twenty minutes to come and leave again just as fast. In one stairwell, a dealer sells knockoff support gear and unlicensed costume parts to hero hopefuls and petty criminals alike, and takes orders for anything harder through a broker. The lanes have no cameras. Two of the dead ends connect through a ramen shop's kitchen, and the cooks let strangers through for a price. Right now the quarter has a guest nobody has placed: Himiko Toga, a fugitive wanted for a string of killings by blood loss, has been sleeping in a weekly room off the Narrow Alley, alone, with no crew and no plan beyond the next night. Her wanted photo is old and her cheer disarms people, so the landlady takes her for a runaway student. Last week a delivery rider was found in the Narrow Alley at dawn, dizzy and pale, with a shallow cut on his forearm; he remembers only a giggling young woman who asked his name and called him cute. The crew's lookouts have seen her walking the roofs at two in the morning and have decided, for now, to leave her alone.

Narrow Alley.description: A lane two arms' widths across, running between six-story buildings to a dead end at a chain-link fence, with a ramen shop's back door, a rusting fire escape and the stairwell to a row of weekly rooms opening onto it. Air-conditioner units drip from above, garbage bins line one wall, and a single caged bulb lights the middle stretch. Cooks step out for smoke breaks between lunch and dinner service and trade gossip about who has paid the weekly fee; delivery riders cut through on foot with their bags. After midnight the alley is empty except for cats and the odd drunk looking for a shortcut, and the bulb throws long shadows past the bins. The walls throw every footstep back, so anyone at the far end hears a visitor coming long before seeing them. The fire escape is the way up: it climbs past the weekly rooms to the Water Tank Rooftops.

Water Tank Rooftops.description: The roofs of the quarter's old four- and five-story blocks, close enough in places to step from one to the next and elsewhere joined by planks someone laid down years ago, each topped with a rusted water tank on steel legs. Residents hang laundry and tend potted plants and foam boxes of herbs up here in the daytime; an old man keeps racing pigeons in a wire coop, and wild pigeons nest under the tanks. The tank platforms look straight down into most of the lanes and, far to the northeast, out to the lit towers of downtown. After dark, lookouts and loners use the tanks as perches, and a phone light blinking from a tank means a patrol has turned into the lanes below. The steel legs creak whenever the wind rises, and the tar paper underfoot goes soft in summer and slick after rain. The fire escape leads back down into the Narrow Alley.

Hole-in-the-Wall Bar.description: A bar so small it fits six stools, behind a sliding wooden door off the Narrow Alley under a hand-lettered sign that simply says bar. Inside is a counter of dark wood worn pale where elbows rest, shelves of shochu bottles with regulars' names on paper tags, a two-burner stove, a small TV on a bracket and a cat that sleeps on the end stool unless someone sits there. The owner, an older woman who has run it since before the rooms upstairs went weekly, pours drinks for about 600 yen, serves boiled peanuts and stewed offal, and takes cash only. Cooks from the ramen shops come after their shifts; laborers and delivery riders drink until two; strangers get a look, a menu and silence until they order a second drink. On Friday nights the owner counts cash into an envelope and puts it in a drawer, and the regulars talk louder while she does it. Nobody here calls the police unless someone is badly hurt, and she keeps a baseball bat behind the counter. A paper sign above the bottles says, in her neat hand, no Quirks, no fights, no questions. Smoke and soy cling to everything. The sliding door opens onto the Narrow Alley.

Manual Hero Agency.name: Manual Hero Agency
Manual Hero Agency.basicInfo: Manual Hero Agency is a small local agency on the second floor of an office building about 3 km east-northeast of Hosu Station, above a dry cleaner and a dental clinic, its name on a modest sign in the window. The pro hero Manual runs it: a courteous, careful hero who does things by the book, explains everything step by step and expects his staff to do the same. His specialty is water-based rescue and support, dousing fires, knocking opponents off balance and screening civilians while flashier heroes take the spotlight. A front desk takes walk-in complaints and police requests from eight in the morning until ten at night; after that a buzzer by the street door reaches whoever is on the night shift. Behind the desk are a few desks, a wall map of patrol routes stuck with colored pins, a whiteboard of shifts, a small kitchen and a locker room. Manual and his small staff patrol downtown Hosu on fixed routes in day and night shifts, alongside Native on Main Street and Chief Tsuragamae's officers, and he accepts interns from hero academies. A player can report a crime, ask for help, apply for part-time agency work, or train here as an intern, which takes an academy's paperwork and Manual's signature; nobody goes out on patrol without him or a licensed sidekick. Downtown and the Station Plaza are about 3 km away by bus, Hosu General Hospital about 4 km. The police scanner on the front desk is never switched off, and the office smells of instant coffee and costumes drying on the radiator.
Manual Hero Agency.hiddenInfo: Manual's agency covers more ground than it can handle. He has asked the large Tokyo agencies for patrol support and has had no answer, and the paperwork eats his evenings; most nights he is still at his desk at eleven, filing case reports so his staff get credit for their work. Right now his night shift is two people short while he hunts the rooftop burglar hitting offices on Main Street, so he would welcome a capable intern or part-time sidekick. On the wall map he has pinned every forced hatch, and the pins cluster near the elevated line: he believes the thief times each break-in to passing trains, whose noise covers a forced lock, and he plans to stake out the roofs by the overpass himself later this week with a single sidekick, which he knows is too few. What he has not pinned is the cut padlock on a roof door where nothing was stolen; it bothers him, and he cannot say why. Native drops in most evenings to compare notes over canned coffee. Manual gives every new hire the same warning: a hero who acts on personal feelings, outside orders, puts the whole agency in breach of the rules, and the supervising hero answers for anything an intern does. He says it kindly and enforces it without exception.

Manual Agency Front Office.description: The second-floor office of Manual Hero Agency, up a narrow stairwell from a street door beside the dry cleaner: a front desk facing the door, a few staff desks behind it, a whiteboard of day and night shifts, a kitchen corner with an electric kettle and a jar of instant coffee, and a large wall map of downtown Hosu, about 3 km away, stuck with colored pins along the patrol routes. The front desk takes walk-in complaints and police requests from eight in the morning until ten at night, and after hours a buzzer by the street door reaches whoever is on the night shift. The police scanner on the desk is never switched off. Manual is usually at a desk behind a stack of case reports, or explaining a form step by step to a visitor; he greets everyone with an almost apologetic bow. Native drops by most evenings with canned coffee to compare notes. Nobody leaves on patrol without Manual or a licensed sidekick. A cluster of pins near the elevated rail line catches the eye of anyone who studies the map for long. The office smells of instant coffee and drying costumes, and the Manual Agency Locker Room is through a door at the back.

Manual Agency Locker Room.description: A narrow room behind the front office: a row of tall steel lockers with names on strips of tape, a bench down the middle, a small shower stall, and a radiator under the window where costumes and towels are always drying. Manual's spare blue-and-white costumes hang in a garment bag at the end, his white helmet on the shelf above, its fin crest polished; the staff lockers hold radios, flashlights and rain gear. Because Manual's water Quirk is useless without a supply nearby, a utility sink by the door has a hose fitting, and filled canteens and water packs stand on a shelf ready to grab before every patrol. The day shift changes here in the morning and the night shift in the evening, and the room is busiest at the handover, when two shifts crowd in and trade news about the rooftop break-ins downtown. Interns get a locker of their own with a laminated checklist taped inside the door in Manual's careful wording: radio checked, license or intern ID on, route confirmed, supervisor told. The air is warm and damp from the radiator and smells of wet fabric and soap. The only door leads back to the Manual Agency Front Office.

Hosu General Hospital.name: Hosu General Hospital
Hosu General Hospital.basicInfo: Hosu General Hospital is the city's main public hospital, a pale multi-story block about 4 km north-northwest of Hosu Station with an ambulance bay on one side and a bus stop on the other. It has an emergency department, surgical and general wards, and staff used to Quirk injuries: burns, crush wounds, poisonings and the side effects of overused Quirks. The city runs it; hospital security controls access, and the wards are open to visitors only during visiting hours, which end at eight in the evening; after that only the emergency entrance stays open. Doctors and nurses work rotating shifts around the clock, and ambulances arrive day and night, busiest after the evening rush. Outpatients fill the lobby in the morning, visitors in the evening. Police officers come to take statements from injured victims and suspects, and heroes stop by to check on people they rescued, which brings fans and the occasional photographer to the doors. A player can be treated, recover, visit a patient, take a hospital job as a porter, cleaner or clerk (or as a nurse or doctor with a license), or ask the staff about recent injuries, though they guard patient details closely. A bus line connects the hospital to Hosu Station, and the downtown agencies are a few minutes away by car. The building is pale and quiet, and the lobby smells of disinfectant and canned coffee.
Hosu General Hospital.hiddenInfo: Someone on the night shift sells word to tabloid reporters: when a pro hero is admitted, the gossip sites know within the hour, and the administration is hunting for the leak. This week it has quietly given slightly different admission details to different night staff, to see which version reaches the gossip sites first, and the night nurses have started to notice that their notes do not match. The emergency department is short of staff, and on bad nights patients with minor injuries wait in the lobby for hours, which has started shouting matches at the reception counter. One room on the ward is kept for injured suspects in police custody, with an officer on the door; detectives use it to question people before they are fit to leave. At the moment it holds a purse-snatcher who broke his wrist running from Native, and the officer on the door is bored enough to chat with anyone who brings coffee. Heroes who bring in a patient usually leave before the paperwork starts, and the staff resent it; the few who stay to fill in the forms, Manual among them, are remembered and treated well. The hospital has no hero on call, and if trouble breaks out inside it, security phones the police box downtown and waits.

Hospital Lobby.description: A wide, bright lobby with a reception counter, rows of padded benches, a pharmacy window and a convenience store by the doors. A ticket machine hands out numbers, and a screen calls them with a soft chime. Outpatients wait here through the morning, elderly regulars greeting one another by name; in the evening the lobby fills with visitors and families carrying fruit and flowers, and police officers wait by the elevators to see a patient. After eight only the emergency entrance is open, and the benches hold people waiting on someone in surgery. Security guards stop reporters at the entrance and check every visitor against the ward list. A wall TV runs the news with the sound off, and when a hero appears on it the whole room looks up. Elevators and stairs lead up to the Hospital Ward.

Hospital Ward.description: A long corridor of shared rooms, four beds to a room, each bed behind a curtain and the window beds the most wanted. Nurses make rounds at set hours and check on patients through the night; doctors come through in the morning with a trail of residents. Visiting hours end at eight in the evening, and the nurses enforce it. Patients recovering from Quirk injuries trade stories, compare scars and watch hero news on the day room's TV, arguing over the rankings. Near the far end, one door has a uniformed officer on a folding chair beside it, and the nurses walk past without looking in. At night the ward is quiet except for monitors beeping, a cough down the corridor and soft footsteps at the nurses' station, where a kettle is always warm. The elevators lead back down to the Hospital Lobby.

Gran Torino's Apartment.name: Gran Torino's Apartment
Gran Torino's Apartment.basicInfo: Gran Torino's Apartment is a cramped, run-down building in an older neighborhood about 8 km southeast of Hosu Station, among low apartment blocks, a shuttered barbershop and a corner shop that sells taiyaki from a griddle in the window. The building has stained walls, a narrow concrete stairwell and a door that often stands unlocked. The retired hero Gran Torino (Sorahiko Torino) lives here alone: a very short old man with spiky swept-back white hair and a domino mask, a pale bodysuit, a high-collared yellow cape, oversized yellow gloves and a cane he barely needs. Almost nobody remembers his hero days. His Quirk, Jet, blasts air from his soles and sends him ricocheting off walls, floor and ceiling at high speed, and the dents in his walls show it. The main room holds a television, a low table, a microwave and a freezer full of taiyaki; the rest of the flat is a tiny kitchen and a futon. He trains whoever he decides to train, in that same room, and turns everyone else away. An unlocked door is not an invitation: he answers when he likes, plays the confused old man to anyone he does not know, and throws out anyone he finds dull. A player can visit, ask for training, bring taiyaki, or try to earn his interest. A local bus from Hosu Station stops a short walk away. The flat smells of sweet bean paste and old tatami, and the television is always on, usually to hero news.
Gran Torino's Apartment.hiddenInfo: His forgetfulness is an act: he pretends not to know visitors' names, or even his own, to see how they react, and he is as fast and sharp as ever. A newcomer usually gets the doddering act, then a surprise attack in the confined room, then one cutting question about what they just did wrong. Long ago he taught at U.A. Academy for one year, and All Might was his student; All Might still goes pale at the mention of his name. Right now he reads every report on All Might's new teaching job and tells any visitor that a great hero is not necessarily a great teacher. He has not heard from All Might since the appointment was announced, complains about it loudly to the television, and keeps the phone within reach of the low table all the same; anything All Might asked with enough guilt in his voice would get a yes. His landlord has sent two warnings about the dented walls; he has ignored both, and the corner shop owner, who has known him for years, quietly suspects the next letter will be the last. In a real emergency he drops the act at once, gives two-word orders and puts himself between the young and the danger, though Jet runs on the air in his lungs, and a long fight tells on an old body.

Gran Torino's Main Room.description: The one real room of Gran Torino's flat, behind a door at the top of a narrow concrete stairwell that often stands unlocked: worn tatami, a low table with a teapot and a cordless phone within reach, a television on a crate that is always on, usually to hero news, a folded futon in one corner, and a microwave and a freezer packed with taiyaki by the kitchenette doorway. The walls and ceiling are dented at odd heights, where something small and very fast has bounced off them many times. This is also where he trains whoever he decides to train, shoving the table aside and turning the cramped space into a test nobody passes on the first try. He answers the door when he feels like it, asks a newcomer who they are more than once, and has been known to forget his own name in front of strangers; visitors who stay long learn not to turn their backs. Mornings he watches the news shows; evenings he complains loudly to the screen about All Might's teaching. Taiyaki from the corner shop, about 150 yen apiece, is the surest way past the doorway. The room smells of sweet bean paste and old tatami. Gran Torino's Kitchenette opens off one side.

Gran Torino's Kitchenette.description: A kitchen barely wide enough for one person, opening off the main room: a stainless sink with a dripping tap, a two-burner gas ring, a dented kettle, and a counter stacked with flattened taiyaki boxes from the corner shop, tied with string for recycling day. A small refrigerator holds milk, pickles and little else, since the taiyaki live in the freezer in the main room, and he heats them in the microwave three at a time, insisting they taste better that way than fresh off the griddle. A teapot and two mismatched cups sit on the drying rack, the second kept for the rare guest he likes. Envelopes from the landlord are pinned to the refrigerator door with a magnet, still sealed. Mornings he drinks strong green tea standing at the window, watching the street; late at night the kettle whistles while hero news plays through the doorway. A visitor who offers to wash up is either thanked gruffly or told they are holding the sponge wrong. The window over the sink looks down the street to the taiyaki griddle in the corner shop's window, and the smell of batter drifts up all afternoon. The doorway leads back to Gran Torino's Main Room.

Kamino Ward.name: Kamino Ward
Kamino Ward.basicInfo: Kamino Ward is an aging ward of Yokohama, about 11 km northwest of the harbor district and some 70 km northeast of U.A. Academy. Half the shops on its covered shopping street have closed, and the backstreets behind it are a tangle of old apartment blocks, two-story wooden houses, small bars, coin laundries, vending machines and empty lots; beyond them lie industrial lots of storage sheds, idle warehouses and yards gone to weeds. Most residents are older people who have lived here for decades, along with day laborers and young people who came for the cheap rent. The ward office runs on a shrinking budget; the prefectural police keep a police box at the shopping street's entrance, and hero patrols pass along the main roads without stopping. Rock Lock, a pro hero whose Quirk locks any nonliving thing he touches in place, is the one familiar hero face on the shopping street, walking it on his own rounds. Mornings belong to shoppers and retirees; at dusk the shutters come down and the backstreet bars stay open late. A player can rent a cheap room by the week, find day labor, drink where nobody asks questions, look for people who do not want to be found, or lend a hand to the old shopkeepers who are still holding on. The nearest station is a few minutes' walk from the shopping street, and its trains can be heard across most of the ward; express lines run from it to Tokyo Station and to the harbor. The ward feels forgotten more than dangerous: quiet, slow and watchful, a place where strangers are noticed and never mentioned.
Kamino Ward.hiddenInfo: Small-time villains from other cities drift into the backstreet bars looking for work, because brokers here are known for jobs that pay cash up front, no questions asked. Most get a phone number and leave town. Right now several wanted people are among the drifters, each one alone: Dabi, a burn-scarred man with blue flames and no past, in the backstreet bars; Magne, loud and big-sisterly, with a huge cloth-wrapped weapon and a Magnetism Quirk, drinking in the same lanes; Twice, a frantic masked man who argues with himself mid-sentence; and Spinner, a gecko heteromorph with a blade of strapped-together knives, who loiters by the electronics shop's game displays. None of them belongs to a crew. This month the phone numbers lead to the same buyer, someone hiring muscle through a broker in Yokohama's Chinatown, paying well and saying nothing. On the ward's northeastern fringe, one bar keeps its lights on but never takes a walk-in customer, and locals have learned not to knock. Northwest of the ward, a sealed warehouse in the industrial lots draws power day and night though nobody is seen going in or out. Brokers rent rooms above the closed shops by the week, cash only, no names asked. The police box is staffed by two officers close to retirement who file as few reports as they can. Rock Lock has noticed the new faces and suspects the ward is turning into a hiring hall; he asked the police for a joint sweep and was told to put it in writing.

Shopping Street.description: A covered shopping arcade three blocks long, its glass roof yellowed and leaking in places, with buckets set out under the worst drips on rainy days. Half the shutters stay down, some sprayed with old graffiti; the open shops are a tofu maker, a pharmacy, a hundred-yen store, a tailor, a pachinko parlor at the far end and an electronics shop whose speakers loop the same jingle all day. Retirees shop here in the morning and sit on the benches to talk; schoolchildren cut through in the afternoon, and the tofu maker sells out of fried tofu by noon. The police box stands at the entrance, its two officers rarely outside it, and the pro hero Rock Lock walks the arcade on his rounds, greeting the shopkeepers by name. After the shutters come down at dusk, the arcade lights flicker over an empty walkway. Gaps between the shuttered shops lead out into the Backstreets. The arcade smells of soy, damp concrete and the tailor's steam iron.

Backstreets.description: Lanes behind the shopping street, between two-story wooden houses, old apartment blocks and empty lots, strung overhead with power lines. Small bars with no signs, a coin laundry, a few vending machines and a shrine the size of a closet are the landmarks, and laundry hangs from balconies over lanes too narrow for a car. Day laborers, bar workers and people renting by the week live here; a labor van collects workers at a corner at 5 a.m., and the bars open at dusk. After dark the bars fill with drinkers who keep their voices low, and the local rule is simple: nobody asks a name, and nobody remembers a face. Newcomers who sit too long or ask too much find the bar suddenly closing for the night. Cats outnumber people on most corners, and an old woman feeds them at the shrine every evening. The lanes wind back to the Shopping Street. The air smells of frying oil, cigarettes and wet wood.

Snack Bar Row.description: A dead-end lane off the Backstreets where a dozen snack bars stack two stories high, each behind a padded door with a glowing name plate the size of a book, the upper ones up steep outside stairs. Inside, each is one counter of eight stools, a karaoke screen, a shelf of bottles tagged with regulars' names, and a mama behind the bar who has run it for decades. The table charge is 2,000 yen, a kept bottle of shochu 6,000, and the mama decides who stays: a stranger gets one drink and a polite word that the seats are reserved. The bars open at eight; day laborers sing old enka off-key after their shift, retirees come early and leave by ten, and after midnight the voices drop. At some counters a man at the far end never sings, and anyone who asks the mama about work gets a phone number written on the back of a coaster, cash up front, no names. Every door has a card asking customers to keep their Quirks to themselves, and one mama keeps a baseball bat behind the bottles anyway. Hero patrols never come down the lane. Air-conditioner units drip on the steps, muffled karaoke leaks from every door, and the lane leads back to the Backstreets.

Late-Night Diner.description: A twenty-four-hour diner on the main road at the mouth of the Shopping Street, its long front window looking across at the police box: red vinyl booths patched with tape, a counter of swivel stools, laminated picture menus and a coffee machine that never cools. The night cook works the grill alone; a curry plate is 650 yen, the morning set of toast, a boiled egg and coffee 400, and refills are free until five. Taxi drivers and night-shift nurses eat here after midnight, laborers fill the counter at half past four before the 5 a.m. van, and retirees take the window booths with their newspapers by eight. In between, the back booths hold people who nurse one coffee for three hours, slide an envelope across the table and leave separately; the staff refill the cups and watch the television. It hangs in a corner playing hero news with the sound off, and the regulars bet coins on the next Hero Billboard Chart. A handwritten card by the register says no Quirks at the table, and a fist-sized dent in the steel counter shows why. The front door opens onto the Shopping Street; a kitchen door at the back lets out into the Backstreets.

Black Market Basement.description: A low basement under one of the snack bars on Snack Bar Row, reached by a steel stair behind the bar's tiny kitchen once the mama has locked the padded door for the night. From about two in the morning until the 5 a.m. labor van, folding tables fill the room under bare bulbs, one for each seller: unregistered support gear in foam-lined cases (grappling launchers, weighted gauntlets, stun batons), forged IDs and residence cards made to order with a week's wait, police-issue Quirk restraints such as heavy cuffs and full-hand mitts gone missing from a transport, phones with no history, and boxes of stolen watches, bags and electronics at a fraction of their price. Buyers come down one at a time on the word of someone the room already knows, and a broker's name at the top of the stair is the only ticket. The rules are taped to the wall and kept by a silent doorman wide enough to block the stair: cash only, no phones out, no names, no Quirks, no haggling above a murmur, no Trigger, and nothing comes back. Anyone who breaks one goes up the stair and is never let down again. A dehumidifier rattles in the corner, and the room smells of mildew, gun oil and the fryer upstairs. A player can buy, sell, fence stolen goods or hear who is buying what. The stair leads back up through the bar to Snack Bar Row.

Kamino Safehouse.description: A single six-mat room over a tobacco shop that closed years ago, its shutter rusted down on a backstreet lane, reached by an outside steel stair at the back. Brokers rent it by the week, cash only and no names asked, and the landlord sends no one up. Blackout curtains are taped at the edges over the one window; there is a futon on the tatami, a low table, an electric kettle, a hot plate, a mini fridge, a sink in the corner and a shared toilet on the landing. A go-bag waits packed by the door: a change of clothes, cash, a burner phone with the battery out, bandages, a cap and a spare mask. The people who sleep here are the ones who cannot sign a hotel register: villains with a warrant, drifters between jobs, people hiding from a debt or a former crew. They come and go after dark, keep the TV low and tuned to the news, and learn which stair treads creak. Through a slit in the curtain the lane below and the corner where the labor van stops are both in view. The walls are thin enough to carry a neighbor's radio and every train at the station, and the room smells of instant noodles, old tatami and stale smoke. A player can sleep, heal, hide, change a look or wait for a phone call. The stair leads down into the Backstreets.

Trigger Dealer's Stairwell.description: A bare concrete stairwell at the back of an emptied apartment block on the Backstreets, five flights with a dead light on every second landing and a steel door propped open with a brick. Trigger changes hands on the third-floor landing: a seller in a hood sits on the steps with a few small glass ampoules in a cigarette tin and takes cash only, and a lookout at the lane mouth whistles if anyone in a uniform turns the corner. Buyers come after dark and do not stay long: day laborers who want one shift's strength, small-time villains before a job, people with weak Quirks who want a few minutes of feeling strong. The landings are scorched, cracked and dented where users tried their boosted Quirks on the walls, and one handrail is bent flat. A user can turn violent at a word and hurt anyone close, and the comedown leaves people slumped on the landings, exhausted and sometimes hurt by their own power. Two or three times a year the prefectural police sweep the block without warning, from both ends at once, and anyone caught holding an ampoule goes to a cell. Rock Lock walks past the lane mouth on his rounds and has started to slow down there. The stairwell smells of stale smoke, scorched concrete and wet cardboard, and every footstep echoes up all five flights. A player can buy, watch, inform, or step in when a user loses control. The door at the bottom opens onto the Backstreets.

League Hideout Bar.name: League Hideout Bar
League Hideout Bar.basicInfo: The League Hideout Bar is a small, dim bar at the end of an alley on the northeastern fringe of Kamino Ward, about 4 km from the shopping street, that no longer serves the public. From the backstreet it is only a steel door with no sign at the end of a dead-end alley. It is the base of the League of Villains, which at the start of the year is two people and almost unknown. Its leader, Tomura Shigaraki, is a thin, pale young man who wears severed hands clasped to his face and body, scratches at his neck when irritated, and talks about villainy as a game; his Quirk turns whatever he touches with all five fingers to dust. Kurogiri, a polite man whose body is dark mist with glowing yellow eyes, tends the bar, does the League's hiring through brokers and opens warp gates with his Quirk. Hired thugs come and go for pay, and most visitors arrive through Kurogiri's gates rather than the door. Kurogiri keeps the glasses polished and the shelves stocked at all hours; Tomura sits at the counter or in the back room playing games. There is no walking in: the door opens only for someone a broker has sent or Kurogiri expects, and a stranger who knocks is turned away through the viewing slot, or worse if Tomura is in a mood. A player can come here to sign on as hired help through a broker's introduction, sell information, or spy on the League from the alley mouth. Inside it is as quiet as a closed shop: low lamps, rows of bottles, a dark monitor on the back wall, and the feeling of being weighed up by people who have already decided what a visitor is worth.
League Hideout Bar.hiddenInfo: Tomura Shigaraki's plans change with his mood and his Sensei's advice; the League pays hired villains in cash through brokers and tells them only what they need. A dark monitor behind the bar carries the voice of the man Shigaraki calls Sensei, who advises him with patience and pays for everything; Kurogiri answers to that voice as much as to Tomura and keeps Sensei's confidences, even from Tomura when Sensei wishes. Kurogiri's mist hides a solid body, and the metal collar at his throat protects it; someone who pins that body can hold him. Tomura's temper is short: when a plan goes wrong he destroys things, and hired help who annoy him do not always leave. Tomura talks about heroes as game bosses and the news as level updates. Kurogiri buys muscle through Giran, the broker in Yokohama's Chinatown, cash up front, and looks hired help over one at a time at the counter. Sensei also supplies the League with Nomu, mindless brutes that obey Tomura and travel by Kurogiri's gates; the hired help are never told what they are or where they are kept. In spring the League is two real members and a borrowed budget; after Hosu it grows to a full crew of recruits, but it stays led by a man learning to lead, and far more dangerous than its size suggests.

Bar Counter.description: A short wooden counter with eight stools, shelves of bottles behind it under a few low lamps, and a dark monitor on the back wall. Kurogiri stands behind the counter polishing glasses at almost any hour, and Tomura Shigaraki sits on the end stool with a handheld game. The few hired villains Tomura wants to meet are brought here to be looked over and given orders, usually after Kurogiri has poured them a drink and asked their price. No music plays; the only sounds are cloth on glass, the click of game buttons and the hum of the refrigerator, and now and then a quiet voice from the monitor that makes Tomura put the game down. Visitors learn fast not to touch Tomura or sit beside him uninvited. A door behind the counter leads into the Back Room, and the steel front door opens on the Alley Entrance. The wood smells of polish and old whiskey.

Back Room.description: A windowless storeroom behind the bar: cases of liquor and soda, a worn sofa, a game console wired to an old television, a folding table buried in printouts, and a cot. Tomura Shigaraki sleeps and plays here when he is not at the counter, and it is where he and Kurogiri argue over plans away from hired ears, with the television paused on whatever stage Tomura was losing. Anything the League does not want its hired help to see is kept here, in folders Kurogiri keeps squared at the corner of the table and Tomura scatters. Snack wrappers pile up by the sofa until Kurogiri clears them without comment. The room smells of dust and stale snacks, and the fluorescent tube overhead flickers on and off. The only door opens back onto the Bar Counter, and hired help are never invited through it.

Alley Entrance.description: A dead-end alley off a backstreet on the fringe of Kamino Ward, too narrow for a car, ending at a plain steel door with no sign and a small viewing slot. Rain gutters drip onto the pavement, a vending machine at the alley's mouth gives the only light, and the buildings on either side have stood empty for years, their windows boarded. Few people use the door: hired villains who were given directions, brokers bringing someone in, and the occasional lost drunk who is sent away. When someone knocks, the slot opens on a pair of glowing yellow eyes in dark mist, and a polite voice asks who sent them; a wrong answer closes the slot for good. For those who are let in, the door opens onto the Bar Counter. Even the neighborhood cats avoid the alley, and the vending machine hums all night with nobody to buy from it.

Corner Booth.description: A horseshoe booth of cracked red leather at the back of the bar, a few steps from the Bar Counter in the same low-lit room, under a dead neon beer sign. It is where the League's regulars sit between jobs: cigarette burns on the table, a deck of cards, Spinner's Stain clippings taped to the wall, Twice's spare masks in a shoebox, empty glasses Kurogiri collects without comment. From here everyone can see the counter, the dark monitor on the back wall and Tomura Shigaraki on his end stool.

Nomu Warehouse.name: Nomu Warehouse
Nomu Warehouse.basicInfo: A plain gray warehouse in a lot of storage sheds and empty yards about 5 km northwest of Kamino Ward's shopping street, out where the ward's old industrial lots run to weeds. From outside it is a long windowless box of corrugated steel on a concrete apron, with welded shutters, a single steel side door with no handle on the outside, a few high vents, and no sign, no company name and no rental notice. Security cameras watch the apron, the door and the gate in the chain-link fence. The neighboring sheds belong to moving firms and a scrap dealer; their workers come and go by day, park their trucks along the fence and leave by dusk, and at night the lot is dark except for one streetlight at the corner and a faint red glow at the high vents. Nobody is ever seen at the door. The building is locked private property: there is no way in without forcing a welded shutter or the door, which is breaking and entering, and nobody nearby has a key or knows who holds the lease. A player can find it only through investigation, and can then watch it, ask the neighbors, dig into who owns it, search it if they find a way in, or report it. Up close, a low mechanical hum comes through the walls day and night, steadier than any freezer, and the steel feels faintly warm to the touch. The place feels empty and occupied at the same time.
Nomu Warehouse.hiddenInfo: Inside, under red standby lights, rows of tall glass tanks filled with fluid hold Nomu: huge, hairless creatures with exposed brains and powerful bodies, kept dormant for the League of Villains and the man Shigaraki calls Sensei, who supplies them. The tank pumps hum in the dark, and that hum is what the neighbors hear. At the start of the year the largest is a massive black-skinned Nomu with a beaked mouth and bulging lidless eyes, built for one job, killing All Might: strength and speed to match his, with Shock Absorption and Super Regeneration. Another is a winged snatcher with batlike wings and four eyes, strong enough to seize a person and carry them off. More tanks hold more Nomu, dormant and waiting. Nobody stays here; the League comes and goes through Kurogiri's warp gates, which is why the door has no outside handle. The building draws heavy power day and night for a place nobody enters, and the utility's meter reader has been paid to stop asking. The warehouse has cameras but no guard; the cameras feed the monitor at the League's bar. While the League holds the place, Kurogiri checks the tanks every few nights. The locks are plain: welded shutters, a steel door barred from inside, a chained fence gate. The danger is plainer: the Nomu do not react to intruders while dormant, but they wake on command and follow Tomura Shigaraki's simple orders without restraint or fear, and stand still without orders. Anyone seen breaking in can expect Kurogiri through a gate within minutes, and a woken Nomu is beyond any first-year and most pros. Right now the night watchman at the neighboring scrap yard has noticed the red glow and the hum and has started writing down the nights lights move inside; he has told no one yet.

Warehouse Loading Dock.description: A cracked concrete apron along the long side of the warehouse, where a raised loading bay meets three roll-up shutters welded shut along their bottom edges, the weld beads rusted to the color of the steel. Beside the bay, a single steel side door sits flush in the wall with no handle, keyhole or bell on the outside. Cameras on short brackets watch the apron, the door and the chained gate in the chain-link fence, and weeds push through every seam in the concrete except the strip in front of the door. By day the moving firms' trucks park along the fence and the scrap dealer's crane clanks next door, and nobody so much as glances at the building; by dusk the lot empties, and the only light is the streetlight at the corner and a faint red glow at the high vents. Up close a low hum comes through the steel day and night, steadier than any freezer, and the wall is faintly warm under a palm. The building is private property: forcing a shutter or the door is breaking and entering, and the nearest police box is a long way back toward the shopping street. A forced shutter or door would open onto the Warehouse Storage Floor.

Warehouse Storage Floor.description: One long dark hall under a high steel roof, lit only by red standby lamps on the pillars. Down the middle stand rows of tall glass tanks full of cloudy fluid, each on a humming pump base fed by thick cables and hoses that run across the floor to a bank of power cabinets at the far end; this is the hum the neighbors hear. In the largest tank floats a massive black-skinned creature with an exposed brain, bulging lidless eyes and a beaked mouth full of teeth, motionless in beige trousers. Another holds a pale, hairless thing with folded batlike wings, four eyes and a plate over its mouth. More shapes hang in the tanks beyond, still and waiting, and none of them reacts to a flashlight or a voice. There are no desks, cots, lockers or food wrappers, nothing to say anyone works here, and the dust on the floor is disturbed only around the tanks, by footprints that start and stop in the middle of the hall rather than at the door. A camera looks down from each corner. The air is warm, damp and smells of chemicals and something like a hospital drain. Whoever forced the way in can go back out to the Warehouse Loading Dock.

Yokohama Harbor District.name: Yokohama Harbor District
Yokohama Harbor District.basicInfo: Yokohama Harbor District is the old port center of Yokohama, about 30 km southwest of central Tokyo and some 70 km east-northeast of U.A. Academy: a waterfront park and seawall promenade, passenger piers, the container docks on reclaimed land, and the painted gates of Chinatown a few blocks inland. Kamino Ward lies about 11 km to the northwest and Takoba Municipal Stadium about 12 km to the west-southwest. The port authority runs the piers and docks, customs officers and the prefectural police watch the cargo, and local hero agencies patrol the promenade and Chinatown. Heroes are a common sight: Gang Orca, the longtime top-ten orca heteromorph whom strangers take for a villain, works the docks with his armored sidekicks; Crust, a rescue-first hero who grows shields from his own body, walks the promenade; and Selkie captains his own patrol ship off the coast on sea-rescue and smuggling cases. Dockworkers keep the container terminal running in shifts around the clock; tourists, couples and school trips crowd the promenade and Chinatown from late morning until late evening. A player can find dock or restaurant work, shop, eat, take a harbor cruise, meet contacts in a crowd, or watch the cargo trade. The promenade and Chinatown are open to anyone; the container terminal needs a port pass at its gate. The nearest station is a short walk from the promenade, with express lines to Tokyo Station. Ship horns, gulls and the smell of salt and diesel carry across the district, and at night the lit cranes and bridges make the whole harbor glow.
Yokohama Harbor District.hiddenInfo: Unlicensed support gear moves through the container docks. Crates declared as machine parts hold grappling launchers, weighted gauntlets and stun batons bound for small-time villains and would-be vigilantes. A customs inspector on the night shift waves certain containers through for cash, usually on the two nights a week when one feeder ship ties up, and the crates leave the terminal through the gap in the seaward fence before dawn. The broker who meets buyers in the private room of a Chinatown restaurant is Giran, the best-known broker in Japan's underworld, who sells introductions, muscle, hideouts and gear to anyone and keeps his records far from that room. One of his steadier clients is a polite man made of mist who buys muscle and pays well for a small group with big talk, and Giran is happy not to ask. Mr. Compress, a masked villain and stage magician who makes people and things vanish into marbles, picks up jobs from Giran and studies the promenade crowds like an audience. Gang Orca suspects something comes off the night ships unseen by customs and has his sidekicks logging which containers leave after midnight; Selkie knows the smugglers' habits on the water and would share them with anyone serious. Hero coverage thins after midnight, when the promenade empties and the docks run on skeleton crews. Chinatown's merchant association pays a local agency for extra patrols during festivals and resents the police for ignoring its complaints the rest of the year.

Harbor Promenade.description: A long seawall promenade and waterfront park with lawns, flower beds and benches facing the water, and passenger piers where ferries, harbor cruises and cruise ships tie up. Joggers and dog walkers use it at dawn, tourists and school groups by day, and couples at night when the cranes and bridges across the water are lit. Street musicians and performers set up near the piers on weekends, and heroes on patrol walk the seawall at regular hours; Crust is the one people stop to thank, and he thanks them back with feeling. The salt wind never stops, gulls work the benches for crumbs, and ships' horns sound across the harbor. Along the waterfront the path runs past fenced lots to the gate of the Container Docks; inland, a few blocks of streets lead to the painted gates of the Chinatown Streets. After midnight the lawns empty and the lamps light only the seawall.

Container Docks.description: A terminal of stacked shipping containers, gantry cranes and straddle carriers on reclaimed land, fenced and gated, with a customs inspection shed by the main gate. Trucks line up at the gate from early morning, and dockworkers, crane operators and customs officers work in shifts around the clock. Entry needs a port pass, shown at the gate booth, though the night crews know a gap in the fence on the seaward side. Gang Orca and his armored sidekicks, who carry cement guns and water for him, are a regular sight on the quay, and Selkie's patrol ship ties up at the terminal between runs. Floodlights keep the yard bright all night, the beeping of reversing trucks never stops, and the container rows form steel canyons where a person can vanish in a few steps. Workers eat at a canteen truck by the gate. The only public way out is back through the gate to the Harbor Promenade.

Chinatown Streets.description: A grid of narrow streets behind ornate painted gates, packed with restaurants, steamed-bun stalls, tea shops, souvenir stores, fortune tellers and a temple heavy with incense. Crowds peak at lunch and in the evening; shopkeepers call out to passersby, and families who have run the same restaurants for generations know every face on their block. Delivery bikes weave through the crowds, and during festivals lion dancers and drums fill the main street. Upstairs rooms over the restaurants are rented for banquets and private meetings, and the staff who serve them are known for never remembering who sat there. Steam from the bun stalls and the smell of roast pork hang in the air, and red lanterns light the streets after dark. The gates on the waterfront side lead back to the Harbor Promenade.

Harbor Jazz Bar.description: A basement jazz bar under an old brick trading house on the street between the seawall and the Chinatown gates, down a flight of worn stairs lined with signed photos of musicians. The room seats forty at small round tables and a long walnut bar, with a baby grand, a drum kit and an upright bass on a low stage under one warm spotlight, and records shelved floor to ceiling behind the bartender. Sets start at seven, nine and half past ten; the cover is 2,500 yen with one drink, and the house rule is no talking during solos. Early sets draw older couples and harbor cruise passengers; later ones bring musicians from other clubs, office workers loosening their ties and the odd sailor off a cargo ship. On Sunday afternoons the stage is open to anyone who signs the sheet, and the only thing the bartender asks musicians to leave at the door is a sound-amplifying Quirk. Off-duty heroes sometimes catch the last set. The room smells of old wood, whiskey and coffee, and a ship's horn now and then lands right on the beat. The stairs climb back to the Harbor Promenade, and the street outside runs inland to the Chinatown Streets.

Waterfront Amusement Pier.description: An amusement park on a reclaimed pier at the far end of the promenade, reached over a short footbridge: a giant Ferris wheel whose hub is a lit clock face, a roller coaster that dives toward the water, a carousel, a drop tower, a game hall and food stands selling crepes, karaage and soft-serve. Entry is free; rides cost 300 to 900 yen by ticket, and a fifteen-minute turn of the Ferris wheel at night is the classic Yokohama date. School trips and families fill it on weekend afternoons, couples queue for the wheel after dark, and the staff close the coaster early whenever the wind off the bay picks up. One ride mechanic's Quirk lets her feel a bolt working loose from across the platform. Each ride posts a sign saying riders who use Quirks to fly, cling or brace will be removed without a refund. A hero merch booth sells Gang Orca plushies to customers who swear they are not scared of him. The pier smells of caramel, popcorn and salt, the coaster's rattle carries over the water, and gulls steal fries from anyone not watching. At ten the lights go off ride by ride, and the footbridge leads back to the Harbor Promenade.

Dockside Safehouse.description: A forty-foot shipping container at the end of a row of retired ones on the terminal's far edge, near the seaward fence, fitted out years ago by a night crew as a break shed and rented now by the week to people who need to lie low. A steel door with a padlock opens on plywood walls, a cot with a sleeping bag, a camp stove, a crate for a table, jugs of water, a bucket behind a curtain and a battery lantern; a vent cut in the roof lets in air and the orange glow of the floodlights. Cash goes to a dockworker who never asks a name, and the key changes hands at the canteen truck by the gate. Smugglers waiting on a ship, sailors who missed one and villains whose faces are on the news have all slept here. The rules are short: no light after dark, no cooking with the door shut, no visitors, and gone before the morning shift whenever the straddle carriers start moving this row. Gang Orca's sidekicks walk the quay logging containers after midnight, so whoever is inside keeps still when boots pass. The hum of the cranes, the beep of reversing trucks and the ships' horns come through the steel, and the air smells of rust, diesel and salt; summer days bake the box and winter nights frost its walls. A player can rest, stash gear, wait out a search or meet one contact. The door opens onto the steel canyons of the Container Docks.

Giran's Chinatown Office.description: A narrow room behind a dried-goods shop on a side street of Chinatown, reached past sacks of dried mushrooms, jars of dried scallops and an old shopkeeper who looks up from her abacus only long enough to nod a customer through the bead curtain. Inside are a desk under a single green-shaded lamp, two folding chairs for clients, a sofa with a cigarette burn on one arm, a wall of cardboard boxes labeled as tea and a small safe that holds cash and nothing written. Giran keeps the hours he chooses, mostly late afternoon into the small hours, and sees clients one at a time: jobs, introductions, forged papers, a week in a hideout, unregistered support gear delivered later to an address he names. He quotes prices with a smile, takes half up front and never says one client's name to another; phones go into a tin box by the door. A heavyset man on the sofa reads a racing paper and does not look up until someone raises a voice. A player can ask for work, buy papers or gear, pay off a debt or ask who is hiring, at Giran's price. The room smells of cigarettes, dried fish and cheap incense from the shop. The curtain leads back through the shop to the Chinatown Streets, and a back door opens on an alley that rejoins the Chinatown Streets two blocks away.

Takoba Municipal Stadium.name: Takoba Municipal Stadium
Takoba Municipal Stadium.basicInfo: Takoba Municipal Stadium is a huge stadium about 12 km west-southwest of Yokohama's harbor and some 60 km east-northeast of U.A. Academy, set among municipal sports fields and parking lots. The municipality owns it, but the Hero Public Safety Commission leases it as a venue for the Provisional Hero License Exam and has fitted it with movable walls and terrain that its crews reshape between sessions. On exam days, more than a thousand examinees from hero academies across Japan gather here, school by school in hero costume, the Commission's examiner Yokumiru Mera reads the rules, and fewer than half the examinees pass: a free-for-all first phase on the arena field, then a rescue phase in the collapsing ruins. Between exams the building is closed to the public except for occasional municipal events, while Commission engineers and maintenance crews work on the terrain; the gates are locked and staffed, and only examinees entered by their academy, Commission staff and hired crews get in. A player can take the exam here when their academy enters them, find work on a maintenance crew or as an exam actor, or scout the facility from the public sports fields outside. Shuttle buses run from the nearest station on exam days, and the parking lots fill with academy buses before dawn. From outside it looks like any big stadium; inside, the field is a landscape of city blocks, cliffs and pipes under open sky. The empty arena echoes with every dropped tool.
Takoba Municipal Stadium.hiddenInfo: Commission engineers are re-rigging the Rescue Exercise Ruins after the last session: one collapse charge failed to fire, and a block of mock buildings is roped off until it is rebuilt. A crew member suspects a contractor wired the charge badly to save money and has kept the faulty part in his locker, unsure whom to show it to. Exam veterans know an unspoken tradition: in the first phase, examinees from other academies go after U.A. Academy students first, because each year's televised U.A. Sports Festival has already shown everyone their Quirks and fighting styles. Actors from the Help Us Company (HUC), professionals who play disaster victims, rehearse here between sessions and score examinees on how they speak to a frightened person as much as on what they do. Pro heroes hired by the Commission may attack during the rescue phase in the role of villains, and the Commission never announces which; Gang Orca, whose judgment of hero candidates it values, is the kind of pro it asks. Every examinee who reaches the rescue phase gets a scored report afterward, with remarks on attitude as well as skill. Yokumiru Mera plans the venue's sessions from his desk in Tokyo and comes out only for the final terrain inspection and on exam days, and the crews work to his schedule, which never has enough hours in it.

Exam Arena.description: The stadium's vast main field, laid out as mixed terrain: a mock city grid, rocky slopes and ravines, a river course, and a block of industrial buildings with tanks and catwalks. On exam days the whole field becomes a free-for-all for more than a thousand examinees at once, and Commission staff watch from the upper levels behind glass, logging every pass and elimination. Between sessions it is empty except for engineers testing the hydraulics and crews hauling rubble, and movable slabs groan as they shift into new layouts. The stands are closed, and every crash or shout echoes back across the field. Dust settles on everything, and wind pours in over the open rim. At the center stands the Waiting Hall, whose walls fold outward onto the field; on the far side, a cordoned district opens into the Rescue Exercise Ruins. Crews wear hard hats and radios, and anyone walking the field without them is stopped within a minute.

Waiting Hall.description: A vast windowless hall at the center of the arena, with bare concrete floors, a small stage and a public-address system. On exam days, examinees in hero costume crowd it school by school, sizing each other up while the Commission's examiner, Yokumiru Mera, reads the rules in a tired voice and mentions how little he has slept. Each examinee is handed the first phase's equipment at the door; old acquaintances from other academies trade greetings, and someone always tries to read the room's Quirks before the rules are finished. When the first phase begins, the hall's walls fold outward and open straight onto the Exam Arena. Between exams it stores equipment: stacked chairs, crates and coiled cable. Empty, it is cold, and every footstep rings off the steel wall panels.

Rescue Exercise Ruins.description: A district of mock buildings rigged to collapse on command, leaving rubble fields, broken water mains and burning wreckage for the exam's rescue phase. Before that phase, actors from the Help Us Company take their places in the debris in convincing wound makeup and play disaster victims who score how examinees treat them; pro heroes hired by the Commission may attack mid-rescue in the role of villains. Between sessions, Commission crews rebuild the ruins and test the charges, and one roped-off block waits for repair. Hidden speakers play sirens, cries and the creak of failing beams on cue, and the footing is uneven enough to turn an ankle. Examinees are expected to set up their own first-aid station and evacuation point, and the actors notice who forgets. The air carries concrete dust and the sweet smell of stage blood. The cordon on its open side leads back onto the Exam Arena.

Deika City.name: Deika City
Deika City.basicInfo: Deika City is a prosperous mountain city built around Detnerat, one of Japan's biggest makers of support items, from hero gear to everyday aids for people whose Quirks make ordinary life hard. Detnerat's headquarters tower and factory campus stand at the edge of downtown, most families have someone on its payroll, and the company pays for the parks, the schools, the festivals and the new city hall. Its president, Rikiya Yotsubashi, a tall, courteous man who bows lower than his guests, is often seen beside the mayor on City Hall Plaza, and the politician Koku Hanabata gives civic talks there that draw large, orderly crowds; the local paper is edited by Chitose Kizuki, a journalist known for getting people to say more than they meant. Crime figures are among the lowest in the country; the few local hero agencies are rarely busy, and neighborhood associations settle disputes before anyone calls the police. Factory shifts change at 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., filling the streets with workers in company jackets; an evening market runs downtown, and by eleven the city is quiet. Detnerat hires temporary workers and runs public factory tours, which need booking a day ahead; the factory floors and the headquarters tower are otherwise closed to anyone without a company badge. Visitors notice the clean streets, the identical banners on every lamppost and the way conversations pause when a stranger sits down nearby. Deika Station has trains to Jaku City (about 14 km east-southeast), Hosu (about 90 km, an hour) and Tokyo (about 120 km, an hour and a half); U.A. Academy is about 150 km south, two and a half hours by rail. Gunga Mountain rises to the northwest, its private villa about an hour's drive away.
Deika City.hiddenInfo: Deika is the living heart of the Meta Liberation Army, a movement the public believes was crushed long ago. Nearly all the residents are sworn members who hold that free Quirk use is a human right; they train in basements and company gyms and cover for one another without being asked. Detnerat's president, Rikiya Yotsubashi, is the son of the army's founder, Destro, and leads it as Re-Destro, with his devoted lieutenant Geten at his side; Detnerat's money and gear supply the members. Two more lieutenants work in plain sight: Koku Hanabata, Trumpet, whose voice strengthens every listener who accepts him as leader, which is why his crowds answer as one; and Chitose Kizuki, Curious, who shapes the local news and researches anyone worth a story. The order is patience: obey the law in public and report any outsider who asks about Destro, the old army or the residents' Quirks. Right now neighborhood associations are vetting every new hire and tenant; anyone who asks the wrong questions gets a friendly visit next morning and is reported up the chain. Younger members are impatient for the day the army shows itself. A new problem walks the Downtown Streets: Muscular, a wanted serial killer who sells his violence to anyone offering a strong opponent, has drifted into town and spends his evenings at the market picking quarrels, and members under orders swallow his insults rather than use their Quirks in public. The associations reported him up the chain, not to the police. Re-Destro wants to know who sent him, and Kizuki has started asking.

Downtown Streets.description: Wide, spotless avenues of offices, cafes and department stores run from Deika Station to the Detnerat campus, lined with young zelkova trees and identical company banners on every lamppost. At shift changes, seven in the morning and seven at night, the sidewalks fill with workers in company jackets; in the evening a street market sets up along the main avenue, with grilled food, secondhand books, Detnerat seconds sold cheap and local crafts. Shopkeepers greet strangers warmly and remember their faces. Residents talk about their Quirks openly, and heteromorph shoppers draw no second looks; doors are wide and benches built for every kind of body. A huge, scarred man in a red tank top has been loitering at the market stalls lately, and people step around him with practiced calm. The same city radio station plays from every shop doorway, and the avenue leads to City Hall Plaza.

City Hall Plaza.description: A broad stone square in front of the new glass city hall, with a fountain, a covered stage and a wall of neighborhood notices. Office workers eat lunch on the benches; neighborhood associations meet in the hall's rooms in the evening; on weekend nights the stage hosts concerts and civic talks that draw large, orderly crowds, Koku Hanabata's most of all. The mayor and Detnerat's community staff often appear together, and the company's president, Rikiya Yotsubashi, sometimes stops to chat with families by the fountain. When a speaker pauses, the whole crowd answers at once, and outsiders find they are the only ones who did not know the reply. The notice wall lists clean-up days, job openings at Detnerat and new arrivals welcomed by name. The Downtown Streets lead back toward the station.

Deika Evening Market.description: Every evening from six, the market fills the pedestrian block of the main avenue nearest City Hall Plaza: two rows of identical numbered white canopies strung with bulbs, under the company banners that hang from every lamppost. Stalls sell grilled squid and yakitori, mountain vegetables, secondhand books, crafts and Detnerat seconds at half price: mobility aids, grip gloves and visors with scuffed paint. A bowl of soba is 500 yen. The rush comes after the seven o'clock shift change, when workers in company jackets stop for dinner; by ten the canopies are down and the street swept spotless. Neighborhood association volunteers in armbands keep order, welcome every stranger, ask where they are staying and how long, and jot the answers in notebooks with a smile. Residents talk openly about their Quirks in the queues. Lately a huge, scarred stranger has been picking quarrels at the grill stands, and the stallholders answer every insult with a bow and an apology. Charcoal smoke hangs over the canopies, and the city radio plays from every pole. The market runs back into the Downtown Streets, and its far end opens onto City Hall Plaza.

Deika Station Cafe.description: A bright cafe in Deika Station's main concourse, glass-fronted toward the ticket gates, with pale wood tables and a pastry case of chestnut cakes. The morning rush comes before the seven o'clock shift change, when Detnerat workers in company jackets queue for a 350-yen coffee and a breakfast sandwich, and the staff know most orders before anyone speaks. Midday brings travelers waiting for the Tokyo and Hosu trains and visitors booked on the factory tour, who are handed a city map with the tour office circled. Evenings are quiet but for commuters and the ticking departure board. Wide chairs, tall stools and a low counter suit every kind of body. The staff are unfailingly warm and curious: a newcomer is asked where they are from, what brings them to Deika and what their Quirk is, as small talk, and by the second visit the staff remember every answer. Conversations at the next table pause when a stranger sits down and pick up again a beat later. The city radio plays from the ceiling, and a framed poster of the company president bowing beside the mayor hangs by the door. The doors open from the concourse onto the Downtown Streets.

Gunga Mountain Villa.name: Gunga Mountain Villa
Gunga Mountain Villa.basicInfo: A large private villa high on Gunga Mountain, about 18 km north-northwest of Deika City, at the end of a private road that leaves the highway at a locked gate with cameras and an intercom. The main house is a modern lodge of concrete and timber with guest wings, a big dining hall and garages, set in cleared grounds with forest falling away on every side. The deeds name a holding company owned by a wealthy Deika family, and people in the valley say only that the owners keep to themselves. A caretaker crew lives on site all year, and a cold, white-haired young man called Geten lives here too and drills the weekend guests; the caretakers defer to him. Most weekends, cars and chartered buses come up the road with guests for what the caretakers call company retreats, and the place is empty again by Monday. Hikers who wander onto the slopes are turned back politely. There is no shop, inn or station; Deika Station is about an hour's drive, and the gate opens only for cars on the guest list or for staff. In April snow still lies on the upper slopes, and the road can close after a storm. Guests arrive Friday evening, drill on the slopes on Saturday and Sunday mornings, eat together in the dining hall and leave on Sunday night; during the week the caretakers do repairs, deliveries come up from Deika, and the house is nearly silent. A player can come here as hired staff, as an invited guest, or over the fence. The air is thin and cold, the silence is total, and from the terrace the lights of Deika look very far away.
Gunga Mountain Villa.hiddenInfo: The villa belongs to the Meta Liberation Army, held through companies tied to Detnerat. Its leaders use it for meetings they cannot hold in the city, and members come up in groups for weekend training on the slopes, where they use their Quirks at full strength with no one to report them. Geten, one of the army's four lieutenants and its truest believer, runs those drills and answers only to Re-Destro. The caretakers are members; cameras at the gate feed a guard room, and anyone who gets past the gate is photographed and their name sent down to Deika. Right now the crew is expanding the cellars and dormitory wings to sleep far more people than any family retreat needs. Something else shares the mountain. In the deep ravines below the drill slopes lives Gigantomachia, a colossal man who serves one master, never named, and keeps away from trails and towns; almost nobody has heard of him. He sleeps for days between orders and ignores anyone who does not block his path. This spring a drill group came back from the lower tracks with stories of cedars torn out by the roots and a landslide rumble that went on and on, and Geten has put the deep ravines off-limits without explaining why. The private road is the only way in for vehicles, and a landslide or heavy snow can close it for days.

Villa Grounds.description: A gravel drive, garages and a paved forecourt in front of the main house, whose long terrace looks down the valley toward the lights of Deika. Caretakers sweep, repair and cook through the week; on weekends the forecourt fills with cars and the terrace with guests in casual clothes who all seem to know one another, and meals in the dining hall run in shifts. Geten, white-haired and wrapped in a long light-blue parka, walks the terrace before the morning drills and sizes up every new guest's Quirk before he looks at their face. A guard room by the garages watches the gate cameras day and night. The grounds are so quiet that every car on the gravel is heard in the guard room before it reaches the house. A path from the edge of the forecourt drops down to the Mountain Slopes.

Mountain Slopes.description: Steep slopes of cedar and beech below the villa, cut by old logging tracks and ravines, with snow lingering in the shaded hollows into April. Some clearings are scorched, frozen solid or cratered where Quirks have been used at full strength. Groups come down from the villa early in the morning to drill and climb back before dark; caretakers walk the tracks in the afternoon.
