Below the drill clearings the ravines run deep and dark, and nobody from the villa goes down there now; from them, now and then, comes a long landslide rumble that never quite finishes. Sound carries a long way here: the thud of impacts and the crack of breaking ice echo across the valley, and the people below have stopped asking about it. The logging track climbs back to the Villa Grounds.

Villa Great Hall.description: The largest room in the villa's main house, at the end of a long corridor past the dining hall: a high hall under timber beams, with a polished concrete floor, a wall of tall windows facing the valley and the far lights of Deika, and a great stone fireplace at the far end. Folding chairs for several hundred stand stacked along the walls between gatherings, and a low wooden dais before the fireplace holds a lectern and a single microphone, with a projector screen that rolls down from the beams. The villa's owners and their guests use the hall for meetings they would not hold in the city: speeches on Friday nights when the buses arrive, plans laid out on maps across trestle tables, and long sessions that end with the whole room on its feet. Guests talk openly here in a way they never would down in Deika, and a stranger who asks the wrong question is remembered. On weekdays the caretakers air it out, wax the floor and restack the chairs, and the sound of a single broom carries from end to end. The fire warms only the rows near the dais, so the back rows sit in their coats, and the hall smells of woodsmoke, floor wax and the cedar forest outside. A player who comes as staff, as a guest or over the fence can hear a speech, meet the people who run the villa or look over what was left on the tables. Double doors at the front open onto the terrace and the Villa Grounds.

Jaku City.name: Jaku City
Jaku City.basicInfo: Jaku is a mid-sized regional city in a mountain basin, plainer and quieter than its neighbor Deika: a compact, busy downtown around Jaku Station and residential hills climbing on three sides. Its best-known institution is Jaku General Hospital, about 4 km northeast of downtown, which draws patients and visiting families from across the region and employs a good share of the city. Downtown, an old covered arcade of family shops runs off the station's south side, business hotels and karaoke boxes crowd the north exit, and a few IT and logistics firms rent offices above the department stores, among them the company whose exacting executive, Tomoyasu Chikazoku, is known around the station cafes for never closing his laptop. Two small local hero agencies and the city police handle traffic accidents, weather emergencies and petty Quirk crime; anything serious brings in heroes from Hosu. Weekday mornings belong to commuters, afternoons to shoppers and hospital visitors with flowers, evenings to the bars around the station; the hills are dark and quiet by ten. Rents are cheap, the hospital and the station hotels are always hiring, and shuttle buses run from the station to the hospital. Trains run to Deika City (about 14 km west-northwest), Hosu (about 70 km southeast, an hour) and Tokyo (about 100 km, an hour and a half); U.A. Academy is about 140 km away, two and a half hours by rail. Spring comes late here: the cherry trees on the hill streets bloom in mid-April, and evenings off the mountains are cold. A player can find hotel, shop or hospital work, rent a cheap room in the hills, shop the arcade, or help the local agencies with a city that has more trouble than it admits.
Jaku City.hiddenInfo: Jaku is less peaceful than it looks. A burglar has hit eleven houses in the residential hills since February, always in daylight while the owners are at work, and has never been seen; the police have one detective on it, and the local agency covering the hills has no leads. Residents have started night watches, and last week a watch group cornered a hospital nurse walking home from a late shift. Downtown, the shopkeepers' association is split over a Deika developer's offer to buy the old covered arcade, and the members who argued loudest against the sale have been getting polite visits from people they do not know, who mention their loan balances and their relatives' jobs word for word from a file. Those files come from Tomoyasu Chikazoku, who as Skeptic runs the Meta Liberation Army's data and surveillance behind his corporate career and treats the arcade as a project to finish on schedule. Separately, a slim young man has been staying at a station business hotel for two weeks, paying in cash and waiting on a job from a broker; the night clerk once saw a gas mask with hoses to a tank in his bag. He is Mustard, a villain who hides in a cloud of knockout gas and backs it with a handgun, and he despises U.A.'s students as pampered elites. The local agencies are stretched thin, and on a bad night help from Hosu is an hour away by train.

Jaku Downtown.description: A compact grid of department stores, chain restaurants, karaoke boxes, pachinko halls and business hotels around Jaku Station, with an old covered arcade of family shops on its south side, where a tofu maker, a tea merchant and a stationer have kept the same storefronts for generations; a petition against the arcade's sale hangs half-signed in the tea shop window. Weekday mornings are commuters and delivery vans; afternoons bring hospital visitors buying flowers and fruit baskets; after dark the side streets fill with office workers in izakaya. A local hero walks the station plaza at rush hour, and the shuttle bus to the hospital leaves from the stand by the north exit. The station's departure chime carries across the plaza, along with smoke from the yakitori stands outside the north exit. Streets and stairways climb from the downtown edge into the Residential Hills.

Residential Hills.description: Narrow streets of family houses, small apartment blocks and terraced gardens climb the slopes above downtown, joined by steep stairways and a single bus route. Retirees, young families and hospital staff on rotating shifts live here. Days are quiet apart from morning walks to school, garbage trucks and the occasional delivery van, and lately neighbors watch every unfamiliar van with suspicion; a hand-lettered sign at the bottom of the main stairway announces the new night watch. By ten at night the streets are dark, neighbors know which car belongs in which driveway, and the watch groups walk past with flashlights. At six every evening a temple bell rings from the top of the hill, and the wind off the mountains carries it across the whole slope. The streets and stairways lead back down to Jaku Downtown.

Jaku Covered Arcade.description: The old covered arcade runs four blocks south from the station under a curved roof of frosted panels, many of them cracked, with a tiled walkway worn into a shallow groove down the middle. Family shops line both sides: the tofu maker selling warm soy milk at seven, the tea merchant roasting hojicha in a drum by the door, the stationer, a fishmonger, a sweet shop selling dango at 120 yen a skewer, and a few shutters down for good. Retirees shop in the mornings, hospital visitors buy fruit baskets and flowers in the afternoons, and most shops close by seven. The petition against the arcade's sale hangs half-signed in the tea shop window, and lately a few of its loudest backers have gone strangely quiet. A sidekick from one of the two local agencies buys lunch at the tofu shop every day. Signs at both ends ask shoppers to leave bicycles at the entrance and Quirks at home. The arcade smells of roasting tea and soybeans, an old radio plays enka at the fishmonger's, and at dusk the mountain wind whistles through the cracked panels. The north end opens onto Jaku Downtown; the south end meets the stairways into the Residential Hills.

Izakaya by the Tracks.description: A row of izakaya built into the brick arches under the raised tracks just east of Jaku Station: each one a single room with a counter and three or four tables, noren curtains, red lanterns, beer crates for extra seats and a menu on paper strips along the wall. Yakitori is 150 yen a skewer, a mug of draft beer 450, a highball 380, and the house rule is to order a drink before sitting down. Trains rumble overhead every few minutes and rattle the glasses, and the regulars pause mid-sentence for every train without noticing. Office workers come straight from work at six, hospital staff off the late shift drift in near eleven, and karaoke stragglers fill the last tables until closing at one. Guests from the station business hotels sometimes eat alone at the counters, paying cash and saying little. The cooks grill over charcoal facing the lane, and smoke sweet with tare sauce drifts out under the arches. A local hero walks the row at closing to settle the odd argument over a bill, and a card by each door says trouble goes to the station police box and Quirks stay out of it. The lane under the tracks leads back to Jaku Downtown.

Jaku General Hospital.name: Jaku General Hospital
Jaku General Hospital.basicInfo: Jaku General Hospital is the largest hospital in the region: a ten-story main tower with an emergency wing, outpatient clinics and a department for Quirk-related injuries and illness, on a rise about 4 km northeast of downtown Jaku. It is well funded and well run, and its director, Kyudai Garaki, an elderly geriatric doctor with an immense white mustache and stacked-lens goggles, is respected across the region; he still makes rounds on the wards, chuckling at his own jokes, and the staff speak well of him. Patients come from Jaku, Deika and farther away, and the emergency department takes Quirk injuries from the whole area. Outpatient clinics run from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.; visiting hours are 1 to 8 p.m.; the emergency department and the wards run around the clock on three nursing shifts. The lobby and wards are open to patients and visitors in those hours; the basement service levels are staff-only behind ID badge doors, and after dark only the emergency entrance is open. A player can work here as a porter, cleaner, clerk or security guard, or as a nurse or doctor with the right license; recover from injuries; visit patients; or look into an accident case. Shuttle buses leave Jaku Station every twenty minutes for the twenty-minute ride, and Deika City is about 17 km away by road. The building smells of floor polish and antiseptic, and the paging system chimes all day.
Jaku General Hospital.hiddenInfo: Heteromorph patients are sent to a separate waiting room and, when admitted, to a separate floor. The hospital calls it specialized care; staff know it began after complaints from other patients, and a heteromorph patients' group is preparing a public protest for May. The emergency department lost two night doctors in March, and on busy nights ambulances are quietly redirected to Hosu, more than an hour away. One of the night porters sells news of injured pro heroes to tabloid reporters, which is why photographers sometimes reach the lobby before the hero's own agency does. Hospital security suspects a leak but has not found it. The director is the other quiet story. Kyudai Garaki will not retire, and the board's polite requests that he name the doctor who will take over go unanswered. He keeps his research office locked and works there alone late at night; what he studies he never discusses. Deliveries addressed to him personally go to that door unopened, and the night porters have learned not to ask. He takes a collector's delight in unusual Quirks, asks to examine any rare case that comes through the Quirk ward, and charms patients into agreeing. Nobody on the staff has ever seen his own Quirk at work; he chuckles off the question. To everyone here he is a kindly, eccentric workaholic, and nothing on the record says otherwise.

Hospital Lobby.description: A tall glass atrium with a reception counter, rows of blue seats, a pharmacy window, a convenience store and a small cafe that sells the best melon bread in Jaku. From 8 a.m. it fills with outpatients holding numbered tickets; afternoons bring visitors with flowers; at night only the emergency entrance is open and one guard watches the doors. Heteromorph patients are directed to a separate waiting room down a side corridor, and the sign pointing them there has been defaced twice this spring. Elderly patients sometimes linger after their appointments in the hope that the director will pass through on his way to the wards. A soft electronic chime and a recorded voice call out ticket numbers all day long. Elevators rise to the Patient Wards, and a staff-only door behind the pharmacy leads down to the Basement Service Levels.

Patient Wards.description: Eight floors of wards above the lobby: general medicine, surgery, a pediatric floor with painted walls, and a Quirk injury ward with reinforced rooms for patients whose Quirks flare under fever or anesthesia. Nurses change shifts at 8 a.m., 4 p.m. and midnight; visitors come from 1 to 8 p.m.; nights are quiet but for rounds and monitors. The elderly director makes his own rounds most mornings, sitting an hour with a lonely patient and lingering longest at the Quirk ward. The Quirk ward's doors are heavy and slow to close, and a card beside each one lists the patient's Quirk for the staff. Day rooms on each floor have a television, a shelf of donated paperbacks and a view over the basin to the mountains. The elevators lead back down to the Hospital Lobby.

Basement Service Levels.description: Two staff-only levels under the main tower: the laundry, central sterile supply, kitchens, the generator and boiler plant, medical records storage, the morgue and the loading dock where supply trucks unload. ID badges open the doors, and porters push carts through long, low corridors at all hours. Days are busy with deliveries; at night the levels are nearly empty except for the boiler engineers and porters taking cigarette breaks by the dock, swapping hospital gossip and the occasional rumor sold on. Sealed crates addressed to the director come in through the dock now and then and are wheeled away without a docket. The air is warm and smells of laundry steam, over the steady hum of the generators. The service elevators and stairs lead back up to the Hospital Lobby.

Wild Wild Pussycats Lodge.name: Wild Wild Pussycats Lodge
Wild Wild Pussycats Lodge.basicInfo: The lodge is a large two-story timber building in a mountain valley, deep in the private forest land owned and patrolled by the Wild Wild Pussycats, a four-hero mountain rescue team that has worked together for well over a decade: Mandalay (Telepath), the calm leader who speaks into many minds at once; Pixie-Bob (Earth Flow), loud and theatrical, who reshapes whole hillsides; Ragdoll (Search), bubbly and exact, who tracks up to a hundred people she has seen; and Tiger (Pliabody), the massive drill instructor who bends his body at impossible angles. They wear matching cat-themed costumes and strike their team pose for every introduction. It is their office, bunkhouse and training base, and Kota Izumi, the small boy in Mandalay's care, lives here with them, scowling under a horned cap. In summer the lodge hosts U.A. Academy's training camp and sleeps about forty guests; the rest of the year the team answers search-and-rescue calls across a wide stretch of mountains. Their day starts at dawn with drills and radio checks, and calls come at any hour; in April, snowmelt, mudslides and lost hikers keep them busy. A player can train here with the team's permission, volunteer as rescue support, help run the lodge, or recover in the hot spring; the land is private, and anyone who arrives uninvited is greeted kindly and asked their business. One mountain road climbs to the lodge from the highway, about 130 km northwest of U.A. Academy, three to four hours by chartered bus; there is no rail line, and the nearest town is far down the valley. Beast's Forest lies to the northwest, about three hours across on foot for the team. The lodge smells of woodsmoke, curry and cedar, and the radio is never off.
Wild Wild Pussycats Lodge.hiddenInfo: The team is busier and poorer than its cheerful act suggests. Four heroes cover hundreds of square kilometers, rescue work pays little, and summer camp fees and merchandise keep the agency afloat. Mandalay's Telepath only sends: she can speak into many minds at once but hears nothing back, so the team relies on radios and on Ragdoll's Search, which tracks the position and weaknesses of up to a hundred people at once, but only people she has seen. Kota disappears for hours most afternoons; Mandalay has never found where he goes, and his contempt for heroes is getting worse. Ragdoll keeps him registered, and Mandalay has asked her not to say where he is unless he is in danger; that is the arrangement between them, and Kota does not know it exists. Pixie-Bob spends her mornings in the forest reshaping trails the winter washed out. Right now a group of video streamers keeps sneaking into Beast's Forest to film the earth beasts; the team has warned them twice. Ragdoll registered the two who argued with her at the road lookout, but the third stayed behind the camera, and she never saw that one. Their car has been parked at the lookout for two nights, and nobody at the lodge has checked it yet; the radio log shows no call. When the team finds out, Mandalay will want every pair of hands on the slopes before dark.

Lodge Hall.description: The main building: an entry hall racked with boots, ropes and rescue packs, a long dining hall with low tables for forty, a map and radio room the team uses as its office, and guest rooms upstairs. Breakfast is at seven and dinner at half past six; at night the team gathers around the map table to plan the next day's searches, and Pixie-Bob complains about her love life until Mandalay cuts her off. Framed team photos line the stairs, decades of the same pose in the same cat ears. Kota eats fast and leaves early. The radio scanner crackles all day, and at mealtimes Mandalay calls everyone in by speaking straight into their heads. Doors lead out to the Outdoor Kitchen behind the lodge, the Hot Spring Bath and the Training Clearing beside it.

Outdoor Kitchen.description: A roofed cooking area behind the lodge: wood-fired stoves, giant rice cookers, long prep tables and stacks of pots big enough to feed forty. During camps the guests cook their own meals here; the rest of the year the team takes turns, cooking curry and stew in bulk for the week, and Kota is often put to work peeling vegetables, which he does in silence and badly on purpose. Ragdoll hums while she chops and greets anyone new at full volume. A woodpile and a chopping block stand at one end, and a hose bib by the sink is the only water. The air smells of woodsmoke and curry, and the house rule is that whoever burns the rice washes every pot. The back door leads into the Lodge Hall.

Hot Spring Bath.description: Outdoor rock pools fed by a natural hot spring, split into men's and women's sides by a tall wooden wall, with a changing house and a covered rinsing area of low stools and wooden buckets. Guests can bathe from four in the afternoon until eleven at night; the team uses the pools after night searches to thaw out, and the morning soak belongs to whoever came back from the latest call. A hand-painted sign asks bathers to rinse first and keep their voices down, and Pixie-Bob ignores the second half. Steam rises into the cold air, the water smells faintly of sulfur, and a mountain stream runs loud just beyond the fence, swollen with snowmelt in April. A stone path leads back to the Lodge Hall.

Training Clearing.description: A wide stretch of packed earth and rock beside the lodge, ringed by forest and a low cliff, which Pixie-Bob reshapes on request into slopes, pits and walls. Tiger runs body-conditioning drills here at dawn, barking short orders and demonstrating rather than explaining; Mandalay and Ragdoll run search exercises in the afternoon; during camps, dozens of students push their Quirks here from morning to dusk under the team's supervision. A rack of stretchers and climbing gear stands at the edge for rescue carries. The ground never stays the same from one day to the next, and yesterday's footprints end at walls that were not there. The lodge's side door leads back into the Lodge Hall.

Men's Bunk Room.description: The larger of the two guest rooms upstairs in the lodge: one long tatami room under the slope of the roof, with sliding paper doors onto the landing, a row of small windows facing the forest, and futons for twenty-some guests stacked in a wall cupboard by day and rolled out edge to edge at night. A low table sits by the window under a single paper lamp; bags, boots and drying towels collect along the walls no matter how often Tiger orders them tidied. During U.A.'s summer camp the Hero Course men sleep here, falling onto their futons after twelve hours in the Training Clearing, too sore to talk, or else talking far too long: pillow fights, a card game on the low table, someone snoring in a way that sounds like a Quirk, and Tenya Iida announcing lights-out at ten and enforcing it alone. The windows stay open for the cold mountain air, the wooden floor creaks on the stairs, and the smell is cedar, liniment and the curry from dinner below. The rest of the year it holds rescue volunteers and the odd stranded hiker. The stairs lead down to the Lodge Hall.

Women's Bunk Room.description: The second guest room upstairs, across the landing from the men's: a long tatami room with sliding paper doors, a row of windows looking down over the Hot Spring Bath's wooden wall to the trees, futons stacked in a cupboard by day and laid out in two neat rows at night, and a mirror and outlets by the door that are always fought over. A kotatsu-style low table holds snacks, a first-aid kit and a fan; Ragdoll has left a hand-drawn welcome card on the wall. During U.A.'s summer camp the Hero Course women sleep here after the day's training: sore arms, muscle cream passed hand to hand, talk about the day's drills and Pixie-Bob's matchmaking, Toru Hagakure's floating pajamas startling whoever wakes first, and a firm rule that the door stays closed after lights-out. Mornings start before dawn when Tiger's whistle carries up the stairs. The room smells of cedar, soap from the bath and the forest through the window screens. The rest of the year rescue volunteers and stranded hikers sleep here. The stairs lead down to the Lodge Hall.

Beast's Forest.name: Beast's Forest
Beast's Forest.basicInfo: Beast's Forest is the dense mountain forest northwest of the Pussycats' lodge, part of the team's private land: steep slopes of cedar, beech and oak, mossy ravines, fast streams and almost no trails. Pixie-Bob uses her Quirk, Earth Flow, to raise beasts of soil and rock that stalk and attack anyone crossing, which makes it one of the hardest training courses in the country. The team runs survival and rescue training here and sends camp guests through on foot, and nobody enters without the team's say; signs at the road and at the lodge's edge mark it as private training land. From the lookout on the mountain road at the forest's far edge, the lodge is a speck across the valley; the team crosses in about three hours, most visitors take all day. In April the streams run high with snowmelt, old snow lies in the shaded gullies, and Pixie-Bob is out most mornings rebuilding the trails and slopes the winter washed out. Camp guests who cross it carry a radio and a whistle, and the team checks every group out at the edge and back in at the far side. A player can train here with the team's permission, cross it as a test, help Pixie-Bob rebuild a washed-out slope, or go in after someone who should not be there; anyone caught inside without permission is walked out and warned. Under the trees the light is green and dim even at noon, the ground is soft with needles and moss, and the only warning a beast gives is the sound of earth shifting where no one is walking.
Beast's Forest.hiddenInfo: The beasts are only soil and rock moving under Pixie-Bob's control: break one and it collapses into dirt, and she can raise another as fast as it falls. She cannot make earth, so a beast raised on wet ground is soft and a beast raised on rock is hard. The beasts are meant to chase and pin, not to maim, and she pulls them back the moment someone is hurt. The real dangers are the terrain and the weather: ravines hidden by undergrowth, a stream crossing that floods after rain, and freezing April nights. A group of video streamers has been sneaking in from the road lookout to film the beasts, and one of them has not come back out. The two Ragdoll registered when she warned them off are back in the valley town, editing footage and telling no one; the third, the one behind the camera, went in alone two days ago to get the shot they missed and is now somewhere in the lower ravines with a twisted ankle, a dead phone and no food. Their car still sits at the lookout. Ragdoll never saw the third, so her Search cannot find them; only boots, a careful eye and the streamers' footage will.

Forest Trailhead.description: The edge of the forest on the lodge's side, where a cut meadow of rough grass stops at a wall of cedar and beech. A weathered wooden board, painted with the team's cat-ear logo, states the rules in plain words: private training land, no entry without the Wild Wild Pussycats' permission, earth beasts active, carry a radio and a whistle, check out here and back in at the far side. Under a little roof beside it hang a clipboard log, spare whistles, a first-aid bag and a bear bell on a cord,. One muddy track leads in and narrows to nothing within a few hundred steps. Most mornings Pixie-Bob strides out from here at first light with a thermos and comes back filthy at lunch, loudly reporting which slopes the winter took; during camps, groups of U.A. students gather here in the morning chill for a team pose and a briefing before the beasts are let loose. In April the meadow is soggy with snowmelt, old snow lies gray in the shade, and the first gust from the trees carries the cold smell of wet earth and cedar. From here the track runs into the Deep Forest, and a side path drops toward the Forest Ravine.

Deep Forest.description: The heart of the forest, where the trails give out entirely and the slopes are a tangle of old cedar, beech and oak, with fallen trunks thick with moss and roots that stand up like steps. The light is green and dim even at noon, the ground is soft with needles, and the only marks of people are a few strips of faded orange tape tied to branches by the team and the boot prints of whoever came through last. This is where Pixie-Bob's Earth Flow does its work: soil and rock heave up into beasts with stone teeth and clumsy, heavy legs that stalk crossers, chase them and pin them down, and collapse back into dirt when they are broken or called off. Beasts raised on wet ground come up soft and crumbling; on rock they come up hard. The team crosses in about three hours, most visitors take all day, and camp groups crossing it are checked over the radio on the hour. In April the snowmelt has left soft patches and fresh slides, and bears are waking hungry. The only warning a beast gives is the sound of earth shifting where nobody is walking. The way back leads to the Forest Trailhead, and the slope falls away downhill into the Forest Ravine.

Forest Ravine.description: A narrow, mossy cut in the forest floor where a fast stream runs between boulders, ferns and walls of wet rock ten or twenty meters high. Undergrowth hangs over the rim and hides the drop until the ground gives way, and the only ways down are a few steep gullies of loose stones and roots. The stream bed is a jumble of slick rocks and fallen logs; one crossing has a fixed rope the team strung years ago, and after a night of rain the water rises over it and goes brown and loud. In April the stream runs high and icy with snowmelt, old snow lies packed in the shaded corners, and the air down here is several degrees colder than on the slopes above. There is no phone signal, and even the radios crackle between the walls. The team uses the ravine for rope rescue drills and stretcher carries, and Pixie-Bob rebuilds the gully steps here after every storm; camp guests are warned at the briefing that the ravine, not the beasts, is what actually hurts people. Voices echo strangely off the rock, and a whistle carries farther along the water than up the walls. Gullies climb back up to the Deep Forest and, farther along, to the Forest Trailhead.

Kota's Secret Hideout.name: Kota's Secret Hideout
Kota's Secret Hideout.basicInfo: A rock ledge high on a cliff on the Pussycats' land, northeast of their lodge and more than an hour's scramble from it, reached by a long scramble up a dry streambed and a last stretch of hand-over-hand climbing. It is a flat shelf of stone big enough for a few people to sit on, with a couple of wind-bent pines, a shallow overhang that keeps off the rain, and a view over the whole valley and the forest beyond. Kota Izumi, the small boy in Mandalay's care, climbs up here when he wants to be away from heroes, which is most afternoons, and goes back down before dark. Nobody gave him permission and nobody knows it is here; there is no path, only the streambed, which starts in the trees behind the lodge's woodpile, and the rock. In April the streambed carries a thin trickle of snowmelt and the last pitch is wet and cold to the touch until midafternoon. A player can follow him at a distance, find the ledge alone, sit and look at the view, or try to talk to him; up here he is the one who knows the way, and he makes sure everyone feels it. A player who follows him will find a small boy who does not want company and says so, with a sneer for hero talk and silence for anyone who expects thanks. The ledge is quiet except for wind in the pines and the faint roar of the snowmelt streams far below, and on clear days the whole valley lies open under it, every road and roof in view.
Kota's Secret Hideout.hiddenInfo: Nobody at the lodge knows where the ledge is; Mandalay only knows that Kota vanishes for hours and comes back before dark. His parents, the pro hero duo Water Hose, were killed two years ago by a villain who, as of the start of the year, has never been caught, and he hates the way people praised their deaths. Under the overhang he keeps a biscuit tin with snacks, a flashlight and a photograph of his parents he will not keep at the lodge. He has a small water Quirk, enough to spray someone from his palms and never to hurt, and he uses it up here only when he is sure nobody is watching. Snowmelt has loosened the last pitch, and this week a slab broke away under his hands; he kept climbing and told no one. After dark the ledge ices over, and the drop below it is long. A late start, a sudden April storm or one more loose hold could leave him stuck above the pitch at nightfall. Ragdoll would know where he is, and Mandalay would hear it first, but he would rather freeze than call for a hero. Whoever helps him should do it as a person, not a title: deeds reach him, praise for heroic sacrifice pushes him away.

Hidden Cliff Path.description: No real path at all: a dry streambed that starts in the trees behind the lodge's woodpile and climbs northeast through the forest for more than an hour, a staircase of boulders, gravel and tree roots between steep banks. In April a thin trickle of snowmelt runs down the middle and the stones are slick with moss. Near the top the trees thin out and the streambed ends at the foot of the cliff, where the last stretch is a hand-over-hand climb up cracks and ledges in bare gray rock; the holds are wet and cold to the touch until midafternoon, and a pale, fresh scar near the top shows where a slab broke away not long ago. There are no signs, markers or tape, only a few scuffs on the rock at the height of a small boy's reach and a snapped twig here and there where someone short pushes through the same branches every day. Most afternoons Kota Izumi comes up this way alone, fast and sure-footed, and goes back down before dark; anyone following him has to keep up without being heard. After sunset the wet rock begins to ice, and the climb is no place to be. The top of the climb comes out onto Kota's Rock Ledge.

Kota's Rock Ledge.description: A flat shelf of gray stone high on the cliff, big enough for a few people to sit on, with two wind-bent pines clinging to its outer edge and a shallow overhang at the back that keeps off the rain. From the lip the whole valley lies open: the forest rolling away toward Beast's Forest, the lodge's roof and its thread of woodsmoke far below, the single mountain road, and on clear days every stream silver with snowmelt. Under the overhang the rock is dry and swept, and a dented biscuit tin sits pushed into the back where the rain cannot reach it. Kota Izumi comes up here most afternoons, sits with his knees drawn up and his horned cap pulled low, and stays until the light starts to go; this is his place, and he makes sure any visitor knows it, with a curt word or a long silence. No hero has a reason to be here, and hero talk gets a sneer and nothing more; a person who just sits and looks at the view gets further. The only sounds are the wind in the pines and the far roar of the streams below. After dark the stone ices over, and the drop beyond the pines is long. The way down is the climb back to the Hidden Cliff Path.

Osaka Downtown.name: Osaka Downtown
Osaka Downtown.basicInfo: Downtown Osaka is the loud, crowded commercial heart of Kansai: the neon of the Dotonbori canal, long covered shopping arcades, street food on every corner and back streets of bars, pachinko halls and small offices. People speak Kansai dialect, bargain hard and joke harder; they cheer heroes loudly and heckle the slow ones. Several established agencies split the patrol districts, and Fat Gum, whose agency is about 5 km north-northeast, is a favorite with shopkeepers, who press food on him wherever he walks. Days are for shopping and office work; evenings are for food and noise until the last trains, after which the back streets belong to bar workers and taxi drivers. Police and heroes are busiest on Friday and Saturday nights, when the canal walkway is packed and the drunk fights start. The streets are public and open at all hours; only the shutters of the arcade shops close at night, and police boxes at the main crossings take reports and give directions. Students from Shiketsu Academy, U.A.'s great rival, turn up here often in their dark uniforms and peaked caps, some to eat and some on conduct patrols of their own. A player can find work in kitchens and shops, pick up street rumors, patrol with a local agency, eat at the canal stalls, catch a hero on PR duty, or follow a whisper into the back streets. Namba Station and the subway serve the district; Shin-Osaka Station lies about 8 km north, Sir Nighteye's agency about 7 km northwest, and the walled Shie Hassaikai compound about 11 km southeast. The shinkansen from Shin-Osaka runs east to Musutafu (about 2 hours) and Tokyo (about 2.5 hours), and west to Fukuoka (about 2.5 hours). The feeling is a party that never quite ends, with something less friendly underneath it after midnight.
Osaka Downtown.hiddenInfo: Trigger is back. The Quirk-boosting street drug, rare for years, has been turning up in the back streets since winter: users get a surge of power and lose their judgment, and two fights in the arcade this month ended with bystanders in the hospital. Street dealers sell it in small doses through layers of middlemen; the people at the bottom do not know who supplies them, but the money runs upward to an old yakuza house outside the city. Right now the busiest seller works the back streets on Friday and Saturday nights after the last train, from a standing bar with a torn red lantern, handing doses through a runner in a delivery jacket who never carries more than three at a time; used injector ampoules turn up in the gutters behind the mahjong parlors on Sunday mornings, and the bar's owner pays for silence by looking the other way. Anyone who buys twice is offered a phone number, and the voice on it never meets a buyer in person. Fat Gum's agency and the prefectural police drug squad are both working the case and share little with each other: the squad wants a dealer arrested with a supply, Fat Gum wants the source. Meanwhile the arcade shopkeepers' associations pay consulting fees to whichever agency keeps their streets cleanest, and some smaller agencies cut corners to win those contracts, chasing off loiterers and ignoring what happens two lanes back. Underworld brokers meet clients in the back-street bars and pay well for anyone who can find things out quietly, carry a bag without asking or keep a stranger company for a night. The Shiketsu students who walk these streets have noticed the arcade fights and the dealers, and the more earnest of them are tempted to do something about it without a license to do it.

Dotonbori Canal.description: A narrow canal lined on both banks with giant neon signs, mechanical shop mascots, takoyaki and okonomiyaki stands and a riverside walkway that is packed shoulder to shoulder from early evening. Tour boats pass under the bridges; crowds gather on the main bridge for photos; heroes on PR duty walk here at peak hours to be seen and filmed, signing autographs and posing with tourists while their sidekicks keep the walkway moving. By day the canal is quieter, office workers on lunch and tourists with maps; from dusk to the last train it is the loudest place in Kansai, and on Friday and Saturday nights the crowd spills across the bridges. Shiketsu students in peaked caps stop here for street food after training. Takoyaki griddles hiss, shop barkers call out in thick Kansai dialect, a giant mechanical crab waves its claws over a restaurant door, and the signs keep the walkway bright long after midnight. The local rule is simple: eat standing, keep walking, and never stop dead on the bridge. The walkway leads into the Covered Arcade.

Covered Arcade.description: A long covered shopping street under a high arched roof, running from the canal district toward the back streets: clothing shops, drugstores, hero merch stalls, cheap eateries, pachinko halls and old family businesses that have sold the same pickles or tea for generations. Shoppers and students crowd it from late morning; local agencies run foot patrols down the middle at set hours, and shopkeepers come out to chat with the heroes they like and grumble about the ones they pay. Shiketsu students drift through in pairs after class. After the shutters come down at night it becomes a dim wind tunnel with a few late bars, a convenience store and the occasional busker. The roof traps every sound, so jingles, announcements and voices merge into one roar, and a fight anywhere along it is heard everywhere. The floor tiles are worn smooth down the center, a fried-chicken stand near the canal end never seems to close, and every shop has a hand-lettered sign saying no Quirks inside. One end opens onto the Dotonbori Canal; side passages lead into the Back Streets.

Back Streets.description: Narrow lanes behind the arcade: tiny bars, mahjong parlors, pawn shops, kitchen doors and vending machines under a tangle of wires and air-conditioner units. Most bars seat six or eight at a counter, with a lantern or a hand-painted sign as the only clue they exist, and the lanes are too narrow for a car. By day it is delivery workers and smokers; after the last train it is bar staff, drunks, touts and people who would rather not be seen on the main streets, and a broker might be holding court in any back room. Patrols pass through but do not linger. Cats sleep on the warm compressor units, a rice-cracker shop that opens at dawn is the only thing here that keeps daytime hours, and a shrine the size of a phone booth gets fresh sake every morning. The air smells of fried food and garbage, air conditioners drip onto the pavement, and everyone notices a stranger who stops walking. The only way out to the main streets is back through the Covered Arcade.

Namba Comedy Theater.description: A big comedy theater a block off the arcade, its frontage plastered with grinning portraits of manzai duos and its lobby lined with souvenir stands. The main hall seats eight hundred on red velvet, facing a bare stage with a single standing microphone for the duos and a painted set for the slapstick play that closes every show. Shows run two to four times a day, about 4,800 yen a seat; bus tours, retirees and families fill the matinees, office workers the evening show, and the audience is expected to heckle back. Upstairs, a small studio stages young duos fighting for a slot, 1,000 yen at the door. Hero jokes are the bread and butter: All Might impressions, villains who trip over their own capes, and a running bit about Fat Gum's appetite that he has laughed at from the front row. A notice at the stage door reminds performers that Quirk acts need a permit filed in advance, and a stagehand with a sound-damping Quirk waits in the wings for the duo whose act is shouting. The lobby smells of fried snacks and floor polish. The front doors open onto the Covered Arcade, and a side street runs north to the Dotonbori Canal.

Kushikatsu Alley.description: A short, roofed alley between the arcade and the back streets where six kushikatsu counters face each other close enough to pass a plate across. Each is a steel counter around a bubbling vat of oil, with boxes of raw cabbage and a shared tin of thin brown sauce in front of every two stools; skewers of beef, lotus root, quail egg and cheese run 100 to 200 yen each, and a beer is 500. Every counter has the same sign in big red letters: no double-dipping in the sauce, and the cooks enforce it with a glare that works on pro heroes too. Office workers stand at the counters at lunch, families take the back tables on weekends, and after the last train the alley feeds bar staff, taxi drivers and anyone heading into the back streets. Shiketsu students in peaked caps come through after training to see who can eat the most, and when Fat Gum's patrol passes, the cooks start frying before he asks. The cook at the far end reads the oil's heat with her Quirk by touching the vat. The air is thick with frying oil and sauce, and paper lanterns turn the walls amber. One end opens onto the Covered Arcade; the other leads into the Back Streets.

Electric Town Arcades.description: A few blocks southeast of the arcade, the electronics street packs its game centers into narrow buildings five and six floors high: crane games and photo-sticker booths on the ground floor, rhythm and fighting-game cabinets above and a retro floor of old cabinets at the top, with parts shops and figure dealers squeezed between. A credit is 100 yen; fighting-game regulars line their coins on the cabinet to claim the next match, and weekend tournaments draw crowds that cheer every combo. Students after class, office workers on lunch and anime fans on weekends fill it from noon until closing at midnight. A life-size All Might statue in one window is the street's most photographed spot. Since winter, staff in vests walk the floors more often: a late-night fight ended with smashed cabinets and a customer whose Quirk was far stronger than his friends had ever seen, and rumors are spreading. A sticker on every cabinet warns that Quirk use on the machines gets a player barred. The noise is a wall of jingles and button clatter, the air smells of hot electronics and fried chicken, and the street leads back to the Covered Arcade.

Amerikamura Club Street.description: West of the main boulevard, the youth quarter's club street runs past Triangle Park, a small paved square where skateboarders, buskers and young people in loud secondhand clothes hang out from afternoon on. Vintage shops, sneaker stores and tattoo studios fill the ground floors; above them, clubs and live houses hide up narrow stairwells papered with stickers. Doors open at ten, the cover is 2,000 to 3,000 yen, and the bouncers check ID and bags. On weekend nights the queues run down the sidewalk and DJs play until the first train. Touts in puffer jackets work the corners, the police box at the park end hands out leaflets about drink spiking, and the rumor on the steps is that an old Quirk-boosting drug is back on the street; the bouncers walk out anyone who looks too wired or suddenly too strong. At closing the curb fills with people eating takoyaki and waiting for the first train, and a local agency's night patrol breaks up the odd shoving match. Shiketsu students on conduct patrol get teased for looking stern. The street leads south to the Dotonbori Canal, and an alley behind the clubs cuts through to the Back Streets.

Fat Gum Hero Agency.name: Fat Gum Hero Agency
Fat Gum Hero Agency.basicInfo: A cheerful, cluttered agency in a low building about 5 km north-northeast of downtown Osaka, a short ride from Shin-Osaka Station, run by the pro hero Fat Gum, the BMI Hero (Taishiro Toyomitsu), a huge, round, good-natured man whose Quirk, Fat Absorption, sinks blows and blades into his body fat and lets him release the stored force. When he spends the stored force he burns through the fat and comes out startlingly lean, and then he eats until he is round again. The agency focuses on drug crime and street violence and patrols the nightlife districts in the afternoon and again late at night; downtown shopkeepers love him and feed him on every round. Tamaki Amajiki, a U.A. Academy third-year and one of its Big Three, does his work-study here, riding in from U.A. on approved days and hiding in the back office until patrol starts. There are snacks on every desk, a rice cooker that never goes cold and a whiteboard of patrol routes covered in food stains. The front office is open to the public from morning until evening, with a sidekick at the front desk to take reports, tips and requests; the back office, the evidence cabinet and the patrol briefings are for staff and interns only. The office empties in late afternoon when the patrols go out and fills again near midnight when they come back. A player can intern, take a sidekick shift, bring a tip or ask for help, and anyone who brings snacks is welcomed. The feeling is a busy neighborhood kitchen that happens to fight crime: loud, warm and serious only when the radio says so.
Fat Gum Hero Agency.hiddenInfo: Fat Gum has been chasing the return of Trigger since winter. He has seen the drug before, and he is sure this supply is organized: the same doses, a steady flow, and dealers too frightened to name anyone. He suspects an old yakuza house but has no proof, and the police want more before they move. He pays a back-street informant out of his own pocket, a nervous bar worker who meets him on Tuesday nights at a standing noodle counter near the arcade and has started asking for more money because he is scared. Right now Fat Gum wants one thing: a live dealer caught holding a dose, with the phone that dealer calls, so the chain can be followed upward. He has two sidekicks rotating on late watch near the red-lantern bar in the back streets on weekend nights, and anyone who can get closer than a hero in costume would be worth his while. The prefectural drug squad shares little with him; it has not told him that Sir Nighteye's agency is building a file on the same house, and neither agency knows how much the other holds. Fat Gum also worries about Tamaki, whose nerves are the weak point of a strong Quirk: Manifest lets Tamaki take on the traits of whatever he has eaten, and he is far stronger than he believes. Fat Gum is quietly looking for chances to put him in front of a real crowd and let him find out. The agency's finances are thin because Fat Gum turns down sponsors he does not like, and the shopkeepers' associations' consulting money keeps the lights on.

Fat Gum Agency Front Office.description: The ground floor of the low building, open to the public from morning until evening: a long front desk where a sidekick takes reports, tips and requests, a row of mismatched chairs for people waiting, and behind the counter a cluster of staff desks buried in paperwork and snack bags. A whiteboard of patrol routes covers one wall, the nightlife districts marked in red and the margins spotted with sauce. A glass bowl of rice crackers on the counter is for anyone, and a hand-lettered card beside it says, in Kansai dialect, that tips are welcome and snacks even more so. Shopkeepers drop by all day with boxes of takoyaki or a bag of buns for the boss, and Fat Gum, when he is in, eats whatever arrives at the desk while he talks. The office empties in late afternoon when the patrols head out and fills again near midnight when they come back loud and hungry, and the police radio on the desk mutters through it all. Interns and visitors sign in here; the back office, the evidence cabinet and the patrol briefings are staff only. A hallway behind the desk leads to the Fat Gum Agency Break Room and down to the Fat Gum Agency Training Mat.

Fat Gum Agency Break Room.description: A narrow staff room off the back hallway with a low table, floor cushions, a battered sofa, a refrigerator covered in takeout menus and a rice cooker on the counter that is never switched off. A shelf holds paper plates, chopsticks and whatever the shopkeepers sent over that day, and a laminated sign over the sink asks whoever eats the last of the rice to start the next pot. Sidekicks eat here between patrols, nap on the sofa after late watches and argue about the best okonomiyaki in the ward; Fat Gum holds informal debriefs at the table with his mouth full, and the jokes stop the moment the talk turns to the street drug the agency has been chasing. On his work-study days, Tamaki Amajiki, the quiet U.A. third-year, often sits at the end of the table nearest the wall, eating deliberately and saying little, until the patrol goes out. Interns are expected to eat with everyone; refusing a second helping counts as rude. The room smells of rice, sauce and coffee, and a small television in the corner plays hero news with the sound low. The hallway leads back to the Fat Gum Agency Front Office and down to the Fat Gum Agency Training Mat.

Fat Gum Agency Training Mat.description: A plain basement room under the agency, floored wall to wall with thick blue mats and lit by bright ceiling panels, with a heavy bag hanging in one corner, a rack of padded batons and practice knives, a scale with a cracked dial and a whiteboard of capture drills. This is where Fat Gum teaches close-quarters work: he invites interns and sidekicks to hit him as hard as they can, lets their fists, batons and practice blades sink into his body and stop, and then explains, kindly and in detail, exactly what went wrong. Restraint holds, takedowns in narrow alleys and how to keep a partner covered are practiced here every morning before the office opens, and again on quiet evenings. Quirk use is allowed on the mat during supervised training only, and a sign on the door says so in words; Fat Gum's other rule is that nobody spars hungry, and a basket of rice balls sits by the door to make sure of it. The mats smell of sweat and disinfectant, and the thud of a body landing carries up through the floor to the offices above. Stairs lead back up to the Fat Gum Agency Front Office and the Fat Gum Agency Break Room.

Sir Nighteye Hero Agency.name: Sir Nighteye Hero Agency
Sir Nighteye Hero Agency.basicInfo: Sir Nighteye's agency fills two floors of an office building about 7 km northwest of downtown Osaka, west of Shin-Osaka Station. Sir Nighteye (Mirai Sasaki) was All Might's sidekick for years before going independent; tall, thin and severe, he runs a precise, analysis-driven agency that takes investigations, surveillance and long cases other agencies drop. His Quirk, Foresight, lets him see a person's future after touching them and meeting their eyes, and he uses it sparingly. His sidekicks are Bubble Girl, upbeat and loud, whose bubbles burst with any scent she has smelled before, and Centipeder, a courteous, centipede-featured man who handles surveillance and restraints. Mirio Togata, a U.A. Academy third-year and one of its Big Three, does his work-study here. The office is full of All Might memorabilia, and Nighteye insists his staff keep a sense of humor; staff who disappoint him end up in his tickling machine. Office hours are nine to six, but investigations run late, and someone is usually at a desk until midnight. Visitors enter through the building's lobby and ride up to a reception counter where Bubble Girl or a clerk asks their business; nobody goes past the counter without an appointment or a case worth hearing, and the case files never leave the office. Applicants are expected to make Nighteye laugh, or at least to try. A player can apply as an intern or sidekick, bring a case, or join a team-up. The agency's reputation is for patience: it rarely makes headlines, but the cases it takes end in arrests that stick. The feeling is a quiet library with a manic streak, where a stern man in glasses watches every visitor from behind a wall of smiling All Might posters.
Sir Nighteye Hero Agency.hiddenInfo: Nighteye has not spoken with All Might in years; they parted over something neither will discuss, and anyone who raises it meets a cold silence. The truth is that Nighteye once used Foresight on All Might, saw what he saw, and begged him to retire; All Might refused, and Nighteye left. He is one of very few people who know how badly All Might was wounded years ago and how short his fighting hours have become, and he guards that secret absolutely. He believes the future he sees cannot be changed, which makes him careful to the point of rigidity, and he pushes Mirio harder than any other trainee because he believes Mirio can become the next Symbol of Peace. Foresight works on one person at a time for about an hour once he activates it, and he will not waste it. Right now the agency is quietly building a file on the Shie Hassaikai: Centipeder has been logging who comes and goes at its compound from a rented room across the street, and Nighteye is tracking who the group buys from and sells to. The file holds two odd threads he cannot yet explain: the house buys sterile gloves, antiseptic and medical supplies by the crate through a supplier in another prefecture, far more than one comatose old man needs, and its members have started meeting underworld brokers in Osaka bars. The police know about the file and want to hear the moment it holds evidence. Nighteye wants to touch Chisaki and look at his future, but a hero who lays a hand on a member of a watched group without cause hands the house a complaint, so he waits for a reason.

Agency Office.description: An open-plan office of neat desks, filing cabinets and case boards, under walls and shelves covered in All Might memorabilia: posters from every year of his career, figures in glass cases, signed photos and rare limited goods, all dusted and arranged with care. Bubble Girl and Centipeder work here between patrols, and Mirio comes in on work-study days, cheerful and loud enough to break the hush. Nighteye's desk faces the door, so he sees every visitor before they see him; the tickling machine stands in one corner, a padded chair with restraints and feather arms that every staff member has sat in at least once. The reception counter by the elevator is where visitors wait to be seen, and Centipeder's surveillance desk by the window holds a row of monitors and stacked logbooks. Mornings are for reports and filing; afternoons for patrol and fieldwork; evenings for the long cases. The room is silent but for keyboards and the occasional forced joke, and the house rule is that anyone who touches an All Might figure without asking will regret it. A door at the back leads to the Meeting Room.

Meeting Room.description: A long conference room with a table for twenty, a projector, whiteboards and a wall of case maps marked with pins and string. Nighteye briefs police and visiting heroes here and plans team-ups; on quiet days he reviews footage frame by frame, and Bubble Girl brings him tea he forgets to drink. The current map is of southeastern Osaka, with surveillance photos and car plates pinned in neat rows. The blinds stay closed, a single framed All Might poster faces his chair, and the unwritten rule is that everyone has read the file before sitting down: anyone who has not is asked to leave and come back when they have. The only door leads back to the Agency Office.

Shie Hassaikai Compound.name: Shie Hassaikai Compound
Shie Hassaikai Compound.basicInfo: The compound is a traditional Japanese estate behind a high plaster wall in a quiet district about 11 km southeast of downtown Osaka: a tiled main house, outbuildings, a raked gravel courtyard and a heavy wooden gate. It is the seat of the Shie Hassaikai, one of the last yakuza houses, listed as a designated villain group since heroes broke up the old gangs; the police keep its members on file and drive past the gate several times a day. The neighbors are elderly householders who keep their curtains drawn and say the house has always been polite. The old boss, who took in outcasts nobody else would have, lies in a coma, and his second-in-command, Kai Chisaki, known as Overhaul, runs the house in his place. Chisaki is polite, cold and obsessively clean: he wears a beaked mask and gloves, cannot stand being touched and calls Quirks a sickness. Hari Kurono (Chronostasis) is always at his side. Members come and go at all hours in dark suits and masks, mostly by car; outsiders are received at the gate or not at all. Access is strict. The gate is guarded day and night, visitors state their business through it and wait, and only those invited are walked across the courtyard to the reception room; the gate closes to visitors at sunset. Nothing deeper than the reception room is open to anyone outside the house, and members never show guests the way below. A hero with no warrant can only watch from the street, and the house complains loudly about anyone who tries more. A player can come here as a recruit, a debtor, a business contact or a hero watching from the street. The feeling is a museum of an old world, swept and silent, where every bow is correct and nobody smiles.
Shie Hassaikai Compound.hiddenInfo: Under Chisaki the house has moved from old-style gambling and protection to dealing Trigger, the Quirk-boosting drug, through layers of street dealers in Osaka, and the money funds a plan to restore the yakuza's power that he shares only with his inner circle. The plan is this: in the Restricted Wing he keeps Eri, a small child, the old boss's granddaughter, whose Quirk can rewind a living body to an earlier state and which she cannot control. Chisaki takes her blood and cells and is trying to refine them into a drug that destroys a person's Quirk outright, and later a second drug to restore one, so that he can sell both and make the underworld depend on the house. The work is unfinished and slow. Eri is frightened, silent and convinced that her Quirk is a curse; she never leaves the wing, and fewer than a dozen members know she exists. The Eight Bullets, hand-picked enforcers sworn to Chisaki personally rather than to the house, carry out his orders, and many wear beaked masks of their own. The old boss's coma did not come from illness: the few who know say it followed an argument with Chisaki, and in truth Chisaki took him apart and put him back together with his own Quirk, Overhaul, which can disassemble and reassemble anything he touches. Tunnels run under the estate from hidden entrances in the main house, and Joi Irinaka (Mimic) can enter their concrete and reshape them at will. Right now Chisaki is sounding out other villain groups for allies and money through brokers, the house is ordering medical supplies by the crate from out of the prefecture, and the police know only that the house spends more than it earns.

Main House.description: A long tiled-roof house of dark wood and tatami: a formal reception room hung with the house crest, offices, a kitchen and members' quarters around an inner garden of raked gravel, moss and one old pine. Low-ranking members clean, cook and stand guard; visitors are seated in the reception room and served tea by men in suits and masks, and a guest who arrives with business waits in silence until Chisaki or Chronostasis decides to appear. The house wakes at dawn, eats in shifts and keeps the old ceremony: formal greetings, bows by rank and sake poured in strict order on the rare nights the house drinks together. The gate closes to visitors at sunset. Everything smells of disinfectant, the floors are wiped several times a day, the masked members change their gloves after every handshake they cannot avoid, and no one offers a hand to shake. Every corridor is lit and every door is watched. Members who know the house go down from here to the Underground Passages; visitors are never shown the way.

Underground Passages.description: Concrete corridors under the estate, lit by bare fluorescent tubes, running in a maze beneath the house and well beyond its wall, with storerooms and steel doors along the way. Some rooms hold crates of supplies, some hold cots for members on night duty, and one long room holds a training floor where the Eight Bullets spar out of sight. Only trusted members come down here, mostly at night, carrying crates between the house and exits nobody outside knows about. The layout does not stay put: Mimic can move into the walls and shift them, so a corridor that was open an hour ago may end in solid concrete, and members who get lost wait where they are until someone comes for them. The air is cold, the tubes buzz, a faint smell of bleach follows every crate, and footsteps echo a long way. Members speak in low voices and never run. Stairs lead back up to the Main House, and a guarded steel door at the deepest end opens on the Restricted Wing.

Restricted Wing.description: The deepest part of the tunnels, behind a guarded steel door: white walls, bright lights, scrubbed floors and the sharp smell of antiseptic. It holds Chisaki's private office and quarters, the sickroom where the old boss lies hooked to monitors, and further rooms that stay locked. Only Chisaki, Chronostasis and a few of the Eight Bullets come here; anyone else needs Chisaki's word, and must wash, glove and mask before entering at a steel sink beside the door, under a sign that lists the order in which to do it. Chisaki works here late into the night, and his office is as bare as an operating theater: a desk, a chair, files squared to the edge. A cart of sealed medical supplies stands in the corridor, restocked every few days. The only sound is the boss's machines, and the lights never dim. The guarded door leads back to the Underground Passages.

Fukuoka Downtown.name: Fukuoka Downtown
Fukuoka Downtown.basicInfo: Downtown Fukuoka is the center of Kyushu's largest city, a port spread along a wide bay: the Tenjin shopping district of department stores and an underground mall, the Nakasu riverside with its evening food stalls and bars, and high-rises along the harbor. It is Hawks' city. Number Three on the chart at the start of the year, he patrols it from the air and is often over a crime before anyone has reported it, so street crime is low, and the local agencies and police handle what he leaves: traffic accidents, lost tourists, drunk fights at closing time. Ms. Joke, the Smile Hero, who also teaches the hero course at Ketsubutsu Academy, is a familiar face in Tenjin, and her student Yo Shindo, quick with a handshake, is often with her. Days are for offices, shoppers and students; the food stalls open at dusk and run past midnight; the port works around the clock. Every street is public and open at all hours; the department stores close at eight, the underground mall's shutters come down with them, and the harbor towers' roofs are reached only through staff access doors. A player can shop, find work in restaurants or at the port, take patrol shifts with a local agency, or hope to catch sight of Hawks. Hakata Station, about 4 km east, has the shinkansen east to Osaka (about 2.5 hours) and Tokyo (about 5 hours); the Hawks Hero Agency is about 4 km northeast. Locals are proud, friendly and loud about their ramen, and they will tell a stranger which stall is best before being asked. The feeling is easy and warm: a big city with a hometown's manners, sure that someone fast is watching over it.
Fukuoka Downtown.hiddenInfo: Hawks' speed has a cost nobody mentions on camera. Fukuoka's smaller agencies resent that Hawks takes every visible case; their rankings and income are falling, and a few of their sidekicks sell reporters tips about where he will appear next. In the port, unregistered support gear comes in hidden among legal cargo, and there are rumors that Trigger has started arriving from Osaka. Right now the container yard on the east side of the harbor has a forwarding company that declares machine parts and ships out boxes of gauntlets, grapple guns and Quirk-dampening collars to buyers who pay through a broker in a Nakasu bar; a night-shift crane operator has seen the crates opened and is deciding whether to tell anyone. On weekend nights, street racers with speed Quirks run the harbor expressway after midnight and bet on whether Hawks will come for them; so far he has not bothered, and the bets are getting bigger and the racers bolder. Last weekend one of them clipped a taxi. The food-stall owners' association looks after its own members and has its own ways of dealing with troublemakers: a stall owner who brings in a dealer loses his pitch, and an outsider who causes trouble finds every stall full. Ms. Joke has noticed how little the local pros get to do and teases them about it, and she would happily lend her students to a smaller agency that wanted a real case. The city police are comfortable and slow, used to Hawks finishing their work before the paperwork starts.

Nakasu Riverside.description: The riverbank facing the Nakasu entertainment island, where dozens of yatai food stalls set up every evening: wooden carts with plastic curtains and a handful of stools, serving pork-bone ramen, yakitori, oden and beer. The stall owners tow their carts in at dusk, light the lanterns and set out their stools in the same spots every night, and each stall has its regulars and its argument about whose broth is best. Office workers and tourists queue from dusk; after the clubs close, hosts, hostesses and taxi drivers eat here before going home, and the stalls vanish before dawn, leaving the bank swept. Across the water, Nakasu's bars and clubs glow until the small hours. Broth steam hangs over the water, neon reflects off the river, and the rule is to eat, drink and give up your stool when someone is waiting. Strangers end up talking shoulder to shoulder, and a stall owner hears more gossip in a night than a detective does in a week. The riverside walk leads up to the Tenjin Shopping District.

Tenjin Shopping District.description: Fukuoka's main shopping center: department stores, fashion buildings, a bus terminal and an underground mall of hundreds of small shops running beneath the main avenue. Students and shoppers fill it from mid-morning; when the stores close at eight, the crowds move to the bars and the underground mall's shutters come down. Hero merch shops sell Hawks goods faster than any other hero's: feather keychains, wing hoodies, and posters of him eating fried chicken. A giant screen at the main crossing plays hero news, and people stop to watch whenever a Hawks clip comes on. Ms. Joke turns up here with Yo Shindo and other Ketsubutsu students, cracking jokes at the crossing and drawing a crowd of her own. Local agency patrols walk the avenue at set hours. Below ground the lighting is dim and the floors are patterned stone, cooler and quieter than the street, and the underground mall smells of coffee and pastry. The avenue leads down to the Nakasu Riverside, and service stairs in the harbor towers climb to the Harbor Rooftops.

Harbor Rooftops.description: The flat roofs of the office towers and hotels along the harbor: water tanks, antenna masts, helipads and the bay spread out below, with container cranes to one side and the ferry piers to the other. Hawks perches up here between calls, where he can see most of downtown; window cleaners, maintenance crews and the odd photographer hunting for him come through the access doors, which are locked to the public and opened with a staff key or a building pass. In the mornings the window-cleaning gondolas hang off the edges; at night red warning lights blink on every mast and the city is a carpet of lights. Heroes with flight or climbing Quirks cross from roof to roof here. The wind off the bay never stops, anything dropped goes over the edge, and a red feather caught on a railing means Hawks was here. The only way down is back through the towers to the Tenjin Shopping District.

Riverside Yatai Stalls.description: Upstream of the main Nakasu row, a quieter line of yatai stands under the willows on the Tenjin bank, a dozen carts along the river wall: each a wooden counter behind a plastic curtain, a gas burner, a pot of cloudy pork-bone broth and eight stools that fill knee to knee. The menus here run past ramen: grilled mentaiko, skillet gyoza, oden and tempura, and one stall is run by a four-armed heteromorph cook who works two grills at once. Ramen is 700 yen, skewers 150 to 300, a beer 600, cash only. Owners light up at six and close past two, and the local rule is one drink, one dish, then give up the stool so the queue can sit. Office workers and couples come early, and Ketsubutsu students share bowls at the end of a patrol. The owners keep a quiet eye on who brings trouble: a stranger who makes a scene finds every stool along the river suddenly taken. Lanterns glow through the curtains, broth steam drifts over the water, the river reflects Nakasu's neon, and everyone looks up when a shadow with red wings crosses the sky. The walk downstream leads to Nakasu Riverside, and a stair by the bridge climbs to the Tenjin Shopping District.

Tenjin Underground Mall.description: Beneath the main avenue, the underground mall runs about six hundred meters north to south in two parallel corridors: patterned stone floors, dark painted cast-iron arches, low warm lamps and hundreds of small shops on both sides selling clothes, cosmetics, sweets and coffee. The lighting is kept dim on purpose, so the corridors feel like an old European street at dusk. Commuters cut through from the subway in the morning; shoppers and students fill it from mid-morning until eight, when the shutters come down with the department stores. Hero goods kiosks sell Hawks feather keychains by the bucket, and a bakery near the middle makes a wing-shaped pastry that is gone by noon. Ramps and elevators serve wheelchairs and big-bodied heteromorphs, and a security guard with a tracking Quirk reunites lost toddlers with their parents faster than the announcements can. Signs at every entrance ban Quirk use and skateboards in the same breath. The air smells of coffee, perfume and fresh pastry, footsteps echo softly on the stone, and a recorded chime marks every half hour. Stairs along its length climb back up to the Tenjin Shopping District.

Daimyo Cafe Street.description: A grid of narrow streets just west of Tenjin's department stores, lined with old wooden houses and low concrete buildings turned into cafes, vintage clothing shops, record stores and tiny galleries. The cafes come in every style: a roastery with a long bar and burlap sacks stacked by the door, a pancake shop with a line down the block on Saturdays, and a quiet second-floor shop where students study for hours over one 550-yen latte. Mornings are slow and smell of roasting beans; lunch fills with office workers; afternoons and weekends bring students, couples and hero fans hunting photo spots. Baristas compete on latte art, and the most requested design is a pair of red wings. Many cafes keep a counter and chairs built higher, lower or wider for heteromorph customers, and some post a sign asking that no Quirks be used on the coffee. Patrols rarely come here, but people still glance up whenever a shadow crosses the rooftops, hoping it is Hawks. Ketsubutsu students hang out here after class. In the evening the cafes turn into wine bars under string lights. The streets lead east back to the Tenjin Shopping District.

Hawks Hero Agency.name: Hawks Hero Agency
Hawks Hero Agency.basicInfo: A small, modern office about 4 km northeast of downtown Fukuoka, north of Hakata Station, home to Hawks, the Number Three hero at the start of the year and the youngest ever to reach the top ten. He is fast, cheerful and casual, flies on large red wings whose feathers he controls one by one, fine enough to sense movement and strong enough to carry people, and is famous for finishing cases before anyone else arrives. His sidekicks take the calls, the paperwork, the press and the cleanup, because Hawks is almost never in the office; when he is, he is usually eating fried chicken. The agency is small and lean: a handful of sidekicks, a dispatch desk that tracks his calls across the city, and a press office answering questions about cases he closed an hour ago. The ground-floor lobby is open during office hours, with a reception desk, a rack of fan mail and a glass case of donated feather art; the dispatch room and the offices upstairs are staff only, and the roof has a landing pad that only Hawks uses. The agency rarely takes interns, and those it does take spend more time chasing the boss than learning from him. Fans wait outside on weekends hoping for a landing, and the staff keep a polite script for them. A player can apply, file a request, sell information, or wait in the lobby in case he drops in. Downtown Fukuoka is about 4 km to the southwest. The feeling is a well-run office built around an empty chair: efficient, friendly, a little tired, and always looking up when a shadow passes the window.
Hawks Hero Agency.hiddenInfo: The sidekicks barely see their boss: Hawks sends instructions by phone, lands only to sign forms and is gone before they can ask questions. They admire him and resent being left behind, and one senior sidekick is quietly interviewing with other agencies in Osaka and Tokyo, taking long lunches on the days he has calls. Sponsorship offers and interview requests are piling up unanswered, and the staff are running out of ways to say he is busy. Behind that lies something the staff do not know. Hawks was found and raised by the Hero Public Safety Commission from his early childhood, trained for hero work before he could choose it, and he still takes quiet assignments straight from the Commission that never appear in the agency's case log. The gaps in his day that dispatch cannot account for are often those jobs. He reports to a senior Commission official by secure phone, keeps his own counsel, and under the easy smile he is sharper, lonelier and more careful than anyone at the agency suspects. He is also a quiet admirer of Endeavor, whom he has followed since long before he could fly. Right now the dispatch chief has noticed that Hawks was logged on patrol for a whole afternoon last week with no call, no sighting and no stray feather to back it up, and she has started keeping her own notes. The press office has a feature interview booked for next month that Hawks agreed to on the phone and has almost certainly forgotten.

Hawks Agency Lobby.description: A bright ground-floor lobby of glass, pale wood and red accents, open during office hours. A curved reception desk faces the door, staffed by a sidekick with a headset and a polite smile, and beside it stands a rack of fan mail sorted by date, some of it decorated with drawn wings. A glass case along one wall displays donated feather art, from framed paintings of red wings to a full-size model of a single feather made of glass beads. Visitors file requests, report incidents, apply to the agency or ask whether Hawks is in; the answer is almost always that he is out, and the staff have a script for saying it kindly. On weekends fans wait on the sidewalk outside hoping for a landing, and the receptionist hands out a printed card with the agency's address for letters. Everyone in the room, staff included, looks up when a shadow crosses the front windows. The lobby smells faintly of fried chicken whenever the boss has passed through, which is how the staff can tell he has been here without seeing him. A staff-only stairway leads up to the Hawks Agency Operations Room and on to the Hawks Agency Rooftop.

Hawks Agency Operations Room.description: The staff-only floor upstairs: an open room of desks under a wall of screens, with a city map of Fukuoka marked with the morning's calls, traffic cameras, police radio feeds and a news channel muted in the corner. The dispatch desk tracks Hawks's calls across the city as they come in and, more often, as they are already closed; a sidekick reads out the incident, a second confirms it with the police, and a third starts the paperwork for a case that ended before anyone finished typing. Along the back wall the press office answers questions about those cases, and a whiteboard lists interview requests and sponsorship offers still waiting for the boss's answer. The room runs from early morning to late at night in shifts, with takeout boxes stacked beside every keyboard, and when Hawks does appear, usually through the roof door, he signs a stack of forms standing up and is gone before anyone can ask a question. One chair at the head of the room belongs to him; it is rarely used, and nobody else sits in it. The phones never stop for long. Doors lead down to the Hawks Agency Lobby and up to the Hawks Agency Rooftop.

Hawks Agency Rooftop.description: The flat roof of the agency building, ringed by a waist-high railing, with a painted landing pad in the middle that only Hawks uses: no helicopter has ever touched it, and the paint is scuffed only by boots. A windsock snaps on a short mast, a steel door leads down to the staff floor, and a couple of potted plants the staff once brought up have long since blown over and been left that way. The view runs over the rooftops around Hakata Station toward the harbor cranes of Hakata Bay, and downtown's towers stand about 4 km to the southwest. Stray red feathers turn up in the corners after a landing, and the staff collect them in a jar by the door rather than throw them out. When Hawks does stop here, he tends to perch on the railing rather than stand on the pad, often with a bag of fried chicken, watching the city while seeming to watch nothing; sidekicks come up to catch him with a form or a question and usually find only the wind. At night the roof is dark except for the pad's edge lights, and the city's noise comes up as one low hum. The steel door leads down to the Hawks Agency Operations Room and the Hawks Agency Lobby.

Hakata Station.name: Hakata Station
Hakata Station.basicInfo: Hakata Station is Kyushu's main rail hub: a huge station building with a department store, a shopping concourse, restaurant floors and a rooftop garden.
