The shinkansen line from Tokyo and Osaka ends here, and local lines, the subway and long-distance buses fan out across Kyushu; the subway also runs two stops to the airport and on to Tenjin. Railway staff run the gates and platforms, and a police box by the main exit takes lost-property and pickpocket reports. Commuter rush runs from seven to nine and five to seven, and the gates stay busy until the last trains near midnight; after that the bus terminal next door takes over with night buses to the rest of Kyushu and back east toward Osaka. The restaurant floors are packed at lunch and dinner with ramen counters, motsunabe pots and mentaiko set meals, and the rooftop garden is a quiet place to eat a bento above the traffic. Access is open: the concourse, shops and rooftop are public during business hours, and the platforms are reached only through the ticket gates. A player can arrive in or leave Kyushu here, work in the shops and ramen counters, or meet anyone passing through. Downtown Fukuoka is about 4 km to the west; the Hawks Hero Agency lies to the north. Osaka is 2.5 hours east, Musutafu about 4.5 hours and Tokyo about 5. Travelers look up when a shadow crosses the glass roof, and locals tell them it is only a crow, usually. The feeling is a gateway that never stops moving, with the smell of pork-bone broth drifting through every passage.
Hakata Station.hiddenInfo: The station police box has orders to watch for couriers carrying Trigger west from Osaka on the shinkansen. Officers check bags at random and have found nothing so far, because the couriers ride the night buses instead. Right now one courier arrives on the overnight bus from Osaka every other Saturday morning just before six, a quiet young woman in a nurse's cardigan with a small cool bag, and walks from the bus terminal through the empty concourse to the subway before the police box changes shift. Her doses go to a bar in Nakasu and from there into the port. The bus terminal's cleaners have seen her often enough to nod hello. A pickpocket crew works the concourse at rush hour; station staff know them by sight but have never caught them in the act. There are three of them: one bumps, one lifts, one walks off with the wallet within seconds, and they work the shinkansen exits on Friday evenings, when tired business travelers come off the trains from Osaka and Tokyo. The police box officers are good at lost umbrellas and slow at everything else, and they quietly expect Hawks to deal with anything serious. The station's lost-property office holds a growing box of items found on the night buses, among them an empty injector ampoule nobody has thought to report upward.

Hakata Station Concourse.description: The main concourse runs straight through the station building from the Hakata exit on the city side to the Chikushi exit on the shinkansen side: a broad, bright hall under a glass roof, with JR gates in the middle, shinkansen gates toward the east end and subway stairs going down toward Tenjin and the airport. Shops sell boxed mentaiko, Hakata dolls and sweets, and pork-bone broth drifts down from the restaurant floors. The police box by the Hakata exit handles lost umbrellas, wallets and travelers. At rush hour commuters cross shoulder to shoulder; on Friday evenings tired business travelers stream off the trains from Osaka and Tokyo, and the police box has taped up a hand-lettered warning about pickpockets at the shinkansen exits. Near midnight the shops close and the hall empties, and in the first hour of the morning it is so quiet that a lone traveler crossing from the bus terminal to the subway echoes. Now and then a shadow slides across the glass roof and everyone looks up; locals say it is a crow, usually. Escalators climb to the Station Rooftop Garden, and the Hakata exit opens toward the Hakata Exit Bus Terminal.

Station Rooftop Garden.description: On the station's roof, a lawn, trees and planters make a small park in the sky: a little railway shrine with a red torii, a miniature train that carries small passengers around a looped track, vegetable plots, benches and an observation deck along the railing. From the deck you can watch the shinkansen glide in from the east and stop at the end of the line, look west over Fukuoka's rooftops toward the bay and, on clear days, follow planes dropping in low over the city toward the airport. Office workers come up at lunch with bentos and canned tea; families ride the little train on weekends; trainspotters with long lenses stake out the railing; in the evening, couples and photographers come for the city lights, and staff close the garden late in the evening. Travelers ring the shrine bell and pray for safe journeys, the wind up here is always stronger than it looks, and the little train plays a jingle each time it passes. Now and then a winged shadow crosses overhead, heading north, and somebody always says it is only a crow. Elevators run back down to the Hakata Station Concourse.

Hakata Exit Bus Terminal.description: Beside the Hakata exit stands the bus terminal, its own building with gates stacked on several floors, joined to the station by a covered walk. Local buses leave from the ground floor for the city and the port, while the upper gates send highway buses across Kyushu, to Kumamoto, Nagasaki, Oita, Beppu and Kagoshima, and overnight coaches back east to Osaka. Ticket windows, plastic seats, a convenience store and departure screens fill the lobby, and upstairs counters serve ramen to drivers between runs. Mornings bring commuters off the suburban routes; after the last trains the terminal takes over, and the station's late crowd drifts in for the night buses. Every other Saturday morning the overnight bus from Osaka pulls in just before six, and the cleaners, who know some of its regulars by sight, nod hello as they walk off through the empty station toward the subway, a little before the police box changes shift. Things left behind on the night buses go to the station's lost-property office, where the box keeps growing. Diesel and coffee smells hang in the stairwells. The covered walk leads back to the Hakata Station Concourse.

Tartarus.name: Tartarus
Tartarus.basicInfo: Japan's maximum-security prison for villains too dangerous for any ordinary facility, built into a small volcanic island among the Izu Islands, about 55 km south-southeast of the Tartarus Transfer Port. It is a national facility: a guard force under the National Police Agency runs custody and transfers, and the Hero Public Safety Commission vets the staff and approves every visit. Nobody casually visits, and there is no public access of any kind. Nobody lands without written authorization, and only by armored transfer boat or helicopter from the port; every arrival is met at the landing by armed guards and escorted from that moment until departure. Visitors pass a chain of checkpoints, surrender phones and belongings, and are scanned and searched more than once; anyone whose papers do not match the day's log goes back on the boat. Inmates live in solitary cells deep inside the island, each built around its occupant's Quirk; they wear restraints that block their Quirks, and automatic guns cover every cell. Inmates leave a cell only in full restraints with an escort of four guards, and no door opens without two officers confirming it. Guards work long rotations on the island in armored gear, eating and sleeping in quarters inside the walls. Only the worst offenders are sent here: serial killers, villains whose Quirks no ordinary cell can hold, and criminals judged too dangerous to live among other prisoners. A player can deliver a prisoner, interview an inmate with approval, work a guard rotation, or investigate a case. Sound is controlled: steel doors seal with a hiss, alarms are tested at set hours, and the sea can be heard only at the landing.
Tartarus.hiddenInfo: Tartarus is nearly full. The number of villains judged too dangerous for ordinary prisons has risen for years, and the guard force works longer rotations to cover it; some guards have not been ashore in three weeks, and mistakes on the night shift are becoming more common: a logged check that was never walked, a door confirmation given by radio instead of in person. A few inmates' files are sealed, and the Commission screens every request to see them. The whole design assumes the restraints, the cell locks and the guns never fail at the same moment, and the backup generators are tested monthly. A guard is under review for passing an inmate's letter out unread; he says he was told it was a note to a lawyer, and the review has not yet found who asked him. Among the inmates is Moonfish, a serial killer under a death sentence, held in the Maximum-Security Cell Block. He murmurs about meat for hours and rarely answers what he is asked, and the guards rotate who brings his meals because he unsettles everyone who stands at his slot. Detectives from several prefectures have requested interviews with him about old cases, and most leave with nothing. To the staff, the danger is not any one inmate but tiredness: a crew that has done the same checks for weeks starts to see what it expects to see.

Guard Control Center.description: The command room at the island's core: a wall of monitors showing every cell, corridor and checkpoint, lock and gun controls behind a second sealed door, an armory, and a duty desk where every arrival, transfer and visit is logged by hand and by computer. A shift supervisor and a full team are on duty around the clock, changing at six in the morning and six at night, and each handover is read aloud line by line. Nothing opens without two officers confirming it, and no one enters alone, not even the supervisor. Arrivals from the landing are brought here first, checked against the day's log and assigned an escort. The room is cold, equipment hums, the coffee is bad, and conversation stays short. Secured corridors lead to the Visitor Interview Room and, through the guarded elevator, down to the Maximum-Security Cell Block.

Visitor Interview Room.description: A bare room split in two by a thick transparent wall. On the inmate's side, the prisoner sits strapped into a fixed chair under automatic guns that fire at any sign of Quirk use. On the visitor's side there is one chair and a speaker grille, bolted to the floor. Visits are approved weeks ahead, limited in time, recorded, and watched by guards on both sides; a clock above the wall counts down the minutes. Before every visit a guard reads the rules aloud: no gifts, no touching the wall, and the visit ends at the first breach. Visitors come in already searched, with nothing in their hands but the papers they were allowed to bring. The light is flat and white, the walls are bare concrete, and the only other sound is the faint whir of the guns tracking the prisoner. A sealed door leads back to the Guard Control Center.

Maximum-Security Cell Block.description: Levels of solitary cells deep beneath the island, reached by a single guarded elevator. Each cell is sealed by a heavy door and built around its occupant's Quirk, with restraints that block it, automatic guns covering the bed, and lights that never fully go off. Meals arrive through a slot at fixed hours; inmates leave only in full restraints with an escort of four guards, for interviews, medical checks or transfers. Guards walk the corridors in pairs at fixed intervals and speak to inmates only to give orders. Each door carries a number, not a name, and a colored stripe that tells the guards how dangerous the occupant is. From one cell a broken voice repeats the same word for hours, and the guards have learned not to answer. The air is filtered, dry and smells of metal. The elevator leads back up to the Guard Control Center.

Tartarus Transfer Port.name: Tartarus Transfer Port
Tartarus Transfer Port.basicInfo: A walled harbor on a headland at the Izu Peninsula's southern tip, 50 km south of Musutafu Station, under two hours by road or rail, where prisoners bound for Tartarus board armored transfer boats. The Tartarus guard force runs it, with prefectural police on the gate. Inside the fence are a helipad, two piers, holding cells, a guardhouse, a fuel depot and a low operations building with a radio mast. One gated road leads in, open only to staff, escorts and approved visitors; everyone else is turned back at the outer barrier, and even cleared visitors are searched and logged before they reach the piers. Transfers run at set hours, usually at night, and stop in rough seas. Tartarus lies 55 km south-southeast: about two hours by boat, twenty minutes by helicopter. Prisoners arrive in armored vans under police escort, are checked against the manifest, held if the boat is not ready, then walked to the pier in full restraints. By day the port is quiet: crews maintain the boats, guards drill on the piers, and supply crates go out on the morning boat. A player can escort a prisoner, wait for a transfer, check a manifest, or report for a guard rotation on the island. Floodlights stay on all night over idling boat engines, the wind off the open sea never stops, and the fishing harbor's lights twinkle on the far side of the bay.
Tartarus Transfer Port.hiddenInfo: Spring storms have delayed several transfers this month, and prisoners are waiting in the port's holding cells longer than intended; the cells were built for a night, not a week, with no proper restraint rigs for long stays and only the guardhouse crew to watch them. The night crew has started skipping the second manifest check to keep the backlog moving, so a prisoner's identity is now confirmed once at the van and not again at the pier. A fishing boat has been seen idling offshore during transfers more than once; the crew suspects a reporter with a long lens, but nobody has checked, and the patrol boats are kept busy escorting the transfers themselves. The boat is local, and someone in the nearest fishing town rented it out for cash. Two prisoners currently waiting in the holding cells are scheduled for the next calm night, and the duty officer has asked the police for an extra escort that has not yet arrived. The port's staff are tired, proud of a record of no escapes, and quietly convinced that the backlog will be fine as long as the weather turns soon.

Port Security Gate.description: The only way into the port: the single gated road ends here at an outer barrier of striped steel arms, concrete blocks and a tall fence topped with wire, with a guardhouse beside it and watchtowers on the headland behind. Prefectural police officers in body armor run the gate around the clock, checking every vehicle against the day's list; anyone not on it is turned back, and cleared visitors are searched, scanned and logged by name and time before they go any farther. A mirror on a pole is run under every car, and phones and bags go into numbered trays while the officers phone the operations building to confirm. Armored prisoner vans come down the coast road under escort, usually after dark, and the arms rise for them without a stop; on quiet days the gate sees supply trucks in the morning, staff cars at shift change and almost nothing else. A sign in plain letters warns that Quirk use anywhere inside the fence is grounds for immediate detention. The wind off the open sea never stops, and the floodlights hum above the barrier all night. Past the gate, the road leads to the Transfer Waiting Hall and down to the Transfer Pier.

Transfer Waiting Hall.description: A long, low room in the operations building, under the radio mast, where everyone bound for the island waits for a boat: rows of bolted plastic seats, a duty desk behind thick glass, a wall clock beside a board that lists the next transfer time and, more often than not, a handwritten note that it is delayed by weather. Escort officers, Tartarus guards reporting for a rotation, lawyers and approved visitors sit here with their papers on their knees, under the eye of a guard by the door. Manifests are checked at the duty desk, names read aloud and matched to faces, and nobody walks to the pier without an escort. A heavy steel door at the far end leads to the holding cells, where prisoners wait when the boat is not ready; it stays shut, and only the duty officer's keycard opens it. A vending machine sells canned coffee for 130 yen, and a television bolted high on the wall shows the marine forecast on a loop. The room smells of floor polish, diesel and wet coats, and the windows rattle when the wind swings onshore. Doors lead back out to the Port Security Gate and, through the escort corridor, down to the Transfer Pier.

Transfer Pier.description: Two concrete piers reaching out into a walled basin, under floodlight towers that stay on all night. The armored transfer boats tie up here, squat gray hulls with sealed cabins and barred ports, their engines idling and the exhaust drifting over the water; police patrol boats lie alongside, and a helipad sits on the headland just above. Prisoners are walked down the pier in full restraints, a guard on each side and more ahead and behind, checked against the manifest and taken aboard; the crossing to Tartarus, 55 km to the south-southeast, takes about two hours, or twenty minutes by helicopter. Transfers run at set hours, usually at night, and stop entirely in rough seas, when the boats strain at their lines and the spray comes over the outer wall. By day crews maintain the boats, guards drill on the piers, and supply crates go out on the morning boat. Yellow lines mark where visitors may stand, and nobody crosses them without an escort. The air smells of salt, diesel and rust, and across the bay the fishing harbor's lights twinkle. The pier leads back to the Transfer Waiting Hall and up the road to the Port Security Gate.

Shin-Osaka Station.name: Shin-Osaka Station
Shin-Osaka Station.basicInfo: Shin-Osaka Station is Kansai's shinkansen terminal, about 8 km north of downtown Osaka: long elevated platforms under a steel canopy where the bullet trains from Tokyo and Musutafu arrive and the line west to Kyushu begins, a busy central concourse of ticket gates, departure boards, bento and souvenir shops and standing noodle counters, and a taxi and bus rotunda outside. Local trains and the subway run on into the city, about a quarter of an hour to the downtown stations. Railway staff run the gates and platforms, and a police box by the central exit helps lost travelers and takes reports. The concourse is busiest in the morning and evening rush and on holiday weekends, when the queues for reserved seats curl around the pillars and families sit on their suitcases eating takoyaki from paper boats. Late at night it empties fast: the last shinkansen leaves before midnight, the shops pull down their shutters, and a few travelers wait for the first train sleeping on benches. Hero Course students on Kansai internships arrive here and ride on to their agencies; Fat Gum's agency is a short taxi ride to the southeast and Sir Nighteye's a short ride to the west. Access is simple: the concourse is open to anyone, and the platforms are reached only through the ticket gates with a valid ticket. Coin lockers line the lower concourse for travelers who want to leave their bags. A player can arrive in Kansai or leave it here, work a shift at a noodle counter or a souvenir shop, meet someone off a train, or ask the police box for directions. Musutafu is about 2 hours east by shinkansen, Tokyo about 2.5 hours, and Hakata about 2.5 hours west. The feeling is a crowd in a hurry, announcements in four languages and the smell of dashi from every counter.
Shin-Osaka Station.hiddenInfo: The station police box keeps photos of Shie Hassaikai members and watches the shinkansen gates for them, so the compound's people come and go by car and night bus instead and are almost never seen here. The officers know this and keep watching anyway, because the photos are their orders. What they are not watching is the bank of coin lockers on the lower concourse by the south passage. Right now a middleman in Osaka's Trigger trade uses three of those lockers as a dead drop: dealers' cash goes in during the week, and every Monday morning, just after the rush, a man in a gray work jacket with a cleaning company's logo empties them, pays the locker fees in coins and leaves by the local line toward the city. He never looks at the cameras and never uses the same locker twice in a row. Station staff have noticed that the same lockers are always occupied but assume a shop is storing stock. A regular at the standing noodle counter by the gates, an old night-shift cook, has noticed the man too and would say so to anyone who bought him a bowl. The police box could stop the drop in a morning if anyone gave it a reason to look. Meanwhile the station sees the usual troubles: luggage thieves on holiday weekends, the odd drunk whose Quirk sparks on the late platform, and travelers who arrive for an internship at the wrong agency and need directions to the right one.

Shin-Osaka Shinkansen Concourse.description: The central concourse sits beneath the shinkansen tracks: a long hall of ticket gates, departure boards, bento and souvenir shops and standing noodle counters, with the bullet trains rumbling overhead. Rush hours fill it with business travelers; on holiday weekends the queues for reserved seats curl around the pillars and families sit on their suitcases eating takoyaki from paper boats. Hero Course students on Kansai internships come through with too much luggage and a printed map, and the officers at the police box by the central exit, who glance from a sheet of photographs to the faces at the gates, spend half their day redirecting interns who set out for the wrong agency. At the standing noodle counter by the gates, an old night-shift cook eats a bowl of udon after every shift, watches everyone and will chat with anybody who buys him another. The smell of dashi drifts from every counter. After the last shinkansen leaves before midnight, a few travelers stretch out on benches to wait for the first train. Escalators lead down to the Shin-Osaka Taxi and Bus Rotary, and a corridor of shops opens into the Station Food Hall.

Station Food Hall.description: Off the concourse, a bright hall of stalls packs Osaka's appetite into a few aisles: takoyaki griddles where cooks flip octopus balls with metal picks, a counter of steamed pork buns whose queue never ends, kushikatsu bars serving fried skewers with beer, okonomiyaki, sushi to take away, and shelves of boxed meals, pickles and sweets packed for the train. A sign over the shared sauce pots says what every Osakan already knows: no double dipping. Travelers grab boxed meals in the last ten minutes before their train and sprint; office workers from the nearby towers come for lunch; interns buy boxed sweets to present at their new agencies, and stall staff happily tell them which box the local pros actually like. In the evening, salarymen stand at the skewer counters loosening their ties, and on holiday weekends the aisles jam with families buying souvenirs. Cooks call to each other in broad Osaka dialect and tease customers who hesitate, and the smell of sauce and batter follows people to the platforms. Most stalls close by ten or eleven at night. The hall opens back onto the Shin-Osaka Shinkansen Concourse.

Shin-Osaka Taxi and Bus Rotary.description: On the ground floor, under the elevated tracks, the station opens onto a broad rotary of taxi lanes, bus bays and drop-off curbs. Black and white taxis wait in a long line that moves fast, and the drivers know every hero agency within a short ride and will tell a nervous intern which one they actually mean. Limousine buses leave for Itami and Kansai airports, highway buses for Shikoku, the San'in coast and Tokyo overnight, and city buses for the northern wards. The passage in from the rotary is the lower concourse, lined with coin lockers in every size; travelers leave suitcases there while they see the city, a few lockers by the south passage never seem to be free, and on Monday mornings, just after the rush, the passage is quiet enough to hear coins drop into the fee slots. Business travelers and interns fill the taxi line in the morning, tour groups crowd the bus bays at midday, and on holiday weekends luggage thieves work the curbs while families wrestle with their bags. Late at night the taxis wait with their roof lights on and their drivers chatting by the doors. Escalators climb back to the Shin-Osaka Shinkansen Concourse.

Kyoto Station.name: Kyoto Station
Kyoto Station.basicInfo: Kyoto Station is the old capital's front door and the city's main rail station: a vast steel-and-glass building of hard modern lines set down in a city of temples, with a canyon-like atrium under a lattice roof and a grand stairway of 171 steps climbing from the concourse to a rooftop garden, its risers lit with changing light pictures after dark. JR West's local and limited-express lines, JR Central's Tokaido shinkansen on the south side, the Kintetsu Kyoto Line and the Karasuma subway line all meet here, and IC transit cards open every gate. The north side, the Karasuma exit, faces the white-and-red needle of Kyoto Tower across the road and the city's main bus terminal, where travelers queue at numbered stands for the city buses to Kiyomizu-dera, Gion, Kinkaku-ji and Ginkaku-ji, with taxi ranks for everything else; the great wooden halls of Higashi Hongan-ji are a five-minute walk north. The south side, the Hachijo exit, holds the shinkansen gates, highway-bus stops and quieter hotels. Under the north plaza runs an underground shopping street; inside the building are a department store, a high floor of rival ramen counters, gift shops stacked with yatsuhashi sweets and green-tea everything, boxed-meal stands, counters that forward suitcases to hotels, and banks of coin lockers that are full by ten in the morning. Early mornings bring commuters and students in uniform; from mid-morning to dusk come tour groups, school trips and rental-kimono strollers; evenings, the stairway lights draw couples and photographers; after the last trains leave, a little after midnight, the halls go quiet and the taxis wait. A police box stands at the Karasuma exit, railway police walk the concourses, and pros from the city's old, dignified agencies pass through on patrol, polite, unhurried and expected to stop for photos. The shinkansen reaches Shin-Osaka in about 15 minutes and Musutafu in about 1 hour 45 minutes; JR lines run to Fushimi Inari, Arashiyama, Nara and Lake Biwa at Otsu, and a limited express runs to Kansai Airport. It feels like a city politely holding its breath: crowded, orderly and always a little too full.
Kyoto Station.hiddenInfo: A pickpocket pair is working the city-bus queues at the Karasuma exit right now, every afternoon between about 3 and 6 p.m., when the lines for Kiyomizu-dera and Gion are longest. One is a woman in a rented lavender kimono who passes for a tourist and asks people to take her photo by the queue signs; the other, a man in a gray rain jacket, has a Quirk that makes anything he touches weigh almost nothing for a few seconds, so a wallet lifts out of a pocket without a tug as the bus doors open and the crowd surges. They strip the wallets in the restroom off the underground shopping street and drop them, cash gone and cards left, in the bin beside the coin lockers on the Hachijo side, where a night cleaner has found eleven in two weeks and turned each one in. The evening officer at the police box is new to the posting, has written every one up as lost property and has not connected them; the cleaner has noticed that the owners all came through the same two bus stands and would tell anyone who asked. How the place really runs: the station belongs to the railways, JR West on the north side and JR Central on the shinkansen side, and each keeps its own guards; the local agency that holds the station patrol contract is short-handed in tourist season and leans on its sidekicks; and the city's tourism office would rather nothing that frightens visitors reach the news, so small crimes here are handled quietly and slowly. After lost luggage, unlicensed Quirk use in the bus crush is the commonest complaint at the police box.

Kyoto Central Concourse.description: Inside the north entrance the building opens into a canyon: a vast atrium of steel and glass under a lattice roof, with the department store rising on one side, the hotel on the other and terraces of escalators climbing away into the light. On its floor lies the central concourse, a wide hall of JR ticket gates, departure boards in four languages, gift shops stacked with yatsuhashi sweets and green-tea everything, counters that forward suitcases to hotels, and banks of coin lockers that are full by ten in the morning. Commuters and students in uniform cross it early; from mid-morning tour groups gather under raised flags and school trips sit in rows on the floor. Railway police walk the hall, and pros from the city's old agencies stop patiently for photos. A night cleaner who empties the bins by the coin lockers turns in every lost thing found there, and lately that has meant a surprising number of empty wallets. After the last trains, a little after midnight, the hall goes quiet. The Grand Stairway and Skyway climb from the atrium's west side, and the north doors open onto the Karasuma Exit Bus Terminal.

Grand Stairway and Skyway.description: From the atrium's west side the Grand Stairway climbs 171 steps through the building, escalators running alongside, past shopping floors and the high floor of rival ramen counters to a rooftop garden of benches and trees that looks out over the city to the hills. High up, a glass corridor called the Skyway is slung across the atrium; from it you can look down on the lattice roof, straight across at Kyoto Tower and, through the north glass, onto the bus terminal's numbered stands and the queues that snake around them. People sit on the steps to eat lunch, wait for friends or rest their feet; tour groups line up for photos, and a few fit locals run the stairs early in the morning before the shops open. After dark the risers become a screen: thousands of lights in the steps play changing pictures, falling maple leaves, cherry blossoms, a festival scene, and couples and photographers sit and wait for their favorite. The ramen floor fills from lunch until late evening, each shop arguing for its own broth. Security staff clear the rooftop at closing. The stairs lead back down to the Kyoto Central Concourse.

Karasuma Exit Bus Terminal.description: Outside the north doors, across the road from the white-and-red needle of Kyoto Tower, the city's main bus terminal spreads out in rows of numbered stands under shelters, each with a sign listing its routes in four languages: Kiyomizu-dera, Gion, Kinkaku-ji, Ginkaku-ji. The police box stands at the corner of the exit. Morning buses carry commuters and students; from mid-morning to dusk the queues belong to tourists with daypacks, school trips and rental-kimono strollers who ask strangers to take their photo by the queue signs. Between about three and six in the afternoon the lines for Kiyomizu-dera and Gion are at their longest, and when the bus doors open the crowd surges forward all at once; regulars hold their bags in front of them. The evening officer at the police box is new to the posting and keeps a growing stack of lost-wallet reports on the desk. Starters in caps call out route numbers through handheld speakers, and buses kneel and hiss at the curb. After the last city buses leave, late in the evening, only the taxis remain. The north doors lead back into the Kyoto Central Concourse.

Nagoya Station.name: Nagoya Station
Nagoya Station.basicInfo: Nagoya Station, Meieki to locals, is the hub of central Japan and one of the busiest stations in the country: a long, broad JR building crowned by twin office towers, with more skyscrapers crowded around it and a maze of underground shopping streets beneath. JR Central's Tokaido shinkansen and its Chuo, Kansai and Tokaido lines share the main building; the Meitetsu and Kintetsu stations sit next door to the south, and the Higashiyama and Sakura-dori subway lines and the Aonami Line toward the port run underneath. The east side, the Sakura-dori exit, faces downtown and the big taxi and bus pools, and the Gold Clock in the central concourse is the city's standard meeting point; the west side, the Taiko-dori exit, holds the shinkansen gates, the Silver Clock, an underground mall of noodle and miso-katsu shops, and the stops for highway buses to Tokyo, Osaka and the Hokuriku coast. Outside the Meitetsu department store stands a giant mannequin, dressed anew for every season and every local cause. On the shinkansen platforms, standing counters sell bowls of flat kishimen noodles, and travelers argue over whether the platform bowl beats the one downstairs. Coin lockers line every passage, and boxed-meal shops sell hitsumabushi eel and tebasaki wings by the case. Weekday mornings bring a flood of office workers and factory commuters; lunchtime fills the underground cafes, many still serving generous morning sets; evenings fill the towers' restaurant floors and the bars around the station; the last trains leave a little after midnight. A police box stands at the Sakura-dori exit, railway police and station guards patrol the concourses, and sidekicks from the downtown agencies stand at the main crossings and wave the crowds through. The shinkansen reaches Musutafu in about 1 hour 15 minutes, Kyoto in about 30 minutes and Shin-Osaka in under an hour; Meitetsu's airport express reaches the Centrair airport on Ise Bay in about half an hour, and the subway reaches Sakae and the castle within ten minutes. It feels big, efficient and practical: a city that builds things and expects its trains to run like its machines.
Nagoya Station.hiddenInfo: Stolen machine parts are leaving the city on the night highway buses from the Taiko-dori side, and it is happening right now. Three or four nights a week, around 11:30 p.m., a delivery rider with a heavy mutant build, gray scales on his forearms and an insulated courier backpack, meets the last overnight buses to Tokyo and Osaka and checks two hard suitcases into the luggage hold under a different passenger's name each time. The cases hold precision bearings and machine-tool heads lifted from subcontractor plants in the southern wards, and they are collected at the far end before the factories notice the gaps. One overnight driver has noticed that the cases are always too heavy for their size and that the ticketed passenger never boards; she mentioned it only to her dispatcher, who told her not to make trouble. A plant foreman whose shop lost a whole crate last week has started waiting in the Taiko-dori underground mall in the evenings, hoping to recognize something, and he is angry enough to try to stop the rider himself, which would end badly for him. How the place really runs: JR Central owns the main building and guards it closely, while the private railways and bus operators each patrol their own ground, so the seams between them, the passages, bus stops and loading docks, are where trouble lives. Downtown agencies split the station patrol by exit and shift, and the night rotation is the thinnest; the police box can call a sidekick in minutes, but nobody watches the bus holds.

Nagoya Central Concourse.description: The central concourse runs straight through the JR building from the Sakura-dori exit on the downtown side to the Taiko-dori exit on the shinkansen side: a long, polished hall of ticket gates, kiosks and coin lockers under the twin towers. At the east end stands the Gold Clock, the city's standard meeting point, and at the west end its partner, the Silver Clock, near the shinkansen gates; people arrange to meet at one and wait at the other. On weekday mornings a flood of office workers and factory commuters crosses in both directions; in the evening business travelers queue at boxed-meal shops selling hitsumabushi eel and tebasaki wings by the case. Railway police and station guards patrol the hall, and sidekicks from the downtown agencies stand at the crossings outside the Sakura-dori exit, waving the crowds through. Announcements are calm and exact. The last trains leave a little after midnight, and the hall empties to cleaners and a few late travelers heading west for the night buses. Stairs go down to the Nagoya Underground Mall, and the Taiko-dori exit opens onto the Taiko-dori Night Bus Stops.

Nagoya Underground Mall.description: Beneath the station's west side runs a bright underground mall of low ceilings and narrow lanes, the start of a maze that ties the Meieki district together. On the Taiko-dori side the lanes are lined with noodle shops, miso-katsu counters pouring thick dark sauce over pork cutlets, kishimen stands, tebasaki bars, cafes and souvenir shops, and the cafes are famous for their morning sets: order a coffee before eleven and toast, a boiled egg and sometimes a salad come with it free. Office workers fill the lanes at lunch, travelers kill time before the shinkansen over a bowl of noodles, and in the evening the crowd turns to beer and fried wings. Lately a man in a factory work jacket sits in one of the cafes every evening over a single coffee until closing, watching every traveler's luggage roll past with a hard, unhappy look; the staff have stopped asking him to order more. The smell of miso and frying oil follows shoppers up the stairs,. Most shops close around nine or ten. Stairs climb back to the Nagoya Central Concourse, and an exit at the west end comes up beside the Taiko-dori Night Bus Stops.

Taiko-dori Night Bus Stops.description: Along the curb outside the Taiko-dori exit, in the shadow of hotels and office towers, a row of highway-bus stops with numbered poles and a small ticket office sends coaches to Tokyo, Osaka, Kyoto, the Hokuriku coast and the mountain towns. Daytime buses carry budget travelers, shoppers and students; after dark the overnight coaches take over, and by eleven the sidewalk fills with backpackers and travelers clutching neck pillows. Drivers load the luggage holds themselves, check each case against a ticket and call passengers by name before the doors hiss shut. The last overnight buses to Tokyo and Osaka leave around 11:30 p.m.; delivery riders still come and go along the curb even then, and one veteran driver has a habit of hefting each case before she loads it, frowning at the heavy ones. Diesel engines idle and convenience-store coffee goes cold in people's hands. Station guards rarely walk this far after dark, and the police box is on the far side of the building. The Taiko-dori exit leads back into the Nagoya Central Concourse, and the stairs beside the stops go down to the Nagoya Underground Mall.

Sannomiya Station.name: Sannomiya Station
Sannomiya Station.basicInfo: Sannomiya is the heart of Kobe and its main rail hub: not one station but a knot of them under and around the elevated tracks, where JR West's Kobe Line, the Hankyu and Hanshin lines toward Osaka, two subway lines and the driverless Port Liner to Port Island and Kobe Airport all meet within a few minutes' walk of each other. The shinkansen does not stop here: travelers from Musutafu ride to Shin-Kobe, at the foot of the mountains, then take the Seishin-Yamate subway one stop, about two minutes, so the whole trip runs about 2 hours 15 minutes. The JR special rapid reaches Osaka in about 20 minutes, the private lines in about half an hour. Around the stations, pedestrian decks and underground passages tie together department stores, a tall fashion building over the JR east exit, the long covered arcade of Center Gai heading west toward Motomachi and Chinatown, and Flower Road running south between trees toward city hall and its flower clock, with the harbor beyond. North of the tracks the streets climb at once toward Ikuta Shrine, a few minutes' walk away, the bar lanes of Kitanozaka and the old Western merchant houses of Kitano, and the green wall of the Rokko mountains stands over everything, so nobody here ever loses north. The bus terminal on the south side sends highway buses over the Akashi Strait bridge to Awaji and Shikoku and airport buses to Kansai Airport; taxi ranks wait at every exit, and coin lockers line the passages. Mornings belong to commuters and students, afternoons to shoppers and bakery lines, evenings to office crowds heading for the izakaya under the tracks, and on weekends the arcades are shoulder to shoulder. Police boxes stand at the JR exits, railway police patrol the platforms, and sidekicks from the city's many agencies direct the crowds at the big crossings. It feels cosmopolitan and quick, the sea air only a few streets away and the smell of fresh bread and grilled meat in every passage.
Sannomiya Station.hiddenInfo: Every evening at about 9 p.m., a soft-spoken man in a good camel coat walks the row of small shops in the passage under the elevated tracks between the JR and Hanshin stations and collects envelopes from at least four of them: a shoe-repair counter, a secondhand-watch shop, a standing bar and a dumpling stall. He works for one of the old loan-sharking outfits that survive in the port's nightlife, and the shopkeepers are paying off debts at interest that never shrinks. Nobody has gone to the police, because the last owner who complained found his shutter fused shut overnight by someone's Quirk and lost a week of trade. The clerk at the watch shop has a Quirk that lets her recall any face she has seen once, and she has begun drawing the collector and the two men who sometimes wait for him by the Port Liner stairs in a notebook she keeps under the counter; she is frightened, looking for someone she can trust, and will not talk to anyone in uniform while he might be watching. The officers at the JR east exit police box know there is loan sharking under the tracks but have no complaint to act on. How the place really runs: several railways and the city's subway share the station area, each with its own guards, and the passages between them belong to everyone and no one; several agencies split the downtown patrol, and the one that covers the under-track passage is small and spread thin. On weekend nights, pickpockets and unlicensed Quirk scuffles in Center Gai keep every patrol busy, and the collector times his rounds for exactly then.

Sannomiya Station Concourse.description: JR Sannomiya's concourse runs beneath the elevated tracks between the east and west exits: a busy, low-ceilinged hall of ticket gates, departure boards, coin lockers and a bakery counter whose fresh-bread smell fills the whole passage. Outside, pedestrian decks and stairways tie it to the Hankyu and Hanshin stations, two subway lines and the driverless Port Liner, all within a few minutes' walk, and the green wall of the Rokko mountains stands over the rooftops to the north. Mornings bring commuters and students hurrying between lines; afternoons bring shoppers; in the evening office workers drift out toward the izakaya under the tracks, and on weekends the crowd barely moves. Police boxes stand at the JR exits, railway police patrol the platforms above, and sidekicks from the city's many agencies direct the crowds at the big crossings. Trains thunder overhead every couple of minutes, and sea air drifts in from the harbor a few streets south. The last trains leave a little after midnight. The west side opens onto the Center Street Arcade, and a passage along the tracks leads into the Under-the-Tracks Shops.

Center Street Arcade.description: Center Gai runs west from the station under a long arched glass roof, a covered street of boutiques, sneaker shops, game centers, drugstores, cafes and bakeries, with the tracks a block to the north and the arcade carrying on toward Motomachi and Chinatown. Shoppers fill it from mid-morning, students in uniform come after classes for crepes and arcade games, office workers cut through at lunch, and street performers set up at the cross streets in the evening. On weekends the arcade is shoulder to shoulder, and on weekend nights pickpockets and unlicensed Quirk scuffles outside the game centers keep every patrol busy; sidekicks in bright vests jog from one incident to the next, and a shout at one end can pull every uniform in the district toward it for a while. Rain drums on the glass roof without ever touching the shoppers, and every shop plays its own music. Most shutters come down around nine, and by eleven only the game centers and convenience stores are lit. The arcade's east end opens back toward the Sannomiya Station Concourse, and short side streets to the north lead under the tracks into the Under-the-Tracks Shops.

Under-the-Tracks Shops.description: In the passage under the elevated tracks between the JR and Hanshin stations, a row of tiny shops fits into the arches: a shoe-repair counter, a secondhand-watch shop with glass cases of old wristwatches, a standing bar, a dumpling stall and a few others barely wide enough for one customer. The ceiling is low and stained, fluorescent tubes buzz, and every train overhead shakes the dust on the shelves. Commuters cut through all day; after six, office workers crowd the standing bar and the dumpling stall, shoulder to shoulder. Around nine in the evening the talk along the row goes quiet for a few minutes, and nobody explains why. One shutter near the end has a rippled, melted-looking seam where it was fused shut one night and had to be cut open, and the clerk at the watch shop sketches in a notebook under the counter between customers, glancing up at everyone who passes. Two men sometimes stand by the stairs to the Port Liner without ever boarding. The shops close by ten. The passage leads back to the Sannomiya Station Concourse, and short side streets to the south lead out to the Center Street Arcade.

Hiroshima Station.name: Hiroshima Station
Hiroshima Station.basicInfo: Hiroshima Station is the gateway to the western Sanyo coast: a long JR West station on the east side of the downtown delta, newly rebuilt so that the city's streetcars glide off a bridge and straight into the second floor of the south building. The south exit faces the city: streetcars leave every few minutes for Hatchobori, the Hondori arcades and the Peace Memorial Park and A-Bomb Dome, about 20 minutes away, and on a slower line toward Miyajimaguchi. In and beside the south building are shopping floors, an okonomiyaki hall where a dozen griddles turn out layered noodle-and-cabbage pancakes all day, oyster and momiji manju counters, boxed-meal stands, coin lockers and tourist information. The north exit, the shinkansen side, is newer and quieter, with hotels, a pedestrian deck and the limousine bus to Hiroshima Airport, about 50 minutes away. The bus terminal sends city and highway buses everywhere, and taxi ranks wait at both exits. The Sanyo shinkansen reaches Musutafu in about 3 hours 30 minutes, Shin-Osaka in about 1 hour 30 minutes and Hakata in about an hour; the Sanyo Line reaches Miyajimaguchi and the Miyajima ferry in about half an hour, the Kure Line reaches Kure in about 40 minutes, and the Geibi and Kabe lines run up into the hills. Ten minutes' walk southeast stands the city's baseball stadium, and on game nights the station fills with fans in red who sing on the platforms. Mornings bring commuters and students; daytime brings tour groups and school trips bound for the peace park; evenings, office crowds head downtown; the last trains leave around midnight. Police boxes stand at both exits, railway police patrol the platforms, sidekicks work the crowds on game nights, and streetcar crews with Quirks clear a stuck switch without stopping traffic. It feels friendly, unhurried and quietly serious: a city that remembers, and also loves its baseball.
Hiroshima Station.hiddenInfo: A bike gang has started using the north side as its meeting point, and lately as a pickup stop. On Friday and Saturday nights at about 1 a.m., after the last trains, six to ten riders on loud, chromed motorcycles gather in the empty lot beside the north exit's bicycle parking, rev their engines for twenty minutes and roar off toward the bypass. One or two of them now stay behind to collect small taped parcels left in the coin lockers along the north concourse during the evening: cash from the resale of oysters stolen off the bay's rafts, which the riders carry to a buyer at Ujina port before dawn. Chalk marks on the third row of bicycle racks show which lockers hold parcels. A taxi driver who works the north rank at night has dashcam footage of one rider, a broad man with a rooster-red pompadour, using a strength Quirk to bend a steel bollard out of his way, and the bent bollard is still there; the driver has not handed the footage over because the gang knows his cab. How the place really runs: JR West owns the station, and its security staff thin to a skeleton crew after midnight; the streetcar operator runs its own floor; city agencies cover the south exit densely and the north side barely, and the north police box often stands empty after midnight while its officer is out on calls. The gang is small-time, but a hero who shuts it down will earn the oyster farmers' gratitude and the attention of whoever has been buying from them.

Hiroshima Station Concourse.description: Hiroshima Station's concourse runs from the rebuilt south building, where the city's streetcars glide in on a bridge to the second floor, past the JR ticket gates to the newer north side and the shinkansen gates. The south end is busy and full of food: an okonomiyaki hall where a dozen griddles turn out layered noodle-and-cabbage pancakes all day, counters of grilled oysters and maple-leaf momiji manju, boxed-meal stands. The north concourse is quieter, lined with coin lockers that are among the last in the station to be emptied at night. Mornings bring commuters and students; daytime brings tour groups and school trips bound for the peace park; evenings, office crowds heading downtown; on baseball nights fans in red flood through singing. Police boxes stand at both exits, and railway police patrol the gates. The smell of sweet sauce and frying cabbage meets every arriving train. The last trains leave around midnight, and after that the station's security staff thin to a skeleton crew. An escalator rises to the Streetcar Platform, and the north concourse leads out to the North Exit Plaza.

Streetcar Platform.description: On the second floor of the south building the streetcar line ends indoors: the city's trams, old green-and-cream veterans and long, sleek low-floor cars alike, glide off an elevated bridge straight into a bright terminal of platforms under a glass roof, so riders step from the JR gates onto a streetcar without going outside. Cars leave every few minutes for Hatchobori and the Hondori arcades, for the Peace Memorial Park and the A-Bomb Dome about 20 minutes away, and on a slower line toward Miyajimaguchi. The cars squeal and ring their bells as they curve out over the street. Morning cars carry commuters and students; daytime cars fill with tour groups and school trips, guides holding flags; on game nights the cars run packed with fans in red. Crews know their routes by heart, and one with a Quirk can clear a stuck switch without stopping traffic, a small daily show regulars hardly notice. The streetcar operator runs this floor its own way, with its own staff and a gentle chime before every departure. The last cars leave late in the evening. The platform opens back into the Hiroshima Station Concourse.

North Exit Plaza.description: The north exit is the shinkansen side, newer and quieter: a pedestrian deck over a broad plaza, business hotels, a taxi rank, the stop for the limousine bus to Hiroshima Airport about 50 minutes away, rows of covered bicycle racks and, beside them, an empty paved lot. Business travelers come and go through the day and hotel guests wheel cases across the deck. After the last trains the plaza goes very quiet; the police box often stands empty after midnight while its officer is out on calls, and on Friday and Saturday nights at about one in the morning the empty lot fills with the roar of loud, chromed motorcycles revving for twenty minutes before they tear off toward the bypass. A steel bollard by the lot is bent nearly flat, and nobody has fixed it; chalk marks come and go on the third row of bicycle racks. Taxi drivers who work the north rank at night keep their doors locked and talk among themselves, and one of them watches the lot more carefully than the others. Streetlights hum over the empty deck. The north concourse leads back into the Hiroshima Station Concourse.

Kanazawa Station.name: Kanazawa Station
Kanazawa Station.basicInfo: Kanazawa Station is the Hokuriku coast's front door, a JR West station on the Hokuriku shinkansen whose east exit is famous in its own right: a huge glass-and-aluminum canopy called the Motenashi Dome, built to hold an umbrella over arriving guests, and before it the Tsuzumi-mon, a towering gate of laminated wooden pillars twisted like the cords of a hand drum. Locals say that even if you forget your lunch you should never forget your umbrella, and the dome earns its keep from November to March, when gray rain, sleet and sea thunder roll in for days. The east exit faces the old city: the bus terminal under the dome sends loop buses and city buses to the Omicho fish market, Kenrokuen and the castle park, the Higashi Chaya teahouse district and the Katamachi nightlife streets, each ten to fifteen minutes away, and taxi ranks wait beside it. The west exit is plainer and more businesslike, with office blocks, hotels, a broad avenue running toward the port and the buses to Komatsu Airport. Inside, the shopping halls sell gold-leaf everything, from lacquer boxes to cakes, along with Kutani porcelain, wagashi sweets, sake, crab and nodoguro boxed meals and thick Kanazawa curry, and the coin lockers fill early on weekends. The Hokuriku shinkansen runs east to Tokyo in about 2 hours 30 minutes, so Musutafu is about 3 hours 30 minutes away via Tokyo, or about the same via Nagoya and Maibara by limited express and the shinkansen through Tsuruga; westward it runs to Tsuruga for the limited express to Osaka, about two hours in all. IR Ishikawa local trains and the Hokutetsu line from its underground platform fill in. Mornings bring commuters and students; daytime brings tour groups and rental-kimono strollers; evenings, office workers and diners head for Katamachi; the last trains leave before midnight. A police box stands at the east exit, and sidekicks from the local agencies patrol the plaza under the dome. It feels elegant, welcoming and a little formal: a craft city dressed for guests.
Kanazawa Station.hiddenInfo: Counterfeit Kutani porcelain is being sold to tour groups at the west exit right now, each weekday morning between about 9:30 and 11 a.m., while the chartered tour buses load. A smiling man in a dark blue happi coat, with a folding table and two rolling suitcases, offers hand-painted Kutani plates and gold-leaf sake cups at a fifth of shop prices, each with a printed certificate of authenticity; the plates are cheap blanks with transfer decals fired on, and the gold is brass foil. He sets up just off station property, on the sidewalk of the avenue, so the station guards have nothing to say, and he packs up the moment a uniform comes near, because his lookout, a woman pretending to study a bus timetable, has a Quirk that lets her hear the tread of patrol boots from the far side of the plaza. A clerk at a genuine Kutani shop inside the station hall bought one plate, looked at it under a lamp and scratched the glaze with her thumbnail; she has written down the certificate's phone number, which reaches only a voicemail, and she wants someone to take it seriously before the craft associations blame the station shops. How the place really runs: JR West owns the station, the city owns the dome and the plaza, and the shopping halls answer to a merchants' committee of old local houses who care about reputation above everything; two local agencies split the station patrol, reliable but stretched thin in tourist season and in the winter storms.

Tsuzumi Gate Plaza.description: The east exit opens beneath the Motenashi Dome, a huge canopy of glass and aluminum lattice built to hold an umbrella over arriving guests, and beyond it stands the Tsuzumi-mon, a towering gate of laminated wooden pillars twisted like the cords of a hand drum. In front of the dome a fountain clock spells out the time in falling drops of water. The bus terminal under the dome sends loop and city buses to the Omicho fish market, Kenrokuen and the castle park, the Higashi Chaya teahouse district and Katamachi, each ten to fifteen minutes away, and taxis wait beside it. Mornings bring commuters and students; daytime brings tour groups and rental-kimono strollers posing between the pillars; evenings, diners head out for Katamachi. From November to March gray rain, sleet and sea thunder roll in for days, and the dome earns its keep. A police box stands at the east exit, and sidekicks from the local agencies patrol the plaza in pairs, their boots ringing loud on the stone under the dome. Glass doors lead into the Kanazawa Station Concourse, and a walk through the station brings you to the Kanazawa West Exit.

Kanazawa Station Concourse.description: Inside, the concourse runs from the dome to the west exit past the JR gates for the Hokuriku shinkansen and the IR Ishikawa local trains, with stairs down to the Hokutetsu line's underground platform. On both sides the shopping halls sell gold-leaf everything, from lacquer boxes to cakes and soft-serve ice cream wrapped in a sheet of gold, along with Kutani porcelain, wagashi sweets, sake, crab and nodoguro boxed meals and thick Kanazawa curry with shredded cabbage. The shops belong to old local houses, and their staff are polite, precise and proud of their goods. Commuters pass through in the morning, tour groups shop all day, and the curry counters fill at lunch; evenings are quieter, and the last trains leave before midnight. In one porcelain shop a clerk keeps a single cheap-looking plate behind the counter beside the real pieces and will show anyone who asks about Kutani how to tell the difference, scratching its glaze with a thumbnail. The halls smell of sweet bean paste and curry. Glass doors lead out to Tsuzumi Gate Plaza, and the other end of the concourse opens onto the Kanazawa West Exit.

Kanazawa West Exit.description: The west exit is plainer and more businesslike than the east: a broad plaza ringed by office blocks and business hotels, a taxi rank, the stops for the airport buses to Komatsu and a wide, straight avenue running toward the port. Station property ends at the plaza's edge, and the avenue sidewalk beyond belongs to the city. On weekday mornings chartered tour buses line the curb and load between about half past nine and eleven while tour groups mill about with shopping bags and guides count heads; street vendors sometimes set up folding tables on the avenue sidewalk just past the station's edge, selling to the waiting groups, and pack up quickly whenever a uniform comes near. A woman often stands by the bus timetable board, studying it far longer than anyone needs to. Office workers cross at rush hour, salarymen smoke in the marked corner, and in winter the wind off the Sea of Japan comes straight down the avenue carrying sleet. Evenings are quiet, taxis idling in the cold. The doors lead back into the Kanazawa Station Concourse, and a walk through the station brings you to Tsuzumi Gate Plaza.

Utsunomiya Station.name: Utsunomiya Station
Utsunomiya Station.basicInfo: Utsunomiya Station is the gateway to Tochigi and the northern Kanto plain: a big JR East station on the Tohoku shinkansen, with the city spread out to the west and the new light rail running east. The west exit faces downtown across a wide pedestrian deck over the bus terminal, where buses leave for the Oya stone quarries, Futaarayama Shrine on its hill in the center of town and the outlying towns; on the deck stands a statue of a woman wrapped in a gyoza skin, carved from Oya stone, which everyone photographs and nobody explains. In and around the station, gyoza shops argue over the best dumpling in a city that takes the question seriously, and boxed-meal and souvenir stands sell frozen gyoza packs, strawberry sweets, kanpyo and Mashiko pottery cups. The east exit is newer, flat and spacious, with the light rail platform at its center, its trams gliding east across the Kinu river to the industrial parks and Haga, and a plaza with a convention hall. Coin lockers line the concourse, bicycle racks fill the streets on both sides, and taxi ranks wait at each exit. The Tohoku shinkansen reaches Tokyo in about 50 minutes, so Musutafu is about 2 hours away with a change at Tokyo; the Utsunomiya Line runs south toward Tokyo more slowly, the Nikko Line reaches Nikko in about 45 minutes, and the Karasuyama Line runs east into the hills; the separate Tobu station for the private line south lies downtown, about a 25-minute walk west. Mornings bring commuters, students and factory shift buses; noon brings gyoza lines; evenings, workers head downtown for the jazz bars and cocktail lounges; the last trains leave before midnight. A police box stands at the west exit, the prefectural police headquarters are in the city, and sidekicks from the local agencies patrol the deck. It feels comfortable, local and unhurried: a capital that is happy to be a short trip from Tokyo and happier still to be home.
Utsunomiya Station.hiddenInfo: A phone-scam crew is using the station to collect its money, and the next pickup is set for this week. Callers somewhere far away phone elderly people in the farm towns, pretending to be a grandson in trouble or a bank officer, then send a collector to meet the victim at the west exit or to pick up an envelope of cash left in a coin locker. The collectors are hired one job at a time through online ads for easy money: right now it is a nervous man in a too-new gray suit who arrives on the shinkansen from Tokyo around 2 p.m., checks his phone constantly and waits by the gyoza statue; he has no Quirk worth mentioning and does not know who he works for. An elderly woman from Nasukarasuyama is coming in on the Karasuyama Line with three million yen in a cloth bag for her grandson's emergency, and her real grandson knows nothing about it. A ticket-gate attendant who has already seen two other old people come through clutching bags and looking for a stranger has started writing down the times; the officer at the west exit police box has been told to watch for exactly this, but is alone on afternoon shifts and also takes the bicycle theft reports, which come in by the dozen. How the place really runs: JR East runs the station, the light rail runs its own east-side platform, and the city owns the decks and plaza; one local agency holds the station patrol and splits its sidekicks between the deck and the bar streets at night, where Quirk brawls at closing time keep them busiest. Bag snatching on the deck peaks on festival weekends.

Utsunomiya Station Concourse.description: Utsunomiya Station's concourse runs through the JR East building between the west exit, facing downtown, and the newer east exit with its light rail platform, passing the shinkansen gates, the gates for the Utsunomiya, Nikko and Karasuyama lines, coin lockers and boxed-meal and souvenir stands selling frozen gyoza packs, strawberry sweets, kanpyo and Mashiko pottery cups. Mornings bring commuters, students and workers heading for the factory shift buses; at noon visitors follow their noses toward the gyoza shops; in the evening workers stream west toward downtown's jazz bars and cocktail lounges. Elderly travelers from the farm towns come in on the Karasuyama Line in the afternoons with their bags held close, looking about for whoever is meeting them, and the attendant at the ticket gate has started writing down the times they pass. Announcements are calm and unhurried, and the smell of frying dumplings drifts in from the west side. The last trains leave before midnight. A short walk past the shops leads to Gyoza Street, and the west doors open onto the Utsunomiya West Exit Plaza and its deck.

Gyoza Street.description: Along the west side of the station building and the streets just beyond it, gyoza shops crowd side by side, each with a hand-lettered sign, a steamed-up window and a line out the door at noon: pan-fried dumplings with crisp, lacy bottoms, boiled gyoza in broth, deep-fried gyoza, sets with rice and soup, and frozen packs to take home. Every shop has its partisans, and in a city that takes the question seriously, regulars argue loudly over whose filling gets the balance of cabbage, garlic and pork right, and whether vinegar and pepper beat soy and chili oil. Office workers and travelers queue at lunch; shinkansen passengers grab a plate before the train back to Tokyo; evenings bring workers with beer and plates stacked high; most shops close around nine. Cooks work in full view, sizzling rows of dumplings in heavy iron pans and lifting the lids in clouds of steam, and the whole street smells of sesame oil and garlic. Some shops have menus with only three things on them and refuse to add a fourth, and first-timers who ask for something else get a patient lecture. The street leads back into the Utsunomiya Station Concourse.

Utsunomiya West Exit Plaza.description: The west exit opens onto a wide pedestrian deck over the bus terminal, with stairs down to the bus stands, bicycle racks and taxi ranks below and the city spreading west toward downtown and Futaarayama Shrine on its hill. On the deck stands a statue of a woman wrapped in a gyoza skin, carved from pale Oya stone, which everyone photographs and nobody explains; it is the obvious place to meet a stranger. Buses below leave for the Oya stone quarries, the shrine and the outlying towns. Mornings bring commuters and students; at noon tourists photograph the statue; in the afternoon, after the shinkansen from Tokyo comes in around two, there is often someone waiting by the statue who checks a phone constantly and does not look like anyone's relative. The police box at the west exit has one officer on afternoon shifts, who spends half of it taking bicycle theft reports, which come in by the dozen. Sidekicks from the local agency patrol the deck by day; at night they split their time with the bar streets downtown, and on festival weekends bag snatchers work the crowds up here. The doors lead back into the Utsunomiya Station Concourse.

Tokyo Bayside Mall.name: Tokyo Bayside Mall
Tokyo Bayside Mall.basicInfo: A waterfront mega-mall on reclaimed land in Tokyo Bay, about 7 km south of Tokyo Station and just over a kilometer southeast of the Tokyo Broadcasting Center, across a narrow channel; the Hero Billboard Chart Hall is about 4 km to the north-northeast and the Best Jeanist Hero Agency about 4 km to the west. A driverless elevated train loops out over the harbor from the city, a footbridge crosses the channel from the broadcasting center's side, and water buses tie up at the mall's own pier. Five floors of shops, restaurants and entertainment run along the seawall, fronted by the All Might Statue Plaza, where a giant likeness of the Number One stands over the boardwalk, and closed at the east end by the Bayside Ferris Wheel, the tallest thing on the island. Inside are a food hall, a hero history gallery with its museum shop, a whole floor of games, fashion and sporting chains, and fittings built for every body: double-width doors, reinforced benches, escalators with clearance for wings and fitting rooms sized for tails and extra limbs. Shops open at ten and close at nine, restaurants and the games floor run until eleven, and the plaza and the boardwalk stay open all night under lamps. Weekday mornings belong to tour groups and school trips; lunch brings staff from the broadcasting center; after classes come students, and weekends pack the island with families, couples, tourists and hero fans, U.A. students among them on a day out an hour from Musutafu. Since the news that All Might teaches at U.A., the statue draws a line of fans from opening to dusk. The management company's uniformed guards carry radios and have no authority to use Quirks; the Metropolitan Police keep a box at the plaza, and small agencies on contract walk the boardwalk in pairs on weekends. A player can shop, eat, ride the wheel, sell footage to the network next door, work a part-time shift or meet friends under the statue. Gulls, sea wind and the plaza's chime on the hour set the mood.
Tokyo Bayside Mall.hiddenInfo: Right now a two-person freelance crew is planning to stage a rescue on the Bayside Ferris Wheel and sell it to the newsroom next door, which pays cash for incident footage and does not ask how a shot was taken. Their date is Saturday at dusk, when the wheel's queue is longest and the statue's first light show turns every phone on the plaza toward the water. One of them, a thin man in a gray windbreaker, has a Quirk that drains the charge from anything electric he holds for about a minute; he has ridden the wheel alone five times this week, filming the drive cabinet beside the boarding deck as his gondola came down, and has timed a full turn at sixteen minutes. The other will run the camera from the Arcade Floor's skybridge. They have promised a rookie licensed hero from a small agency across the bay a cut of the sale and a clip that could lift his approval for months; he believes the stall will be a harmless pause of a minute or two. It will not be: when the drive loses power the brakes lock every gondola in place until engineers reset the system, which took fifty minutes the last time, when an elderly rider fainted at the top. Clues are there for anyone who looks: the wheel attendant remembers the solo rider and his camera, the drive cabinet's lock was found scratched on Wednesday, and the rookie's sidekick has twice asked the plaza police box what time the lights come on. The officers there would act on a name; the mall's guards would rather hand it to anyone else. Meanwhile management is quietly haggling over the license fee for the statue's likeness, and the museum shop's manager suspects that some signed cards consigned to her are forged.

All Might Statue Plaza.description: A broad plaza of pale paving at the front of the mall, open to the bay on one side, where an All Might statue about eighteen meters tall stands on a stone plinth in his familiar blue, red and gold costume, one fist raised to the sky and his grin turned to the water. The plaque on the plinth carries his famous words, I am here, and fans touch his boot for luck until the toe shines. This is the island's arrival point: the elevated train's station opens onto one corner, the footbridge from the broadcasting center lands on another, and water buses tie up at the pier steps. A photo line forms by ten and runs until dusk, longer since the news that he teaches at U.A., and a staffer with a megaphone keeps it moving at one photo per group. At sunset the statue lights up, and a short light show plays across it every hour until ten. A police box sits by the train exit, and the guards ask fliers not to perch on his shoulders. Sea wind, gulls and the hourly chime fill the air. Glass doors open into the Bayside Food Hall, escalators climb to the Hero Museum Shop and the Arcade Floor, and the boardwalk runs east to the Bayside Ferris Wheel.

Bayside Food Hall.description: A long ground-floor hall behind a glass wall facing the bay, with about thirty food counters around shared tables and a wooden deck outside where diners eat in the sea air. The counters cover the whole country: monjayaki and okonomiyaki griddles, conveyor sushi, tempura bowls, ramen, curry, Korean barbecue, crepes, soft-serve and a bakery whose melon bread sells out by two. A bowl or a set runs 800 to 1,500 yen, and the hall's hero collaboration menu changes each season; this spring it is an All Might hamburger steak with a gold-flecked egg and a paper flag of his grin. Lunch brings staff from the broadcasting center across the channel, talking shop in their lanyards; after classes come students who stretch one drink across an afternoon; weekends fill every seat by noon. One section has wide benches and tables bolted to the floor for big and heavy heteromorph diners, and a card on each table asks guests not to use Quirks to heat, cool or fetch their food. Gulls patrol the deck railing for dropped fries, and the griddles hiss out the smell of soy and butter. The hall opens back onto the All Might Statue Plaza.

Hero Museum Shop.description: A gallery and shop on the second floor, laid out like a small museum. A timeline along one wall runs from the first Quirk births through the years of chaos to the founding of hero licensing, with glass cases of old costumes, worn capture tools and old front pages; a room at the end belongs to All Might, with his famous rescues looping on screens and a life-size cutout that fans stand beside for photos, most of them reaching his chest. The gallery is free. The shop beyond it sells licensed figures from 3,000 to 20,000 yen, replica capes, trading cards and signed goods in sealed frames, each with a holographic license seal so buyers can tell them from street fakes. Weekday mornings bring school trips and tour groups; afternoons bring collectors who know the stock better than the staff; weekends bring families, and since the news about U.A. the All Might shelves are restocked twice a day. Staff wear white gloves, and a sign asks visitors to keep Quirks away from the cases. It smells of new cardboard and floor polish. Escalators lead down to the All Might Statue Plaza and up to the Arcade Floor.

Arcade Floor.description: The whole third floor is one big game center under a black ceiling strung with colored lights. By the escalators stand rows of crane machines stocked with plush heroes, All Might in every size at the front, then photo-sticker booths with hero frames and curtained stalls; deeper in are rhythm games, a taiko cabinet, fighting-game cabinets and a medal corner with a jackpot tower. The showpiece is a rescue simulator, a padded booth with screens on three sides where players dodge and reach through a collapsing city to carry virtual civilians out, 500 yen a run, with the day's top scores posted outside. Most other games cost 100 yen. Students crowd the cranes after classes, fighting-game regulars arrive after dinner, and weekends bring families who leave with armfuls of plush. It stays open until eleven, after the shops close. Staff in vests unjam machines, and a notice on every cabinet says Quirk use means a lifetime ban. The noise is a wall of jingles and pouring medals. Escalators lead down to the Hero Museum Shop and the All Might Statue Plaza, and a glass skybridge at the east end crosses to the Bayside Ferris Wheel.

Bayside Ferris Wheel.description: At the island's east end stands the tallest thing on the waterfront, a Ferris wheel about 110 meters high with sixty-four gondolas, two of them with glass floors, turning above a boarding deck. A turn takes about sixteen minutes and costs 1,000 yen; the glass-floor gondolas cost more. From the top the whole bay opens out: the broadcasting center's helipad close by to the northwest, the towers of central Tokyo to the north, container cranes and ships to the south and, on the clearest winter days, Mount Fuji far to the west. It runs from ten until ten at night and stops in high wind. Tour groups ride in the morning, students in the afternoon, and at dusk the queue fills with couples waiting for the spokes to light up in slow waves of color. Wider gondolas with reinforced floors carry heteromorph riders, and a sign at the gate reminds fliers that nobody leaves a gondola in the air. An attendant in a windbreaker checks every latch by hand, and the motor hums under the clank of doors. The boardwalk leads back to the All Might Statue Plaza, and the skybridge crosses to the Arcade Floor.

Umeda Station Complex.name: Umeda Station Complex
Umeda Station Complex.basicInfo: A department-store and station tower over Osaka's northern rail terminals in the Umeda district, about 3.5 km south of Shin-Osaka Station: the loop line and the private railways meet beneath it, subway platforms run underneath, and underground shopping streets spread from its basements in every direction. Fat Gum's agency lies about 3 km to the northeast and Sir Nighteye's about 4.5 km to the northwest. The complex stacks everything in one building: the Grand Atrium, a glass hall over the tracks where half of Osaka arranges to meet; the depachika food floors in the basement; seven floors of fashion, cosmetics and homeware with a hero goods corner; restaurant floors near the top; and the Sky Garden Deck on the tower's roof, about 170 meters up. Trains run from about five in the morning until after midnight, the store opens at ten and closes at eight, the restaurant floors serve until eleven and the deck stays open until half past ten. Commuters pour through the atrium from seven to nine and five to eight; office workers fill the basement at lunch; shoppers, tourists and students take the afternoons, and weekends are shoulder to shoulder. Shiketsu Academy students in peaked caps are a common sight on their days off. Station staff run the gates, the store's guards in navy blazers walk the floors with radios and no authority to use Quirks, and a police box by the central gates takes reports; local agencies split the district's patrols with the police, and shopkeepers expect any hero who passes to stop for a photo and a joke. The building was made for every body: double-width gates, ramps, freight-sized lifts for wings and tails, and benches reinforced for heavy builds. A player can shop, eat through the basement, catch a train to anywhere in Kansai, work a counter or a stockroom shift, meet a contact under the atrium clock or ride up to the deck at sunset. Announcements chime, the crowd roars softly, and somebody is always haggling, even where the prices are fixed.
Umeda Station Complex.hiddenInfo: Right now someone is using the Grand Atrium to shop for muscle. On weekend afternoons a folding booth appears under a banner for a Quirk aptitude survey, staffed by two young women in matching windbreakers who offer a 1,000-yen gift card to anyone who fills in a form: name, phone number, Quirk type, how strong it is, and whether it has ever hurt anyone. The permit taped to the table carries a stamp the store's events office never issued, and the booth sets up in a different corner every weekend, so the floor guards never see it twice. At closing the forms leave in a paper bag with a man in a cap who waits by the north exit, and on Sunday nights they reach a broker in a back-street bar near the terminals who sells lists of strong, broke Quirk users to anyone who needs quiet work done. Three people who filled in the form, all with fighting Quirks, have since been called and offered cash for night moving jobs; one of them, a delivery rider, took the offer and has not come home since Thursday, and his sister has been asking at the police box. The two women believe they do market research for a staffing agency and are paid 5,000 yen a day.
