Clues: gift cards that the store's own counters refuse, a guard who remembers the same booth in the opposite corner last week, and a sister with her brother's photo on her phone. The police box would act on anything firmer than a hunch, and Fat Gum's agency, a short ride away, listens to anyone who brings snacks. Meanwhile a deck attendant lets couples linger past closing for a tip, which management has not yet noticed.

Grand Atrium.description: A glass hall eight floors high that bridges the station's north and south buildings over the tracks, so trains slide past beneath floor windows and a giant clock hangs from a steel bridge overhead. The ticket gates for the loop line and the private railways open onto its ground level, subway stairs drop from its corners, and escalators climb its walls. Under the clock is where half of Osaka arranges to meet, and on weekend afternoons people hold their phones up to find each other. A big screen loops hero news and store sales; weekends bring seasonal markets, a hero signing at a folding table or a local agency's safety talk, and Shiketsu students in peaked caps sometimes stop to listen with their hands behind their backs. Station staff watch the gates, store guards in navy blazers walk the balconies with radios, and the police box by the central gates hands out maps and takes reports. Every announcement chimes twice, and the wind of passing trains rises through the floor grilles. Stairs lead down to the Depachika Food Floor, escalators climb to the Umeda Fashion Floors, and express elevators rise to the Sky Garden Deck.

Depachika Food Floor.description: Two basement floors of food counters under bright white light, packed so close that the aisles become one long queue: pickles in wooden tubs, wagyu boxed meals, grilled eel, tempura, dumplings, fruit in gift boxes priced like jewelry, rice crackers, takoyaki and the delicate sweets Osaka people carry as gifts. Clerks in white caps call out welcomes and prices, pass samples on toothpicks across the glass and wrap gift boxes in seconds. Office workers fight for boxed lunches at noon; afternoons belong to retirees and regulars who know which counter is best each season; in the last hour before the eight o'clock close, markdown stickers go onto the boxed meals and the crowd becomes a polite stampede. A boxed meal runs 800 to 2,500 yen; a melon in a gift box can cost ten times that. Hero collaboration sweets sit by the stairs, this spring All Might castella in gold boxes and round buns shaped like Fat Gum from a local bakery. A sign at the takoyaki counter asks customers not to use Quirks to reach over the queue. The smell of sauce, dashi and burnt sugar is everywhere. Stairs and escalators climb to the Grand Atrium.

Umeda Fashion Floors.description: Seven floors of fashion, cosmetics and homeware above the atrium, from perfume counters and handbags on the lower levels to young labels, menswear, kimono and clothes for small children higher up, with a hero goods corner on the top fashion floor. Each floor rings an open well, so shoppers on the escalators can see the crowds above and below. The cut matters here: a tailoring counter alters suits and dresses for tails, wings, horns and extra arms while customers wait, and the larger fitting rooms have wing space and reinforced hooks. The hero corner stocks Kansai favorites, Fat Gum plush among them, beside the national stars, and its All Might teacher goods sold out the week the news broke. Weekday mornings bring retirees; after work come office workers; weekends bring couples, families and students hauling bags. Clerks banter even where prices are fixed, and customers bargain back for the fun of it. A guard in a navy blazer stands at the head of each escalator. The music is soft, the light is flattering, and every floor smells faintly of the perfume counters below. The escalators lead back down to the Grand Atrium.

Sky Garden Deck.description: An open-air garden on the tower's roof, about 170 meters up, reached by express elevators from the Grand Atrium. A ring deck runs around the edge behind a chest-high glass windbreak, with planters of grasses and maples, wooden benches, a small cafe counter and coin telescopes. Entry is 1,200 yen. The view runs all the way around: the Yodo River and Shin-Osaka's tracks to the north, the dense towers of downtown to the south, the bay and its cranes to the west under the Rokko mountains, and on clear evenings city lights spreading to the hills on every side. Mornings bring tourists and retirees with cameras; at lunch office workers eat boxed meals from the basement; at sunset couples take the benches facing west, and the deck stays open until half past ten. When the wind picks up, sensors close the outer ring and an attendant ropes it off. A sign by the elevators says fliers may not take off from or land on the deck, and the guards add that the rule goes double for umbrellas. The wind hums in the glass and carries the faint sound of trains far below. The express elevators lead back down to the Grand Atrium.

Hakata Canal Mall.name: Hakata Canal Mall
Hakata Canal Mall.basicInfo: A curving mall built around a man-made canal between Hakata and Nakasu, about a kilometer east of downtown Fukuoka's riverside, with Hakata Station about 3 km to the southeast and the Hawks Hero Agency about 3 km to the northeast. Its buildings bend along both banks of a canal about 180 meters long, joined by bridges and terraces painted in warm reds, ochres, plums and blues, with a hotel, a cinema, a theater and a whole floor of ramen under one roof. Its heart is the Fountain Stage, a round stage at the canal's widest point where jets leap in time to music every half hour and free shows play on weekends; the Canal Walk follows the water past shops and cafes; the Ramen Floor sits on top; and at the far end the Canal Theater Hall stages touring musicals and hero shows. Shops open at ten and close at nine, the restaurants and the Ramen Floor stay open until eleven, and the canal terraces are public ground until midnight. Mornings bring retirees walking laps and tourists off the airport subway; lunch brings office workers from Hakata; after classes come students, Ketsubutsu Academy's among them; weekends and holidays fill every terrace with families, tour groups and couples. Hawks goods outsell everything here, and people glance up whenever a shadow crosses the open sky above the canal. The mall's guards carry radios and have no authority to use Quirks; the prefectural police keep a box at the gate on the Hakata side, and a small local agency holds the mall's security contract and walks the terraces in pairs in the afternoons. Bridges and ramps are wide enough for heteromorph shoppers, the escalators have clearance for wings, and the restrooms include wide stalls. A player can shop, eat, watch a show, work a counter or a stage-crew shift, meet someone by the fountain or follow the canal to the theater. The water is the sound of the place, splashing under the music, and in the evening the whole curve glows.
Hakata Canal Mall.hiddenInfo: Right now the mall is a retail counter for the port's unregistered support gear. On Saturdays and Sundays a pop-up stall on the Canal Walk sells legal training goods, weighted vests, grip trainers and resistance bands, run by a wiry man with a sunburned neck and a cheerful patter about hero fitness. Customers who ask the right questions are shown a catalog on his phone of wrist grapples, compressed-air gauntlets and Quirk-amplifying gloves at 30,000 to 80,000 yen in cash, and told to collect from a car on the third level of the parking garage after eight. The gear comes through the forwarding company at the harbor that declares it machine parts, and none of it is registered or tested. His buyers are local students and would-be street heroes who cannot get licensed gear; one of them, a Ketsubutsu student, burned his palm last week when a gauntlet misfired on the river path, and he told the clinic it was a cooking accident. Clues: cardboard boxes stamped machine parts under the stall's table, a cook on the Ramen Floor who put ice on that burn and asked no questions, and a mall guard who has seen the same car on the third level every Saturday night. The small local agency that holds the mall's security contract has a sidekick who noticed the stall weeks ago and wants to make the arrest himself, for the credit his agency badly needs; he has told nobody, not even his boss, and he watches alone from the Fountain Stage terraces. If the seller spots him, the stall will simply move to another mall. Meanwhile the theater's stage crew is short two hands for the hero musical's run and hires anyone who can lift a flat and keep quiet backstage.

Fountain Stage.description: A round stage at the widest point of the canal, half ringed by curving terraces that climb five floors like the tiers of an amphitheater, with shops and restaurants along every balcony. The water in front of the stage hides rows of jets that leap to music every half hour from ten in the morning to ten at night, in arcs, walls and columns; after dark the show adds lights and a mist screen that throws pictures onto the spray. Weekends bring free shows on the stage: street performers, school bands, idol groups, and now and then a local agency's safety demonstration that ends in photos. Families claim the lowest terrace steps early, and the front row gets wet on purpose. The police box at the Hakata-side gate is a minute's walk away, and mall guards stand at the railings during shows. Performers may not use Quirks on stage without a permit from the management office, which keeps the paperwork short and the answer usually no. Splashing water and a countdown from the speakers set the rhythm. The Canal Walk runs off along the water, escalators climb to the Ramen Floor, and a covered bridge crosses to the Canal Theater Hall.

Canal Walk.description: A promenade about 180 meters long that follows the canal's curve between walls painted in reds, ochres, plums and sky blue, with shops and cafes on two levels and small bridges crossing the water every few dozen meters. The canal is shallow and clear over a tiled floor, and coins glint under the bridges. The shops run from fashion chains and sneaker stores to stationery, character goods and a hero goods shop whose window is mostly Hawks: feather keychains, wing hoodies and posters of him eating fried chicken. Retirees walk laps before the shops open at ten; office workers cut through at lunch; students drift along after classes, and weekends bring tourists photographing every bend. On Saturdays and Sundays pop-up stalls set up along the wider stretch, selling crafts, phone cases and training gear. A guard with a long-handled net fishes dropped phones out of the water and refuses every tip. The walk is wide enough for heteromorph shoppers. Water slaps softly against the stone edge, and music from the stage carries along the curve. The walk leads back to the Fountain Stage and ends at the doors of the Canal Theater Hall.

Ramen Floor.description: The top floor of the mall belongs to ramen: eight counters from different corners of Japan around a shared waiting hall, each with its own cloth curtain, meal-ticket machine and line. Hakata's own cloudy pork-bone broth gets two counters, and the others rotate every few months: Sapporo miso with butter and corn, Tokyo soy, dipping noodles, a spicy Kumamoto garlic bowl. A bowl runs 900 to 1,300 yen, and at the Hakata counters customers order their noodles by firmness and call for a second serving of noodles, 150 yen, before the broth goes cold. Office workers rush the floor at noon, tourists queue all afternoon with phones out, students come up after classes in groups, and the late crowd from Nakasu climbs up before the eleven o'clock close. Locals argue loudly with visitors about which counter is best and expect to be asked. Some stools are wider and bolted down for heavy heteromorph diners, and a sign at each counter asks customers not to use Quirks to cool their broth. Steam fogs the windows, pork fat and garlic hang in the air, and the cooks call orders in rhythm. Escalators lead down to the Fountain Stage.

Canal Theater Hall.description: A theater of about 1,100 seats at the far end of the canal, with a curved glass lobby over the water, a red-carpeted auditorium on three levels and a box office by the doors. It hosts touring musicals, comedy nights and concerts, and this spring a hero musical on tour from Tokyo, with an actor in gold and blue striking All Might's pose under a spotlight; on Sunday mornings a cheaper hero show for small children has costumed performers rescue volunteers from the audience. Tickets run from 3,000 yen in the upper balcony to 12,000 for the best seats; matinees start at half past one and evening shows at six, and same-day returns go on sale at noon. Retirees fill the matinees, office workers the evenings, and on Sundays the lobby is crowded with strollers. Flying and fire effects come from wires and machines, since the hall has never paid for a permit for Quirk effects. The ushers carry small flashlights, and wide seats at the end of each row take heteromorph patrons. The lobby smells of coffee and the lilies in the cast's bouquets. The lobby opens onto the Canal Walk, and a covered bridge crosses back to the Fountain Stage.

Musutafu Highway Outlets.name: Musutafu Highway Outlets
Musutafu Highway Outlets.basicInfo: An open-air outlet mall on Musutafu's west side, about 3 km west-southwest of Musutafu Station, built beside the expressway interchange so drivers can pull straight in off the highway: about a hundred discount stores in low buildings along open-air lanes, with a big parking lot, a bus stop and a food terrace at the center. Dagobah Municipal Beach Park is about 3.5 km to the southwest, Musutafu General Hospital about 3.5 km to the west-northwest and Kiyashi Shopping Mall about 4.5 km to the south. Where Kiyashi is the city's everyday mall, the outlets are where people go for bargains: last season's clothes, sneakers, kitchenware, luggage and sporting goods at thirty to seventy percent off, and a block of sports and hero gear stores that sells training wear, shoes and licensed hero goods cheaper than anywhere else in town. It opens at ten and closes at eight, and the gates to the lanes are locked overnight. City buses run from the station's bus terminal every twenty minutes, and on Saturdays and Sundays a weekend shuttle starts at the stop outside U.A.'s Main Gate, calls at the station and runs straight here, so U.A. students signed out for the weekend can be shopping within half an hour. Weekday mornings belong to retirees and tour buses on their way to the Izu coast; weekday afternoons are quiet; weekends fill the lanes with families, couples, drivers off the highway and U.A. students hunting for cheap training shoes. The management company's guards carry radios and have no authority to use Quirks; a police box opens at the main gate on weekends, and one of the small agencies on Hero Agency Row sends a patrol across town on Saturday afternoons. Ramps run everywhere, the lanes are wide enough for heteromorphs of any size, and the restrooms include wide stalls. A player can shop, eat, take a weekend shift, ride the shuttle with classmates or watch the highway traffic from the terrace. Wind from the bay blows down the lanes, and the sale banners snap all day.
Musutafu Highway Outlets.hiddenInfo: Right now the outlets' far parking rows are being worked by a pair of car thieves who come every Saturday afternoon. They drive in off the highway in a small white van between one and three, park in a different row each week, and walk the rows along the expressway fence, where the cameras are oldest. One of them, a soft-spoken woman in a sun hat, has a Quirk that opens any lock she touches without leaving a mark, so the cars show no broken glass; her partner lifts shopping bags, sneaker boxes and laptops from back seats and carries them to the van in outlet bags of his own. They leave by the on-ramp before half past three. Because nothing is forced, the insurers and the police box both half suspect the owners, and nine reports in a month have been filed as possible losses. The attendant in the north lot, an older man in a reflective vest, has written down the van's plate twice and has nobody who will take him seriously. The goods are sold the following week through a pawn counter near the station's back alleys. The patrol from Hero Agency Row arrives around four, an hour after the van has gone, and nobody has thought to ask it to come earlier. Meanwhile, in the sports block, one store has begun selling blue tracksuits with the U.A. crest as factory seconds at 4,000 yen. U.A. never licensed them, the stitching on the crest is wrong, and the store's manager bought the stock from a man who would only take cash and did not leave a card. Students from up the hill have started to notice, and the academy would want to know where they come from.

Outlet Gate and Bus Stop.description: The front of the outlets faces the parking lot and the expressway interchange: a broad timber arch hung with sale banners, a turnaround with three bus shelters, a taxi stand and a bank of coin lockers where shoppers stash their first bags. City buses from the station's bus terminal arrive every twenty minutes and take about fifteen; on Saturdays and Sundays the weekend shuttle, which starts outside U.A.'s Main Gate and calls at the station, pulls in at the first shelter every half hour, and groups of U.A. students signed out for the weekend spill off it already arguing about routes. An information booth hands out maps and coupon books and lends wheelchairs, including a wide one for heteromorph builds. Tour buses unload retirees on weekday mornings. A police box opens at the gate on weekends, and the guards under the arch carry radios but cannot use Quirks. The hum of the highway never stops, and on clear mornings Mount Fuji shows above the parking lot to the northwest. Through the arch run the Outlet Lanes, the Sports and Hero Gear Outlets stand beside the gate, and a path leads straight to the Outlet Food Terrace.

Outlet Lanes.description: Open-air lanes of low two-story buildings with pale clapboard fronts and covered walkways, laid out in a loop with benches and planters down the middle. About a hundred stores line them: fashion and denim, sneakers, luggage, kitchenware, clothes for small children and a factory store for heteromorph cuts, with tail-slit trousers, wing-back jackets and four-sleeved shirts at a third of department-store prices. Racks of marked-down stock stand outside the doors, and clerks call out time sales through handheld speakers. Weekdays are slow; weekends fill every lane by eleven with couples, families pushing strollers and U.A. students carrying more bags than they meant to. The stores close at eight, and the gates lock soon after. A guard on a bicycle circles the loop, and on Saturday afternoons a patrol from one of the small agencies on Hero Agency Row walks through, stopping for photos with anyone who asks. Wind off the bay snaps the banners and tugs at the bags. The lanes lead back to the Outlet Gate and Bus Stop, open onto the Sports and Hero Gear Outlets, and meet the Outlet Food Terrace at the center of the loop.

Sports and Hero Gear Outlets.description: A block of larger stores at the gate end of the lanes, where Musutafu buys its training gear cheap: outlets for running shoes, team sports and outdoor gear, a training-wear store with whole walls of compression shirts, and a hero goods outlet selling last season's figures, replica capes and sealed trading-card boxes at half price, each with its license seal. The shoe store keeps a shelf of reinforced soles for Quirks that wear through footwear, and the training-wear store will hem, slit or reinforce for tails and wings while customers wait. A rubber test strip outside lets customers jog in new shoes, and a sign at its head says no Quirks on the strip. Weekday afternoons bring local students and club teams; weekends bring U.A. students, who come for cheap training shoes and stay to argue over the figures, and a rack of blue tracksuits with the U.A. crest, marked as factory seconds, draws long looks from them. Staff in team jerseys help with sizing, and the hero outlet's clerk can name every figure's release year. The block smells of new rubber. Doors open onto the Outlet Gate and Bus Stop and back into the Outlet Lanes.

Outlet Food Terrace.description: An open-air food terrace at the center of the loop, under white sail awnings, with long tables, a dozen food stalls around the edge and a small stage for weekend events. The menus lean local: Fujinomiya yakisoba from a flat griddle, black Shizuoka oden simmered in dark broth and dusted with fish powder, sakura shrimp fritters, curry, crepes and green-tea soft-serve that melts fast in the bay wind. A plate runs 500 to 1,000 yen and a soft-serve 400. Weekday lunch is drivers off the highway and store staff on their breaks; weekend lunch is chaos, with families circling for seats. Some tables are wide and low for heteromorph diners, and a sign on every pole asks guests not to use Quirks to cool their food or chase off the crows, which are bold and well organized. The terrace looks over the parking lot to the expressway and, on clear days, to Mount Fuji. On weekends the stage hosts a local band or a hero quiz with coupons for prizes, and the quizmaster's All Might impression gets worse every week. Oden broth and griddle smoke drift across the tables. Paths lead back to the Outlet Gate and Bus Stop and into the Outlet Lanes.

Okuto Island.name: Okuto Island
Okuto Island.basicInfo: Okuto Island is a small, thinly settled island far out in the Pacific south of the Izu chain: a fishing harbor with a breakwater and a few dozen low houses, a coast road around rocky shores, and a steep green interior of scrub and old cedar climbing to a weather station on the summit. Ferries call twice a week when the sea allows; most residents fish, keep small gardens and know every visitor by sight. In bad weather the island is cut off for days.
Okuto Island.hiddenInfo: Its isolation makes it a place heroes could use to separate dangerous people from crowds: a warp route dropped onto its open ground would put a fight far from any city, with nobody to save but whoever is already there.

Harbor and Breakwater.description: A small concrete harbor with a long breakwater, fishing boats tied two deep, net sheds, a fuel pump and a ferry ramp. Gulls, diesel, salt; the harbor office's radio is the island's only link when the cell tower fails.

Coast Road.description: A narrow road around the island between black volcanic rocks and the sea, with a few houses, a shrine at a bend and long stretches of nothing but wind and surf.

Island Interior.description: Steep ground of scrub, bamboo and old cedar rising from the coast to an open grassy summit with a weather station, cut by gullies and a single switchback track.

Mount Fuji Battlefield.name: Mount Fuji Battlefield
Mount Fuji Battlefield.basicInfo: The open lower slopes and plains at the foot of Mount Fuji, northeast of Fujinomiya: wide grassland and lava fields scattered with pine woods, farm roads and a few closed tourist rest stops, with the mountain's great cone filling the sky above. On a clear day the summit snow is bright from every direction; in bad weather cloud swallows everything above the tree line.
Mount Fuji Battlefield.hiddenInfo: The plains are empty enough, and far enough from any city, that heroes planning a last battle would choose them to keep a catastrophe away from people.

Lava Plain.description: A broad plain of old black lava and coarse grass under the mountain, open in every direction, with nowhere to hide and nothing to break apart but stone.

Pine Woods.description: Windbreak pine woods along the edge of the plain, dark and quiet, cut by a farm track and a dry streambed.

Rest Stop Road.description: A two-lane road past a shuttered rest stop with a parking lot, vending machines and souvenir stands, the last built place before the open ground.
